News.title: Police make 169 arrests at Notting Hill Carnival as cops probe sex offences, drugs & knife attacks at world-famous party
News.content:
POLICE made 169 arrests on the first day of Notting Hill Carnival as thousands arrived for the world-famous street party.

As of 7.45pm on Sunday, the arrests had been made for offences including possession of drugs, possession of weapons, assaults and sexual offences.



The annual west London carnival is Europe’s biggest street party and billed by organisers as “the greatest community-led event on the planet”.

In a statement on Sunday evening, the Met Police said the majority of arrests had taken place within the event perimeter.



Officers had responded to two knife assaults, a slashing to the leg and one to the hand, neither of which resulted in life-changing or threatening injuries.

Commander Claire Smart, who is in charge of the policing operation, said: “We have been working closely with Notting Hill Carnival Ltd and other partners for many months ahead of this weekend’s event.

“The organisers have stepped forward significantly across the event, including crowd management, and we have seen the positive progress today.

“While we have seen a significant number of arrests and interventions by officers, the result of that proactive approach is a welcome reduction in the levels of serious violence seen at the event in previous years.



“Nobody involved in the delivery of the event is complacent, however.

“There are still many officers deployed across the footprint to ensure crowds disperse safely.

“We will have officers on duty through the night and tomorrow we will go again to ensure we can continue to tackle the minority who want to come to Carnival to spoil the celebration for the majority.”

Earlier this week, the force said more than 7,000 officers would be deployed to west London over the bank holiday weekend.

The carnival includes parades, live music, street food and sound stages and is celebrating its 60th anniversary this year.



But while officers today responded to a number of incidents, they said “the mood has been overwhelmingly positive and celebratory”.

In 2025, the Met said it made 528 arrests across the two main days of the carnival, including 167 for drug offences, 50 for possession of an offensive weapon, 21 for sexual offences, four for violence with injury and 49 for other violence.

In 2024, there were eight stabbings, including the murder of 32-year-old mother Cher Maximen, with the same number the previous year, and seven including a murder in 2022.

Day two of this year’s event is set to take place on Bank Holiday Monday.

The festival, which first took place in 1966, got off to a colourful start today as partygoers filled the streets.

Today’s Family Day saw thousands of people flock to the event which is celebrating its 60th anniversary.

News.title: Murdered gang kingpin Ross Monagahan’s cousin nailed over £20M global drug trafficking ring
News.content:
A COUSIN of murdered Lyons gang kingpin Ross Monaghan has been nailed for his role in a multi-million pound global drugs cash operation.

Michael Monaghan, 37, was busted by cops probing a major narcotics trafficking mob with “international links” and is now locked up with four associates.





A judge heard he was in cahoots with fellow Scot Anthony Carroll, 57, who was in charge of the cartel’s vast illicit income — which hit almost £20million in a little more than five months.

Details of the case emerged 15 months after Ross Monaghan, 43, was gunned down at his bar in Fuengirola, Spain, with fellow hood Eddie Lyons Jnr, 46.

Michael Monaghan, of Drumchapel, Glasgow, ran one of the gang’s “cash counting houses” and reported to Carroll, the High Court in the city was told.

Others involved were Carroll’s son Anthony Jnr, 37, Ryan Carberry, 46, and Marc Cooper, 34.

Monaghan’s arrest, and those of the others, came while his cousin was in Spain with mob boss Steven Lyons, 45 — who is locked up in the Costa del Sol where he faces trial over an alleged dirty cash and organised crime plot.

Prosecutor Leanne Cross told the court Carroll Snr was in charge of counting, storing and distributing payments the mob received for cocaine, heroin and hash.

She said: “He also directed the other four to carry out this work on his behalf.

“He, in turn, answered to those at the top of the organised crime group who were, by and large, based overseas.”





Police raided Carroll Jnr’s home in Glasgow’s Maryhill and found £780,000 hidden under floorboards in May 2020.

They uncovered phones, £5,000 and €1,000 from under a cooker hood at Carroll Snr’s house in the city’s Milton.

Carberry, of Kirkintilloch, near Glasgow, was described as a “cash collector” involved 75 pick-ups totalling £6million.

A raid on his partner’s home led to £195,000 being found in two rucksacks.

The hoods were snared as part of Operation Venetic, the long-running probe into the encrypted phone network EncroChat smashed by Dutch crimefighters in 2020.

One EncroChat message from Cooper, of Maryhill, stated he had counted £1.8million between May and June 2020.

Ms Cross stated Carroll Snr documented £4million as income for January 2020, £3million the following month, £2.6million in March, around £4million in April and £4.8million in May.

She told the court: “This operation was well organised with everyone having clear roles and responsibilities.

“Cash collectors passed to the counters before everything was funnelled to Carroll Snr. He passed on to safehouse holders for onward transportation.”

The five were paid £500-£1200 per week “wages”. They all admitted being involved in organised crime.



Judge Lord Scott deferred sentence and remanded them in custody.

Two others linked to the gang were jailed in April. Alistair MacKenzie, 60, of Glasgow’s Knightswood, and Daniel Kerrigan, 56, of Maryhill, were handed just over nine years between them.

News.title: Inside ‘totally lawless’ estate home of ‘joyriders’ killed in crash with cops where gangs are rife and all hope is lost
News.content:
DUSK falls on the Grangetown estate near Middlesbrough, and a boy aged around eight whizzes past on a push bike, flicking the middle finger at anyone he does not like the look of.

He has already learned to act tough in a town where the brutality of gang warfare last week burst out into the open like a festering wound.



It began with tit-for-tat house rammings and ended in the tragic deaths of two Cleveland Police officers and five young men, whose car was speeding the wrong way down a dual carriageway, and a woman and seven-year-old girl in a house fire.

At the putrid heart of it all lies a drugs war in an area where jobs are scarce and all hope is lost — with locals now looking to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the so-called “King of the North”, for a lifeline.



For many in the affected areas, community is all that is left to cling to, so they have turned a blind eye to the tasteless vigils for the five men, which included setting vehicles alight and sparking fireworks and flares.

They were in stark contrast to the quiet church service for PC Matthew Blades, 37, a former teacher, and PC Tom Clough, 38, a former soldier who had served in Iraq and Afghanistan.



The officers were killed when their armed response car was hit by the men’s Volkswagen Passat as it fled a high-speed police chase on the A66 on August 22.

The five occupants were Michael Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-old Cole Worthy.

The estates at the centre of the crisis — Grangetown, South Bank and Eaton — serve as symbols of Broken Britain, and it is clear to see why.

There has been no proper investment in the Redcar and Cleveland communities for years.



Green spaces where kids should be able to play are scorched earth where arsonists have set fires, while old sofas, furniture and piles of clothes form rubbish heaps behind shops and along verges.

Bins are overflowing, graffiti is daubed across walls, and houses are boarded up with steel plates.

Hooded teenagers ride around on e-scooters and residents are acutely aware, and suspicious, of strangers who set foot in their neighbourhood.



Those who spoke to me begged not to be named for fear of reprisals.

Within hours of our arrival, cops were scrambled to a house amid reports of a man’s fingers having been chopped off in a savage attack.

When we asked one local if he thought it was related to the crash, he laughed and told us: “That happens just about every day here.

“There are loads of people walking about without fingers, or fingers with nerve damage, ’cos they’ve been smashed in. It’s just a form of punishment for something or other.”

There is a shocking level of deprivation, but there are decent people here too — families who make ends meet without turning to crime.



The area’s increased notoriety sits uncomfortably with them.

As one woman pointed out: “Being poor doesn’t mean you have to be a scrote. There are plenty struggling who don’t rob or deal drugs to put food on the table.”

You cannot help but admire her sense of pride in an area that has seen better days.

Having grown up on a council estate, it is a notion I understand.



I wear my estate “badge” with honour, proud of the fact it taught me the values of looking out for others in need, never looking down on anyone and knowing that not everyone is as tough as they look.

But something has gone terribly wrong in Grangetown and its surrounding estates beyond the lack of work prospects and money. The small minority who have been making life a misery for everyone else have taken control of the streets.

One woman told me: “I’ve lived here for 32 years and it’s been getting worse and worse.

“It was once a nice place, where people kept their gardens nice, their houses tidy and their kids in school.



“Now it feels alien with rubbish dumped everywhere, people wandering about in dressing gowns in the middle of the day and loads of kids who stopped going to school through Covid and never managed to return full-time.

“There’s addicts everywhere and, if it’s not drugs, it’s drink. It’s an embarrassment.” Drugs are the main issue, with turf wars raging. There is talk of postcode gang divisions, but it is not quite that clear cut.

In January, Cleveland Police officers found a “significant firearms haul” after an eight-day targeted search in Grangetown.

The guns and ammunition were seized as part of Operation Galvanise, a multi-agency initiative tackling organised crime.

A source told us that what followed were months of cars ramming into various homes.



Four of the five dead men in the Passat had criminal records, and it is alleged they were being “groomed” by criminals with links to the travelling community. Our source said: “This is about drugs, family warfare and long-time grudges, not stolen cars and joyriding.

“The lads who were killed were being influenced by people who are known to them, older and more experienced in crime.

“They didn’t go off on some solo venture to get cops to chase them. They were sharks for bigger players.”



Police have encouraged people in the area to keep reporting crime, but there is a deep sense of mistrust — and the feeling that locals just are not listened to.

One man told us: “People just don’t trust the police, and why would they? Had they got on top of the problems at the start we wouldn’t be here.

“They don’t listen either. Everyone knows that there’s no point reporting the small stuff because they just open an incident report, close it and you never hear from them. It’s a waste of time.”

Hundreds of extra police from neighbouring regions have been sent to Middlesbrough to deal with the gang warfare, but some residents fear it will make things worse.

One said: “It’s totally lawless. The police have ignored the problems in the area for years and now they want to come in heavy-handed. It won’t go down well.”



Residents in Middlesbrough say it is more like Beirut than the ’Boro, the once-proud port town at the heart of industrialised Britain.

It has been ranked the most dangerous town in England and Wales, with 150 crimes per 1,000 residents, compared with the national average of 72.

People living in Teesside are more likely to be murdered than anywhere else, with a homicide rate of 21.7 per million people. The average is 8.1.

Stockton-on-Tees, ten miles from Grangetown, was the location for Channel 4’s controversial documentary Benefits Street, which focused on economically deprived areas.

But Middlesbrough is just one of countless towns across the North that have been left behind. Grimsby, in Lincolnshire, was rated one of the worst for benefit scroungers, while Blackpool has been left scarred by the demise of seaside towns, and Oldham is now infamous for its grooming scandal.



But they are just the tip of the iceberg.

People in Grangetown feel abandoned by successive governments, and one local businessman told me how most do not even bother voting.

“Westminster means nothing to people here. Most are just trying to get by, day-to-day. Covid made things much worse.



“Kids used to at least have school, but most don’t bother going now. So they barely get a good education, never mind know about what’s going on in politics.”

It is a tragedy that Middlesbrough was once a booming town known as Ironopolis thanks to its iron and steel production.

The area suffered its last wave of devastating economic decline in the 1970s and 80s when automation and global competition led to mass closures in heavy manufacturing, shipbuilding and steel.

The final nail in the coffin came with the closure of the mighty Redcar steel works in October 2015, with the loss of around 2,200 jobs at the plant and nearly 1,000 additional jobs across the local supply chain.

Today, the main road to the docks is mostly used by kids to race cars and e-bikes.



One Grangetown takeaway worker summed it up when he said: “There’s no money and there’s no hope.

“The estates are full of kids having kids and they’ve no idea how to bring them up.

“There’s no work to be had, no money and nothing to do but try and make it in other ways.

“There are decent people around and we’ve got used to the area’s bad reputation, but it’s not great, is it?

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Where’s the so-called King of the North, Andy Burnham?



“The whole area has been failed and forgotten by politicians and it just feels like there’s no going back.”

News.title: Fury as Burnham ‘caves to trade union power’ by handing £70k train drivers that take him to Manchester a bumper pay rise
News.content:
ANDY Burnham has been accused of capitulating to militant unions by handing train drivers a bumper pay rise.

The PM has signed off an inflation-busting 3.6 per cent increase to avert strikes on the Avanti service that takes him back to Manchester.



The Aslef union had rejected a previous offer and threatened industrial action.

Avanti drivers, who start on £70,000 salaries, will be able to earn more for working weekends under the deal, according to the Sunday Times.



In return, the union has agreed to accept rotas digitally rather than printing them out.

Shadow Transport Secretary Richard Holden said: “Andy Burnham has caved to union power.



“Labour have already handed over billions with no strings attached, and passengers have seen services decline and taxpayers a bigger bill. This settlement just makes it worse.”

The Avanti West Coast is the line Mr Burnham would take to his new No10 North if he chose to go by train.

It is the worst-performing train company in the country.

The Department for Transport said: “This deal will avoid highly disruptive bank holiday strike action, reduce short-term cancellations, and modernise work practices.”



Accounts show Aslef donated more than £300,000 to the Labour Party in 2024.

News.title: Fury as prisoners being let out under Early Release Scheme are returning to jail at rapid rate after PC Harper outrage
News.content:
PRISONERS who have been released under the early release scheme are returning to jail at a rapid rate, prison governors have claimed.

They say that many released under the scheme in 2024 have returned after re-offending, with one describing it as a “revolving door”.



The next early release scheme is due to begin in October, with the first offenders freed in tranches over the next 10 months in a bid to ease prison overcrowding.

But more than 51,000 lags were recalled in the year to March 2026 after breaching their release conditions – a staggering 28 per cent increase on the previous year.



One governor from a prison in the north of England told the BBC the government’s plans to ease overcrowding were “short term solutions” and more needed to be done.

“We see the same people coming back after being released early and reoffending again, or breaking their [release] rules,” they said.



A second prison governor from the region also urged action on the overcrowding crisis or the “criminal justice system will grind to a halt”.

They said: “You release someone to serve the rest of their sentence in the community and you think ‘now I have some extra room’, but then they’re back again and you just go round in circles.”



He added it was a “big problem” and had concerns around what would happen when prisoners are freed from October onwards.

One of the governors also cited concerns around gang rivalries due to the lack of space as prisoners from different areas of the country are held in the same prisons.

Meanwhile, they also had “serious health and safety concerns” with some facilities facing staff shortages and some forced to hold two prisoners in a one-man cell.

To make matters worse, they were also worried about the “fragile infrastructure” of England’s prisons, meaning many cells are left out of use.

“We have too many cells we can’t use because there’s something wrong with them which seems ridiculous when you have an overcrowding crisis,” they said.



It comes after PM Andy Burnham announced that PC Andrew Harper’s killers would remain behind bars after it was revealed they were eligible for early release.

Bowers and Cole were jailed for 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper, 28, who was dragged for more than a mile behind their car when he responded to reports of theft in 2019.

Plans to let out the killers in January – under Labour plans to release up to 5,000 prisoners over ten months from October – had sparked fury with a petition to stop their release reaching more than 1million signatures.

Now, Mr Burnham has said “hundreds” of people will remain in prison as part of changes to the scheme designed to ease prison overcrowding.

Prisoners convicted of historic child sex offences will also be blocked from changes.



The Prime Minister ordered a review of the changes to the Sentencing Act, which is being undertaken by Justice Secretary Alex Norris and is set to be published when Parliament returns from summer recess this week.

The changes increase the risk of the Government running out of space in jails, with only around 1,600 spare places available in men’s prisons.

Mr Burnham said extra space in prisons would be created by deporting foreign prisoners.

Full details of the latest changes are expected to be revealed by the Justice Secretary when Parliament returns.

It was also reported on Friday how prisoners could be freed just a sixth of the way through their sentencing under new proposals.



Proposals being examined by the Ministry of Justice could see home detention curfews (HDC) revived, forcing offenders to remain indoors from 7pm to 7am while monitored by electronic ankle tags.

News.title: Murder investigation launched after death of newborn baby as seven arrested as cops promise to ensure ‘justice’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TOT TRAGEDY Murder investigation launched after death of newborn baby as seven arrested as cops promise to ensure ‘justice’

A NEWBORN baby has died with police launching a murder investigation as seven people are arrested.

Police were called to a Sheffield property at around 5:58am on Sunday following concerns for the baby girl’s safety.



Tragically, despite the best efforts of emergency services, the tot died at the scene.

It is not currently known how the baby passed away, but officials have asked the public to avoid speculation.



Seven people have now been arrested on suspicion of murder and remain in custody.

Senior Investigating Officer Detective Chief Inspector Emma Knight said: “We have a dedicated team of detectives and officers hard at work to ensure justice is secured for the baby girl at the heart of this investigation.



“As part of our investigation seven people have been arrested on suspicion of murder.

“All of them remain in police custody at this time. We are working to determine the ages of some of those arrested.

“Our investigation is in its early stages and we would like to remind people to avoid speculating about this incident.”

Anyone with any information has been asked to call 101 quoting incident number 194 of 30 August 2026, or contact Crimestoppers anonymously.

News.title: Beloved ex-mayor and 3 family members ID’d as victims of horror small plane crash into lagoon near remote Alaska town
News.content:
AIR DISASTER Beloved ex-mayor and 3 family members ID’d as victims of horror small plane crash into lagoon near remote Alaska town

A BELOVED former mayor and three of his family members have been named as those killed in a horror plane crash earlier this week.

Everyone on board the small aircraft lost their life after the plane plunged into icy waters near a remote town in Alaska.



Eric Middlebrook, 68, had served as mayor of Bethel – a tiny Alaskan town of 6,000 people – from 2006 to 2011.

He had been piloting the plane with three Californian residents – Daniel Simons, 82, of Los Gatos, Ronald Schmidt, 65, and 20-year-old Lance Schmidt, both of San Jose.



All four victims were related, according to public records.

The tragedy unfolded on a trip from Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, to the tiny town of Seldovia.

The Piper PA-24-260 went down at around 1.15pm on Wednesday.

Alaskan troopers and an emergency helicopter scrambled to the scene – but they were unable to reach the submerged craft for several hours.

The small plane had sunk to a depth of around 15ft in frigid 38F (3°C) waters.

Rescue teams only reached the wrecked plane at around 6:30pm – more than five hours after the crash.



Tragic footage shows several boats and first responders recovering the bodies of the dead from the submerged wreckage.

Tributes to the victims have poured in from across social media.

Bethel city council member Mark Springer recounted that his former mayor was “a real hardworking guy”.



Eric had been a refrigerator technician with his own business, and Mark recounted how he frequently flew to villages to help them fix their refridgerators as part of his business.

“He was a fixture in the community and he was a respected guy”, he said, adding: “He was known all over the [Yukon–Kuskokwim] Delta. It’s a tragic loss.

“He was a pretty cool guy. He was well-known here in Bethel and well-liked.”

Eric was killed alongside his brother Ronald Schmidt, a marketing representative at Cisco Systems in San Jose, California.

Ronald had previously told local paper The Appeal Democrat that his brother Eric was “very talented and very smart, but no one ever guessed politics as his forte”.



US Senator Dan Sullivan, from Alska, said he was “praying for the families and loved ones of those who were killed”.

“These tragedies are heartbreaking and unacceptable, which is why aviation safety and infrastructure in Alaska continue to be a top focus of mine.”

He has vowed to “get to the bottom of this tragedy”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It comes just days after another plane plummetted and crashed in western Alaska, killing all eight people on board.

Rescue teams raced to the scene of the tragedy near an Air Force site in Cape Newenham – but later confirmed there were no survivors.

News.title: What Bank Holidays do we have left in 2026? All the dates plus what we have next year
News.content:
BRITS making the most of the August long weekend may already be starting to look ahead to their next stretch of time off.

Following the Summer Bank Holiday on Monday, August 31 in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the countdown is on for the final public holidays of 2026 and a brand-new calendar of breaks in 2027.



Whether you are plotting a getaway, or simply curious about when shops and banks will be closing, here’s everything you need to know about the remaining UK bank holiday dates for 2026 and what to expect next year.

Remaining UK Bank Holidays in 2026

After the late August holiday, the bank holiday calendar slows down until the festive season.



Scotland gets an extra regional day off in late November for St Andrew’s Day.

But the rest of the UK will have to wait until late December for a festive four-day weekend, thanks to Boxing Day falling on a Saturday and moving to a substitute weekday.



Date Holiday Regions Monday, August 31 Summer Bank Holiday England, Wales, NI Monday, November 30 St Andrew’s Day Scotland only Friday, December 25 Christmas Day All UK Monday, December 28 Boxing Day (Substitute) All UK

(Note: Scotland observed its Summer Bank Holiday earlier in the month, on Monday, August 3).

UK Bank Holidays for 2027

Looking ahead to 2027, the year kicks off with a long weekend right out of the gate as New Year’s Day falls on a Friday.

Easter comes earlier than usual in 2027, landing in late March.

Meanwhile, Christmas 2027 promises another four-day holiday block.



Because Christmas Day and Boxing Day fall on a Saturday and Sunday, substitute bank holidays move to Monday, December 27 and Tuesday, December 28.

News.title: Kyrenia ferry LIVE: Eight dead as boat capsizes off Cyprus with 267 on board - Crew arrested
News.content:
An ambulance arrives at the port of Kyrenia in the Turkish occupied northern part of Cyprus after a ferry overturned off the coast

Eight people have died after a passenger ferry carrying 267 people capsized off northern Cyprus, with a search underway for 17 missing people

Kyrenia ferry LIVE: Eight dead as boat capsizes off Cyprus with 267 on board - Crew arrested

Eight people have died and 17 are missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus - with the boat's captain and seven crew members arrested.

Prime Minister Unal Ustel confirmed the fatalities following the disaster off the port of Kyrenia, which saw over 230 people rescued and sparked an urgent search effort.

The vessel capsized early on Sunday afternoon after "taking in water" just 15 minutes into its journey to the Turkish port of Tasucu.

Mr Ustel said the ferry faced adverse weather conditions and began sinking off the coast of Diana beach before a call for help was made.

Turkish Cypriot and Turkish coastguard crews have been deployed, along with rescue helicopters and other vessels, as efforts continue.

News.title: Emmerdale's Dawn star Olivia Bromley sobs at shock exit and reveals hidden secret of final scenes
News.content:
Emmerdale star Olivia Bromley shed real tears when she filmed the tragic death of her character, Dawn Fletcher, tonight. Due to marry bad boy Joe Tate, their plans were scuppered when Jimmy King crashed into the wedding marquee, causing a big explosion, and pregnant Dawn was rushed to hospital.

Sent into premature labour, while Dawn gave birth safely to a baby boy with Joe at her side, she had a serious internal bleed. Suddenly, without warning, she crashed and, despite medics’ best efforts to resuscitate her, she died.

In her first interview since the explosive scenes, Olivia, 30, who was originally signed by Emmerdale for just 12 episodes in 2018, tells The Mirror: “It was the toughest storyline I've done during my time in the soap.

"I was surprised by how emotional I found it and it was way more emotional than I was expecting. I did cry. It is very strange to kill off your character as an actor and in front of your colleagues. But that said, what a gift to be given. Often people leave and just slip off.”

‌



View 5 Images Emmerdale lovebirds Dawn and Joe

The actress was told earlier this year her character would be at the heart of a huge exit storyline during the soap’s biggest week of the year. Having reached a crossroads playing Dawn, she says it was almost a relief to have the decision over what to do with the role made for her.

She says: “This is a good time for me to go on a personal level. I had felt ready for the character to go. This character felt like she had done so much and I didn't know what direction she could go in next. I had played her for a long time, and it felt like I needed to do other things. I am proud this was such a big finale to my time in the soap.”

But news that Dawn was being killed off came as a bolt from the blue and she confesses she would have liked to have left the door open to one day return.

‌



Despite the initial shock, she says: “Psychologically, now I have had time to reflect, I know it's good for me, because I can say bye to my Emmerdale chapter. It’s been brilliant. I was originally only signed up for 12 episodes and I’ve stayed eight years!”

View 5 Images Happier times, Emmerdale's Dawn delivers a healthy baby boy

And if viewers found her final scenes surprisingly realistic, she can now share the secret - that real life paramedics, rather than actors, were used to make the medical scenes convincing. She says: "They had real life paramedics and intensive care workers who came in to play those parts. Emmerdale is a fast-paced soap and we often don't have time to train actors up, so they bring supporting people in with a lot of experience."

Likening it to an "out of body" experience, she adds of her character’s death scenes: "They had rehearsed the crash response with Ned [who plays Joe Tate] and the supporting artists first and, right at the last minute, they put me in the scene. I had no idea what was going on.

‌



“They went into the crash response, and it felt like an out of body experience lying there. They were all so professional and brilliant at what they did."

But Olivia is sad that Dawn’s life ended so tragically. She says: "Even though she was able to cradle the baby with her children and Joe by her side, nobody had picked up on her bleeding internally. Finally, she had got what she wanted and so it was a sad end for her."

View 5 Images Billy, played by Jay Kontzle, and Dawn, played by Olivia, share a tense moment on the soap

Dawn originally arrived in the village as a drug addicted sex worker. Her big storylines included finding her long lost son and her on-off romance with her big love, ex-husband Billy. But she fell for Joe Tate in January 2025, after embarking on an affair behind Billy’s back.

‌



They got engaged in December 2025 and by February 2026 discovered they were expecting a baby. But in recent months, Dawn, who had two other children and an adopted daughter, had been troubled by her lingering feelings for Billy.

And when he was attacked last month, she believed Joe was responsible and had planned to escape with Billy, rather than marrying the bad boy. However, in a massive plot twist, it became apparent Billy had actually been attacked by Kev - making Dawn want to marry Joe after all.

Olivia says: “Only a few weeks ago, she was talking about escaping with Billy, but in the end chose Joe. If Dawn hadn't returned to Joe at the end, she would still be alive now. Billy is her true love but ultimately, she is an addict and she was drawn to Joe.”

View 5 Images Olivia on This Morning. She says she's sad to leave the soap, but the time is right to go (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

‌



She continues: “I've loved playing Dawn and I've enjoyed watching her develop and change. I've made many friends too and I am going to miss them a lot - especially everyone at Home Farm and Jay, who plays Billy. We are like brother and sister; we get on so well.”

Away from Emmerdale, Olivia lives happily in Leeds with her partner, who she keeps out of the public eye. She says: "My life has changed since joining the show. It has given me stability and, alongside the character, I've grown and changed. It's made me ambitious in different ways and taken my life in a different way."

After graduating from Oxford School of Drama, Olivia moved to London to work in theatre, before the call from Emmerdale came. She says: "This did change things for me and to be a working actor for eight years has been very special.”

And she would love to continue working in TV drama. She says: "I want to try some new things. It's an exciting time and I would love to do a period drama or a gritty 9pm drama like Line of Duty."

‌



Now awaiting auditions, she has her leaving party to look forward to next weekend. She says: "It's themed and I think we all deserve a drink after such a chaotic, complex end for Dawn. I'm also looking forward to just being me and not Dawn!"

As for Emmerdale without her? Olivia says: "The audience will go on a rollercoaster I am sure! I will always be so grateful to Emmerdale for giving me this role and to have been able to play Dawn fully until the end has been so much fun."

*Emmerdale airs every weekday on ITV1 and STV1 at 8pm. Episodes can also be downloaded on ITVX.

News.title: Teen, 16, one of two arrested after man, 46, 'shot in the stomach' at house in quiet village
News.content:
Teen, 16, one of two arrested after man, 46, 'shot in the stomach' at house in quiet village

A 46-year-old man suffered injuries to his abdomen in Gainford with police arresting two males, aged 16 and 20, on suspicion of attempted murder

View Image Police and forensic officers at the scene on Balmer Hill (Image: North News & Pictures Ltd)

A 16-year-old boy and 20-year-old man have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after an alleged shooting in County Durham which left a man critically injured.

The 46-year-old suffered "birdshot injuries" consistent with being shot with a shotgun to his abdomen at an address on Balmer Hill in Gainford just after 8.10pm on Saturday, August 29, police said.

Emergency services were called following reports that the suspects had allegedly driven to a property and fired at it from a car before fleeing the scene.

The man was taken to hospital, where his condition has been described as "critical but stable". No one else at the address was injured and officers remain at the scene today, reports Chronicle Live.

A statement from Durham Constabulary said: "A 20-year-old man and a 16-year-old boy have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. The boy has also been arrested on suspicion of theft, failing to stop and driving without a licence.

Article continues below

"They both remain in custody. An investigation is ongoing and anyone with information is asked to call 101 quoting incident reference 479 of August 29."

Crimestoppers can also be contacted anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Secret to avoiding high blood pressure discovered - and it's great news for anyone that loves a weekend lie-in
News.content:
Secret to avoiding high blood pressure discovered - and it's great news for anyone that loves a weekend lie-in

A seven-year study presented at the world’s biggest heart conference found people who slept in late at the weekend were less likely to have high blood pressure

View 3 Images Scientists say no need to feel guilty for staying in bed (Image: Getty Images)

Weekend lie-ins could protect against high blood pressure, new research suggests.

‌



Scientists say people should not feel guilty about sleeping in at the weekend as it could be the body’s way of recovering. A seven-year study of 41,000 adults found people who slept in late at the weekend were less likely to have high blood pressure.

‌



Analysis identified the perfect amount of catch-up sleep - with a one hour and 27 minute lie-in resulting in the most benefit. Someone getting this amount of extra sleep would be 9% less likely to have high blood pressure.

‌



Study author Dr Nawon Lee, of Korea University in Seoul, said: “Not getting enough sleep puts extra stress on the body. It keeps the heart and blood vessels working harder and can increase blood pressure.

View 3 Images Between an hour and two of catch up sleep is good for us, study suggests (Image: Getty Images/Westend61)

How to get perfect night's sleep as one third of Brits experience problems at least once a week READ MORE :

Study suggests sleeping well keeps middle-aged people fit to stay in work longer READ MORE :

“Getting some extra sleep on the weekend may give the body a chance to recover and reduce some of that stress.

‌



“People should not feel lazy or guilty for sleeping a little longer on the weekend. If they have not been able to get enough sleep during the week, some extra sleep on the weekend may simply be the body’s way of recovering from that sleep loss.”

The average British adult gets between 6 and 6.4 hours of sleep per night - below the recommended 7 to 9 hours. Not getting enough sleep is known to prevent blood pressure from dropping at night, which increases the risk of developing high blood pressure.

Officially known as hypertension, it is referred to in medical circles as the “silent killer” because it is often symptomless despite increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

‌



Around one in three UK adults - or 13 million people - have hypertension but many are unaware.

View 3 Images Dr Lee presenting her findings at the ESC Congress in Munich

Previous research had stressed the importance of having a regular bedtime and wake-up time and many experts dismissed the idea that you should catch up on missed sleep at the weekend.

‌



However the new research presented at the European Society of Cardiology showed that getting some catch-up sleep could boost heart health - whereas getting too much could be harmful. People getting over four hours extra sleep at the weekend were at greater risk of hypertension.

Dr Lee added: “I think moderate weekend catch-up sleep may have a protective effect because, in people who are sleep-deprived during the week, the benefit of compensating for insufficient sleep may outweigh the potential harm from having an irregular sleep schedule.

“However when weekend catch-up sleep becomes excessive, the degree of sleep irregularity and circadian disruption may increase, which could offset that benefit.”

‌



She added: “Keeping a regular sleep schedule is still important, but getting a moderate amount of catch-up sleep may be beneficial rather than something to feel bad about.”

Study participants who had any duration of catch-up sleep at the weekend were 6% less likely to have high blood pressure on average.

A greater benefit of weekend catch up sleep was seen in people who didn’t get enough exercise and were considered to be physically inactive. They were 6.9% less likely to have hypertension if they had weekend lie-ins.

‌



Participants were deemed inactive if they did not get the World Health Organization’s weekly recommended 150 minutes of moderate exercise, or 75 minutes vigorous exercise, or a combination of both.

It comes after previous research had shown regular bedtimes and wake-ups reduced the risk of a stroke. The study by the University of Ottawa in Canada tracked more than 72,000 volunteers' sleeping habits using activity trackers. Irregular sleepers were 26% more likely to suffer a stroke, heart failure or heart attack than regular ones.

This latest study shows that catching up on sleep at the weekend can help even if it means disrupting the body clock, known as the circadian rhythm.

Article continues below

Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, clinical director at the British Heart Foundation and consultant cardiologist, said: “Many of us struggle to get enough sleep during the week due to work, family and social commitments, so it’s natural if we find ourselves enjoying a lie-in at the weekend in an effort to catch up on missed sleep.

“This study is not a green light for physical activity to take a back seat but for now perhaps we don’t need to feel guilty about getting up late at the weekend.”

News.title: Big Church Festival recap: Pastor killed by falling sign named and pictured as tributes pour in
News.content:
Pastor Robert Guanco was killed after a sign fell on him at Big Church Festival.

A 41-year-old pastor killed after a sign fell at Big Church Festival has been named and pictured for the first time, as tributes pour in.

Big Church Festival recap: Pastor killed by falling sign named and pictured as tributes pour in

A 41-year-old man killed after a huge wooden sign came “crashing down” onto people at Big Church Festival has been named and pictured for the first time.

Robert Guanco, from Eastbourne, was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church, which described him as a “faithful servant of God”, loving husband and devoted father.

The sign, which reportedly carried the words “Everything’s Unmissable”, fell near a tented area at the Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday afternoon.

Six other people were injured in the incident, with four taken to hospital for treatment.

One eyewitness said he and his wife were walking just a few paces behind when the sign came down. He said they rushed to help lift it off those underneath and gave first aid alongside others until paramedics arrived.

The festival, which had been due to continue until Sunday, was cancelled by organisers following the incident.

The Archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, said she was “sad and shocked” and offered prayers for Mr Guanco’s family, those injured and others affected.

This live blog has now ended.

News.title: Energy Secretary says 'no one should doubt our resolve' on tackling climate change as she hits back at criticism
News.content:
Energy Secretary says 'no one should doubt our resolve' on tackling climate change as she hits back at criticism

EXCLUSIVE: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said Britain’s communities 'will not forgive us if we do not act to protect them' after the UK was ravaged by heatwaves and wildfires this summer

View 4 Images Climate activists at a demonstration in August calling on the Government to block more drilling in the north sea (Image: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

The Energy Secretary has said “no one should doubt our resolve” on tackling climate change as she hit back at criticism.

‌



Miatta Fahnbulleh said Britain’s communities “will not forgive us if we do not act to protect them” after the UK was ravaged by heatwaves and wildfires this summer.

‌



New PM Andy Burnham faced criticism over the summer for not being explicit enough on the climate emergency facing the country - and the long-term action needed.

‌



Firefighters tackled nearly 200 wildfires in the first 10 days of August alone, while droughts ruined farmers' crops. Nurses warned the extreme heat was making the NHS an "impossible environment" to care for people and schools were forced to close or send students home early.

4 View 4 Images Miatta Fahnbulleh said Britain’s communities 'will not forgive us if we do not act to protect them' (Image: TIM ANDERSON) 4 View 4 Images Miatta Fahnbulleh was appointed as Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero by Andy Burnham (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Mr Burnham called an emergency Cobra meeting and announced a temporary ban on disposable barbecues. He also announced a package of support to help farmers manage the impacts of the dry weather.

But leading climate organisations - including Greenpeace, WWF and Green New Deal Rising - wrote to the PM and accused him of “remaining silent” on the climate crisis, noting how a statement released after his Cobra meeting failed to mention climate change.

Asked about the criticism, Ms Fahnbulleh told The Mirror: “Well, I think it was a bit unfair because, to be fair, he'd only been in the job for a couple of weeks, and there's only so much that you can cover.

‌



“Look, I know Andy. He is as committed to climate change as I am. I think people should judge us by our actions. There has never been a Labour government that hasn't made climate transition an imperative.

“We are a global leader in climate action. We always have been, and that is an action that the last government took under Labour, and it is an action that we are taking now.

“So no one should doubt our resolve about it. And the reason I say it matters is because it's happening here, and ultimately, our communities will not forgive us if we do not act to protect them. That's the first job of government, and that is why we're taking it seriously.”

‌



View 4 Images Firefighters tackle a blaze in Sheffield in August (Image: Paul Atkin / SWNS)

She said tackling the climate crisis was "absolutely a priority" for Labour, adding: "You can't have gone through the last summer - we've seen heatwaves, we've seen droughts, we've seen wildfires.

"For me, the reason I care about this is that if we do not do our job as government of both protecting people by mitigating the impacts of climate change, but also adapting - because it is here - in order to respond and be resilient, that's families, that's homes, that's businesses, that are communities that are impacted in the here and now today. But it's also our kids. So we've got a responsibility to do this and do it well."

‌



Ms Fahnbulleh - who resigned as a minister under Keir Starmer after losing confidence in him - defended Labour's steadfast support of renewable energy, saying the Tories and Reform are “in the wrong place” on their climate policies.

Kemi Badenoch has declared the 2050 Net Zero target impossible. In July, the Conservative leader said the plan to go carbon neutral by 2050 was “a political fiction bankrupting the country”.

Net Zero is the policy aimed at balancing out the amount of greenhouse gases with those being removed from the atmosphere. The 2050 target was set under Theresa May's Tory government in 2019.

‌



Richard Tice has repeatedly labelled the plans "Net stupid Zero", claiming there is no evidence the strategy will work. The Reform UK deputy leader also faced criticism after saying people should be less “doom and gloom” about the hot weather and celebrate the benefits it could have on English wine.

Asked if Labour was losing the fight on Net Zero, Ms Fahnbulleh said: “My personal view, and that's backed up by the science, is that I think some of our colleagues and other political parties have got themselves into a slightly nonsense position on this. That's not where the public is.

“We are constantly testing this, polling, speaking to the public. The majority of the public supports action on climate, and they are seeing the impact on it in their lives and their communities.”

‌



The newly appointed Cabinet minister said the UK must "diversify our energy" to move away from international markets and protect British families' bills from global shocks like the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

She added: "The thing I say to the Tories and Reform is, when you say let's not do renewables, even though we know it's cheaper, when you say let's not do clean energy at a time that we can see that the thing that is driving up bills is gas, what is your answer on affordability? And they don't have one."

As Parliament resumes next week, Ms Fahnbulleh and Mr Burnham must soon make a decision on drilling in the north sea. Unions are in favour of approving Rosebank, an oil field north-west of Shetland, and Jackdaw, a gas field east of Aberdeen, as they say it will protect jobs, while green campaigners say signing them off would lead to devastating environmental impacts.

Article continues below

Asked how she feels that she will upset people no matter the decision, Ms Fahbulleh said: “I think the debate has become a little bit too polarised. The way that I see it is, we've been really clear and really pragmatic that oil and gas are part of the mix as we do the transition.”

She admitted jobs were decimated in the north sea under the Tories and said Labour will ensure there is “a proper plan for Aberdeen that is about protecting and preserving jobs now, but also creating jobs for the future”.

But she also admitted more drilling will not make energy bills more affordable. “If you care about affordability, and that's my number one priority, the reality is that because (Margaret) Thatcher sold off the North Sea, because oil that is drilled in the North Sea is sold on global markets that we have no control over, it doesn't solve the problem of affordability.”

News.title: Sons of police officer killed in horror A66 crash lead out dad's beloved Man Utd vs Ipswich
News.content:
Sons of police officer killed in horror A66 crash lead out dad's beloved Man Utd vs Ipswich

Manchester United fan PC Matthew Blades was killed in a horror head-on collision with a vehicle that was speeding down the wrong way of the A66 in Teesside last week

View 3 Images The boys were invited to lead Manchester United out today (Image: Getty Images)

The sons of a police officer killed in a head-on crash on the A66 have led Manchester United out at Old Trafford for their Premier League clash against Ipswich Town.

‌



PC Matthew Blades, described by the club as a "proud Red," was killed alongside colleague PC Tom Clough in a head-on crash with a vehicle travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank, in Teeside, last weekend. Middlesborough FC also paid tribute to the officers and their colleagues at Cleveland Police on Saturday, and United invited Blades' two sons and his wife to their home match against Ipswich.

‌



The children led the United squad as mascots, with the club expressing "great sadness" at the deaths of the two officers in the matchday programme. United said: "Matthew was a proud Red, a devoted family man and a police officer who dedicated his life to helping others.

‌



View 3 Images Matthew Blades was a fan of Manchester United (Image: Facebook)

Sky News presenter forced to cut live broadcast after being 'hassled' on air READ MORE :

"For Matt, some of his happiest times were spent watching United with his boys. His wife Sarah and two children will be at today's game, with his sons leading out the Reds as mascots."

‌



An image of Blades with his two sons at Old Trafford featured in the programme, along with a tribute from an unnamed close friend and colleague. "For Matthew, United was a lifelong love, a passion he shared with his family," the tribute read.

"Since Matt's tragic death there has been an extraordinary outpouring of grief and support. That love has been seen in countless tributes and acts of kindness.

View 3 Images The two boys led Manchester United out today against Ipswich

Article continues below

"Today, we remember a fellow Red. A husband. A father. A son. A brother. A friend. A police officer. A man who gave his life in the service of others. Forever our superhero."

Across the Pennines, match officials at Elland Road for Leeds United's fixture against Brentford wore black armbands as referee Tony Harrington was a friend of PC Blades. There was a minute's applause on Saturday in the memory of the two police officers. Pictures of the two men were displayed on screen.

The occupants of the vehicle headed the wrong way down the A66 were Robert Cahill, 23, Jakob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17. All of them died in the crash.

News.title: Parents handed airport boost but there is a catch
News.content:
Parents handed airport boost but there is a catch

Families should be aware of some important rules before they travel

View 2 Images The change came into force on July 8 (Image: Akabei via Getty Images)

Heathrow has issued a summer travel update telling families they can now benefit from a major change to Britain’s airport border controls.

‌



The airport said: “Get ready for easier arrivals for families. Children aged 8 and 9 will now be able to use the eGates. They will need to have an eligible passport and be travelling with an adult". The change could prove a welcome boost for parents returning to Britain from their summer holidays – potentially cutting the time they spend queuing at passport control.

‌



Children aged eight and nine can use UK eGates, bringing them into line with older children who are already eligible to use the automated border gates.

‌



But there is an important catch. The youngsters must have an eligible passport, be travelling with an adult and, under the Government’s rules, be at least 120cm (3ft 11in) tall.

The change came into force on July 8, just as the summer holiday travel season was getting into full swing. And the Government estimates that up to 1.5 million more children could become eligible to use eGates over the next year.

For parents facing the prospect of tired youngsters after a long flight, the prospect of avoiding a lengthy passport-control queue could be particularly welcome. Heathrow has urged passengers travelling with younger children to check airport signage or speak to staff if they are unsure which lane they should use.

‌



View 2 Images The change could prove a welcome boost for parents (Image: Europa Press News, Europa Press via Getty Images)

What parents need to know

The expanded eGate access applies to eight and nine-year-olds who meet the requirements.

They must:

‌



Be aged eight or nine

Be at least 120cm tall

Have an eligible passport

Be travelling with an adult

The Government says the change covers more than 290 eGates across the UK and at so-called juxtaposed ports, where British border checks are carried out in Europe. Millions of passengers already use eGates each year.

The Government says using one typically takes only a few minutes – and increasing the number of people who can use them should also help reduce queues for passengers who still need to go through staffed passport control.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Major change for families

The move was announced by the Home Office in May as part of a wider programme to transform the UK’s border system. Migration and Citizenship Minister Mike Tapp said: “Travel with young children can be stressful for parents.”

He said expanding eGate access would allow more families to have a “swifter and smoother journey home” while keeping Britain’s borders secure.

‌



Border Force Director General Phil Douglas said eGates were an “essential part” of keeping the border secure.

He said the expansion would deliver safe and smooth journeys while freeing officers to concentrate on intercepting people who pose a threat to the UK.

Karen Dee, chief executive of AirportsUK, welcomed the change, saying it would give more families the opportunity to use the technology and could reduce waiting times.

Article continues below

Part of wider border overhaul

The change comes alongside the Government’s wider push to modernise Britain’s borders. The Electronic Travel Authorisation scheme has also been introduced for eligible travellers, with almost 25 million ETAs issued, according to Government figures.

The longer-term ambition is for a more “contactless” border, with facial comparison technology being used to verify travellers’ identities.

News.title: Prisoners freed early are returning to jail at rapid rate, governors tell BBC
News.content:
Prisoners who were freed under the government's last early release scheme are returning to jail at a rapid rate, prison governors have told the BBC.

They say they are seeing the same inmates, who were let out as part of the 2024 early release scheme to ease overcrowding, coming back after reoffending - including for breaching their conditions.

"The churn is what stresses me out," said one governor in the Midlands, describing it as a "revolving door".

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the next early release scheme, starting in October, following outrage that the killers of PC Andrew Harper were among those eligible to be released.

On Sunday, Burnham announced that they will not be, telling the BBC that anyone convicted of unlawful killing will be excluded from the scheme.

He conceded that it means "hundreds" more people will stay in prison - as prisons in England and Wales reach breaking point at more than 97% full.

The government says there are plans to create more prison space by deporting foreign inmates and releasing some who are serving indefinite sentences, but they are unlikely to create much more space by the time the first batch of inmates are released in October.

BBC News spoke to three serving prison governors in England to gauge the state of correctional facilities and how staff are dealing with overcrowding. Prison staff are not supposed to speak to the media so their names and the prisons they govern will not be mentioned to protect their identity.

One governor from a prison in the north of England said the PM's plans to ease overcrowding "is all short-term solutions and we need space now".

"Providing additional cells in existing prisons will mean more prison staff needed to monitor that - it's not easy," they said, adding that staff shortages mean "prisoners are not living in a safe and decent environment".

The governor also said they were frustrated by the rate of prisoner recalls, saying: "We see the same people coming back after being released early and reoffending again, or breaking their [release] rules."

News.title: Sons of officer who died in A66 crash lead out Man Utd as mascots
News.content:
The two sons of a police officer killed in a crash on Teesside led out the Manchester United team as mascots for Sunday's Premier League match against Ipswich at Old Trafford.

PC Matthew Blades, described as a "proud Red" by United, was a regular at Old Trafford.

The club paid tribute to him in Sunday's match programme, while his widow attended the game with their children.

PC Blades and his colleague PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision between their police car and a vehicle going the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough early on 22 August. Five people in the other vehicle also died.

United said they learned of the deaths of the two officers "with great sadness".

"Matthew was a proud Red, a devoted family man and a police officer who dedicated his life to helping others," said the club, in a tribute in the programme.

At Elland Road, match officials for Leeds United's Premier League fixture against Brentford on Sunday wore black armbands as referee Tony Harrington was a friend of PC Blades.

On Saturday, there was a minute's applause in memory of PC Blades and PC Clough before Middlesbrough's Championship encounter with West Brom at Riverside Stadium. Pictures of the two men were displayed on a screen.

People also gathered to pay tribute at Seaton Carew FC's game against FC Hartlepool. PC Blades had been a junior football coach at both teams.

Earlier this week, 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash, bringing the total number of arrests to 24.

The occupants of the other vehicle, a Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17, also died.

News.title: Church names pastor killed by falling sign at Christian festival
News.content:
The man killed at a Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday has been named by his church as Robert Guanco, 41.

He was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.

Six other people were injured at the event by a falling sign at the Big Church Festival, near Steyning, four of whom were taken to hospital for treatment.

In a statement, his church said: "Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love, and his service to God will never be forgotten."

On a fundraising page for Guanco's family, pastor Norman Ponce from Jesus the Living Water Worldwide Church, said he was a "faithful servant of God".

"What was meant to be a time of worship, fellowship, and celebration became an unimaginable tragedy," he added.

Ponce said Guanco was a "beloved son, cherished brother, loving husband" and "great father".

"He was also a good friend, mentor, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched," Ponce said.

"His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion, and service. Through his ministry, kindness, prayers, and encouragement, he touched many lives."

News.title: British woman killed in stabbing at German railway station
News.content:
A British woman has died after being stabbed at a railway station in southern Germany in the early hours of Sunday morning, police have said.

The 31-year-old woman was attacked at the station in Rosenheim, Bavaria, shortly before 01:00 local time (00:00 BST). She was taken to hospital where she died as a result of "severe" injuries, the Bavarian Police said in a statement.

Officers arrested a 27-year-old German man at the scene immediately after the incident. The background and motive for the attack is under investigation, the statement added.

Police have asked anyone who may have witnessed "an argument or physical altercation" at the station late on Saturday or early on Sunday to contact them.

The suspect, from the FÃ¼rstenfeldbruck district, will be brought before magistrates later on Sunday, according to German news agency DPA.

It is unclear whether the two knew each other or what the woman was doing in Bavaria, DPA also reported.

Rosenheim is one of the largest cities in Upper Bavaria and is a busy rail hub for passengers travelling to Austrian cities including Vienna, Salzburg and Innsbruck.

The Rosenheimer Herbstfest - an event similar to the Oktoberfest beer festival - is currently taking place in the area.

Responding to the attack, Rosenheim Mayor Abuzar Erdogan said "there are no indications of a security threat in our city or of any link to our Herbstfest".

"The criminal investigation department is working closely with the public prosecutor's office to investigate the circumstances and motive behind the crime as a matter of urgency," he wrote in a statement.

A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local authorities."

News.title: Police release one of two men arrested over fatal house fire
News.content:
A 31-year-old man arrested on suspicion of murder over a fatal house fire has been released with no further action while a second man, aged 23, continues to be questioned.

Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of Wednesday, along with her niece Valentina Foster, seven.

Cleveland Police said a 48-year-old woman had been left in a critical condition in hospital and another three people had injuries that were not life-threatening.

The force added enquiries were ongoing.

Natalie's mother, Lisa Kirton, described her as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".

Valentina, who was known as Tina, was staying at the house for the summer holidays and had been "dancing around the living room" only the previous night.

"She was a cute little kid," Kirton said. "I can't believe it, seven years old - it's just a disgrace."

In an update on Friday afternoon, Cleveland Police ACC Dave Sutherland said the force was not currently linking the fire to a crash on the A66, in which seven people died, including two police officers.

News.title: Seven arrested after death of newborn baby girl
News.content:
Seven people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after the death of a newborn baby girl in Sheffield, police said.

Officers were called at about 06:00 BST on Sunday to a property on Holywell Heights in the Wincobank area following reports of a concern for the safety of the baby.

South Yorkshire Police said, despite the best efforts of officers and paramedics, the baby was pronounced dead at the scene.

Det Ch Insp Emma Knight confirmed the force was "working to determine the ages of some of those arrested".

She said: "We are aware news of this will be deeply concerning and I want to reassure our local communities that we have a dedicated team of detectives and officers hard at work to ensure justice is secured for the baby girl at the heart of this investigation."

Knight added: "Our investigation is in its early stages and we would like to remind people to avoid speculating about this incident."

News.title: Lola Young surprises Reading Festival with final day set
News.content:
Fans at the final day of Reading Festival were treated to a surprise set from singer Lola Young.

"I am backstage, the cat is out of the bag and I am going to be performing so see you... at the Grid stage," she teased on Instagram, before treating fans to hits including number one single Messy and One Thing.

Her performance marks the latest step in a return to the spotlight after she had to cancel a string of shows last year following an on-stage collapse in September.

Young also pulled out of the 2025 Reading festival due to a scheduling clash.

The weekend festival concludes on Sunday with a line-up including performances by drum and bass duo Chase & Status, and Florence + The Machine.

After Charli XCX ushered in her own new era with an electrifying set following her latest release Music, Fashion, Film, Young's return was welcomed by festival-goers in Reading on Sunday.

Young had cancelled her scheduled appearance at Reading Festival last year due to an "unavoidable scheduling conflict".

A month later, Young dropped her microphone, collapsed backwards and had to be helped off stage in front of a festival crowd in New York.

A few days later, she cancelled all shows "for the foreseeable future".

"I really hope you'll give me a second chance once I've had some time to work on myself and come back stronger," she posted in a message to fans at the time.

Young has sought treatment for drug dependency and told the Guardian, external in 2025 that addiction had dogged her for "a long time".

The pop star has since returned to performing with a small run of shows in the UK, starting with a London gig in March.

"It felt so right being back on stage," she wrote on social media shortly after, but said: "As tempting as it is to jump on a big tour I'm going to continue taking things slowly despite feeling so ready to perform more."

Before touching down in Reading, Young performed at the Electric Picnic Festival in the Republic of Ireland on Saturday.

Although she has returned to performing and released reflective single From Down Here in May this year, fans are still awaiting a fourth album.

Reading Festival winds down on Sunday night with a star-studded cast including indie icon Florence and the Machine, R&B hit-maker Loyle Carner, and Irish rap group Kneecap.

The festival's other site in Leeds, meanwhile, closes after performances from singer-songwriter Raye and multi award-winning rapper Dave on Sunday night.

News.title: Head teacher evacuated 900 children minutes before Nepal floods hit school
News.content:
Students and teachers initially moved a few hundred metres uphill to safety before making their way to a neighbouring village.

With roads cut off and transport disrupted, many remained stranded for two nights before rescue efforts reached them.

The principal and Yunisha, who both live across the river from the school, were eventually airlifted back to their home village.

Meanwhile parents were desperately trying to contact their children and relatives.

Yunisha's mother, Sabina Kumari Shrestha, says she repeatedly tried to call both her daughter and husband, but neither could be reached.

Her husband, Yubaraj Amatya, immediately headed towards the school.

"Soon after the flood news spread, I tried my daughter's number, but she was not reachable, then I was afraid," he said.

"Within a few minutes I rushed toward my daughter's school and Trishuli Bazar was all swept by the flood, then I thought my daughter was no more. I was so horrified, stopped my scooter, there was flooding but I could not think of returning without my daughter."

For nearly an hour, he had no idea whether she was alive and kept calling her without success. Then the phone finally connected and Yunisha answered.

"Finally, my daughter received my call and I couldn't stop myself, broke out... two relatives that were with me also cried and hugged me," he said.

Yunisha appears tearful as she recalls that moment.

"After I had reached the top of the hill, I received a call from my father. He was tearful and I could not speak a word then," she said.

Back home, her family waited anxiously for her return.

"Even my younger daughter couldn't sleep. But I felt so good to see her after three days (Friday), I am so happy and relieved," her mother said.

Yunisha says she is now thinking about what comes next.

"Now I am worried about my further studies," she said.

"If I had to change my school, I would have to miss my old friends and will face difficulties to make new friends. I am sad about my further studies."

Head teacher Dawadi says better warning systems, including sirens and evacuation alerts, could have helped residents respond sooner.

But he believes his decision to act immediately prevented a catastrophe.

"Had I decided to close the school after the period, nothing might be left, only the bell would be ringing at 9:30."

News.title: Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?
News.content:
The prime minister's announcement that he will keep hundreds of criminals behind bars who would otherwise have been released early is one he has wanted to make for weeks.

Andy Burnham had already expanded the list of people ineligible for early release and had consistently said he wanted to go further.

What is not clear is exactly what has changed to allow him to do so.

Earlier this month, the Ministry of Justice warned that exempting any more prisoners risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing".

The prime minister himself previously said he had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

In his exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham picked out the release of people on controversial indefinite sentences and the deportation of foreign criminals as measures that had made his latest intervention possible.

It is understood extra capacity will also be created by immediately beginning work to create new cells in existing prisons.

But none of these are short-term solutions.

Ending indefinite sentences will require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.

Previous governments have struggled to quickly deport foreign offenders and there are not thought to be any new returns agreements with other countries. The case of grooming gang ringleader Shabir Ahmed, who Pakistan has resisted attempts to deport, is one example.

Retrofitting prisons to create more cells is also expected to take months.

People in government concede that in the short-term, Burnham will only be able to follow through on today's announcement by making prisons even more full.

With the adult male prison estate already running at 98% capacity, it is a move that could worry some in the sector.

But in the end, the prime minister believed he simply had to act.

The extra exemptions Burnham has announced are being described within government as a "political decision".

That is not surprising given the intense pressure that had built up, especially around the potential for PC Andrew Harper's killers to be released early.

Burnham's inner circle are mindful that political misjudgements at the start of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership caused long-lasting damage.

They believe Sir Keir never recovered from early rows over freebies and winter fuel payments, and point to a lack of major mishaps in Burnham's first six weeks in office as evidence of a more slick political operation.

There was some surprise in Downing Street about how much media attention the issue of early release received over the summer.

That is one reason why the prime minister's aides are relishing the new parliamentary term, when news stories come along at a faster rate and so are less likely to linger in the headlines.

After the initial flip-flopping on whether the government would be able to exempt more prisoners, the mother of PC Harper told BBC Breakfast that the handling of the situation had been a "hash".

Government officials working on the plans have spoken to the families of victims, who made it clear they did not want the new measures to be dripped out in leaks to the media.

Instead it was decided one big announcement would be the neatest option.

It had seemed likely that would come in the form of a parliamentary statement on Tuesday from the justice secretary.

Instead, the prime minister decided to make the announcement himself in an interview with BBC Breakfast.

It is understood Burnham was mindful of mounting speculation and wanted to give victims and the public as much certainty at the earliest possible opportunity.

In doing so, he may have risked the ire of the Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle, who is generally disdainful of governments that make major announcements outside of Parliament.

He may also have offered up ammunition to the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has already accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who finds it difficult to say no to people.

That characterisation is likely to be tested again when more stories inevitably appear about the victims of prisoners who will still be released early.

It already started on Sunday morning, when the domestic abuse commissioner said she remained "deeply concerned about the number of abusers" still set to be freed.

While this is not the first time Burnham has said he has pushed the system to the limit, Whitehall sources are now adamant there will be no more additional exemptions.

News.title: Two missing as French trawler sinks in Channel
News.content:
Searches have been carried out for a second day for two crew members after a French fishing boat sank in the English Channel, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency said.

A coastguard rescue helicopter, fixed-wing plane and RNLI lifeboats began searching an area south-west of Eddystone Lighthouse off Plymouth, Devon, after the crew of the trawler the Maranello made a distress call at 18:00 BST on Saturday.

The intensive multi-agency search continued on Sunday before it was "suspended pending further information", coastguards said at 20:20 on Sunday.

HM Coastguard said three people rescued from the boat and taken to hospital were "currently travelling back to France".

The French authorities said the stricken fishing vessel had contacted another trawler, the Stradale, to say it had a problem with its fishing gear.

The Stradale managed to recover three of the five crew members before the Maranello sank, the French naval prefecture for the Atlantic added.

One of the rescued sailors was evacuated by helicopter and treated in hospital in Truro, Cornwall, while the other two were taken to Plymouth for medical attention.

RNLI lifeboat crews from Falmouth and Newlyn in Cornwall, as well as from Plymouth and Salcombe in Devon, have been involved in the operation.

A large number of civilian vessels had also assisted in the "intensive search" for the two remaining crew members, a UK coastguard spokesperson added.

They said a coastguard aircraft "equipped with the latest technology including a multi-function search radar and high resolution cameras" was also involved, and that mayday relay broadcasts had been sent out, "requesting vessels in the area to keep a sharp lookout."
