World.title: From the archive: Learning Spanish? Don’t be shy or afraid of making mistakes
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article, for example — originally published in November 2019 — explores the leap of faith required when learning Mexican Spanish.

When I first arrived in Mexico, I had two years of college-level Spanish under my belt. While I was an enthusiastic learner, I was also a very self-conscious speaker, terrified of making embarrassing mistakes and generally sounding like a 2-year-old.

I did, in fact, sound like a 2-year-old at first, as there’s simply no way around being a “baby” when one is first learning. Happily, I survived that stage and now speak at least as well as a know-it-all 13-year-old.

Part of my apprehension with the language was the sense that Mexico’s love-hate relationship with the United States would lead to some situations in which I’d be mocked for my accent or mistakes that I would inevitably make.

After all, most people here know very well how Latinos are treated by certain segments of the U.S. population when they’re on the other side of the border, so I’d imagined that the temptation to dish some out to us collectively would be at least a little irresistible.

For the most part, that didn’t happen. It’s also possible that I simply didn’t realize it was happening, but I think most of us humans have a pretty good sense of when others are laughing at us.

Once in a while someone will have a longish conversation with me (in Spanish) and then say something like, “So, you don’t speak Spanish, eh?” or they’ll point out that they “could tell right away that I was American because of my accent” which always makes me bristle, as I’m pretty sure my accent is, while definitely existent, not obviously American.

(My Mexican friends may disagree with me on that one; I’d ask them, but the answer might be too painful for me to hear.)

There’s some sting in it, but I do my best to chalk up any unflattering comments about my Spanish to cosmic justice and not take it too personally.

In the part of Mexico where I live, English is not considered an essential skill the same way it is in the north or in tourist areas. Because of this, most foreigners in my area do their best with the language: they take classes, they practice, they work hard to get better.

Learning a language is sign of respect

They understand, above all, that learning the language of your hosts, if you are able, is a matter of respect.

When I traveled to Los Cabos recently to visit a friend, I saw how different things were in a town that depends on tourism from their English-speaking neighbors: I was addressed in English at all times, and if I answered in Spanish it almost seemed to startle people, as if they’d come into contact with a dog that had learned to produce human sounds.

For the most part, Mexicans are charmed when we non-native speakers at least try. They’re patient and encouraging, and try their best to be helpful. Mexico really is an ideal place to learn Spanish, as I can’t imagine another place in which more impromptu and consistent support among the general population would be given.

That said, I know many of my compatriots are shy about learning — and especially about using — the Spanish that they know already. I completely understand: there’s nothing that makes us feel quite as vulnerable as not being able to “prove” that we are smart, complex, discerning individuals.

There’s no way around sounding like a simpleton when we’re on that long uphill trajectory, and simply put, it can be a humiliating experience.

But again: at least attempting to learn the local language, if one is able, is a matter of respect. “Well then, what about all the people in the U.S. that haven’t bothered to learn English? I bet you don’t go around preaching to them about respect, do you?”

The short answer is that no, indeed I do not. Because here’s the difference: most people who go to the U.S. without already speaking English are in survival mode, just trying to make it from one day to the next, often working a dizzying number of hours both to both survive, and likely to send money back home.

Most Americans and Canadians, however, come to Mexico either in vacation or retirement mode. Some, sadly, come because their spouses or loved ones have been deported and they want to keep the family together.

If one is on vacation, of course, learning the language won’t be expected. But if you settle here, an effort must be made.

Find a school, or find a teacher. Find someone to sit and help you practice. Spend time just listening to people with no intention of adding to the conversation. One of the best pieces of advice I’ve ever received for learning a language is literally to pretend to be a baby: listen to the sounds, watch people, let whole social situations piece themselves together and come into focus slowly.

Babies, after all, spend at least a couple of years listening and observing before they try to string together a sentence with more than four words in it.

On my first plane ride into Mexico, my nervousness increased with each sentence given in Spanish by the flight attendants: the more they spoke, the more I realized I wasn’t catching anything at all that they were saying.

Since then, I’ve made about a million mistakes, linguistically embarrassed myself in every way imaginable, and surely sounded much less sophisticated than I imagine myself to be.

But I’ve gained the ability to talk to most people on this side of the world and have developed some of the closest relationships of my lifetime in this language.

Hands down, totally worth it.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: A governor takes a U-turn, CJNG loses more ground and business booms
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 24 in Mexico began on awkward footing following a Morena party faux pas in Sinaloa. Rubén Rocha Moya, currently under investigation in the United States for alleged collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel, briefly reclaimed the Sinaloa governorship after months on leave, only to retreat again two days later. Meanwhile, several storm systems dumped rain on most of the country, and an investigation into fuel theft in Tamaulipas turned up a startling menagerie of exotic animals.

Also this week, President Sheinbaum revealed new reforms and a US $6M windfall for Guerrero schools as she prepares to soon give her second annual report to the nation.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum weighs in on Rocha’s status in Sinaloa

President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the week fielding questions about the fallout from Rocha Moya’s brief return to the Sinaloa governorship from Aug. 21–23 and the future of Sinaloa’s leadership.

At Monday’s mañanera, as Sonora’s cattle trade with the U.S. reopened, she addressed the episode directly for the first time, saying she learned of Rocha’s Friday return through his social media post and had no prior knowledge of his plans. “I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” she said, later calling the decision “imprudent.” She credited Rocha’s renewed leave request — approved unanimously by Sinaloa’s Congress that Sunday — as “the best thing for Sinaloa,” and dismissed rumors that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador had encouraged Rocha’s return as “political fiction.”

Sheinbaum extended the same standard to other Morena officials swept up in the same U.S. indictment. Asked on Tuesday about Senator Enrique Inzunza — one of 10 Sinaloa-linked officials accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking ties, who had signaled he might return to the Senate — she said the same principle applied. “Yesterday I gave my opinion on the case of the governor of Sinaloa, who is now on leave. I feel the same way about all 10 cases under investigation by the Attorney General’s Office,” she said. Inzunza subsequently separated from Morena’s Senate caucus on Wednesday, though he remains in office as senator.

Multiple CJNG busts across three states

Security forces delivered a string of blows against the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) this week. A coordinated operation across Hidalgo, Jalisco and Michoacán from Aug. 21–23 resulted in 20 arrests and the seizure of weapons, drugs and exotic animals tied to the cartel, with authorities raiding 36 properties and confiscating firearms, fentanyl, methamphetamine, 113 vehicles and a drone jammer.

That action followed a separate military-led operation in Michoacán targeting alleged CJNG leader Heraclio “El Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez last week, which produced roughly a dozen more arrests, including relatives of the suspect. Combined, the two operations brought the week’s tally of alleged CJNG detentions to 32, part of what Security Minister Omar García Harfuch described as an effort to systematically dismantle the group’s operational and financial capacity rather than simply rack up arrests.

Confusion and concern in Mexicali

A U.S. security alert warning of a possible “August 25 threat” in Mexicali created a tense but ultimately murky standoff between caution and normalcy. The alert prompted the U.S. Mission to suspend official travel and activity in the border city, reportedly linked to fears that the crime gang Los Rusos might retaliate after a 120-kilogram fentanyl seizure — roughly 4 million doses — from a property connected to the group.

Mexican officials responded by increasing patrols around public buildings, but as Tuesday came and went without a major incident, the federal security cabinet said it had found no evidence of a specific or imminent threat to the public. Residents described a largely normal day, and the Mexicali-Calexico border crossing remained open throughout, leaving the alert’s basis and its practical necessity still unclear.

Economic data: Record highs alongside warning signs

Revised GDP figures showed the economy grew in the second quarter but contracted in June, with the primary sector contributing the steadiest growth. Foreign direct investment in Mexico yielded US $34.968 billion in FDI in the first half of 2026, its highest semester total ever recorded, up 2.1% year over year, even though the second quarter alone saw a 3.5% annual decline. Manufacturing captured 38.6% of that investment, and the United States remained the dominant source at $16.871 billion.

Trade data added to the good news: July exports hit a record US $81.4 billion, up 43.7% annually, driven by a 134% surge in electrical and electronic equipment shipments tied to U.S. demand for AI and data-center infrastructure inputs. At her Wednesday press conference, Sheinbaum cheered the numbers as proof of a “strong” economy, pointing to record FDI, 60 million people employed and a firm peso, and argued that years of minimum-wage increases had not triggered the inflation or capital flight critics once predicted.

That optimism gained further support when Mexico placed among the OECD’s fastest-growing economies, ranking sixth with 1.4% quarterly growth against an OECD average of 0.5%. But the jobs report complicated the picture: Mexico posted its best monthly job gain of 2026 in July, yet the increase was driven entirely by informal employment, with more than 1.08 million informal jobs added while over 412,000 formal positions vanished. Informality climbed to 56.2%, its highest level since December 2021 — a reminder that headline growth figures can mask deteriorating job quality.

This week’s investment announcements

Schneider Electric announced a major expansion of its operations in Querétaro, reinforcing the state’s role as an industrial and technology hub. Danish firms unveiled a US $510 million renewables project set to boost Campeche’s clean energy supply, adding to the country’s growing green energy portfolio. And Jalisco is set to host Mexico’s first solar panel recycling plant, a facility in Ciudad Guzmán capable of recovering up to 95% of materials from the roughly 1.6 million panels already installed statewide.

A fresh framework for environmental protection

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena presented a bill to put environmental justice at the center of Mexican law, proposing reforms to the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection. The initiative would require more forward-looking assessment of major projects, close loopholes that let developers split projects to dodge full environmental review, strengthen restoration and remediation requirements and add specific protections for environmental defenders and Indigenous, Afro-Mexican, rural and urban communities.

Foreign Minister strengthens ties in South Korea and Washington

Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco kept a packed international schedule this week. In Seoul, he met with South Korean officials and executives from Samsung, Hyundai, LG and Posco to promote investment in technology, semiconductors and education, part of groundwork for a 2026–30 bilateral action plan ahead of a planned visit by South Korea’s president. He then traveled to Washington, where he held his first face-to-face meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both sides publicly stressed cooperation against drug and arms trafficking, Bloomberg reported that Washington privately pressed Mexico to do more to stop its own citizens from crossing into the U.S.

Aura farming battles debut in Mexico

A new social-media-driven trend reached Mexican public squares this week: aura farming battles, in which participants strike poses, dance and reference memes to project confidence and style while crowds judge who accumulates the most “aura.” Events popped up at Mexico City landmarks as well as in Xalapa and Torreón, though at least one Veracruz municipality banned the contests in public parks on administrative grounds.

Sheinbaum proposes dual-citizenship ban

Sheinbaum also unveiled a constitutional amendment that would bar dual nationals from running for president, governor or Mexico City mayor unless they renounce their other citizenship before registering as candidates. The government argues current constitutional language contains a loophole and that the country’s highest offices should be held only by people with unambiguous national allegiance — a proposal likely to draw scrutiny over its impact on Mexican-born citizens with binational ties.

Mexican athletes shine internationally

Cyclist Isaac del Toro won the Tour of Germany, becoming the first Latin American rider to capture the race, finishing 53 seconds ahead of France’s Louis Barré.

Mexico won two gold medals and a bronze at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam: Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez took gold in women’s lightweight double sculls, Kenia Lechuga won gold in lightweight single sculls, and Alexis López earned bronze in men’s lightweight single sculls.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test whether this week’s political and security cracks widen further. In Sinaloa, the ongoing conflict between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos remains unresolved, complicating the search for a permanent successor. Pressure is also unlikely to ease on other Morena-aligned officials named in the same U.S. indictment, amid broader questions about the party’s exposure to organized crime in states beyond Sinaloa. With Sheinbaum’s second annual report to the nation approaching, how she navigates these overlapping crises could shape both her security narrative and her party’s credibility heading into the fall.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Activists rally to stop luxury project on Yucatán dunes
World.content:
A proposed luxury real estate development along a protected beach community in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula has sparked protests and backlash online. It’s the latest in a string of projects that activists have sought to stop, saying the developments will have detrimental impacts on their communities.

Las Dunas tourist complex is a planned luxury real estate and tourism venture that aims to encompass 92,000 square meters (more than 22 acres) of virgin beach area less than an hour’s drive from Mérida, the state capital of Yucatán, including more than 70 apartments spread across six towers.

Given its size and scope, activists say the project will have a significant economic and environmental impact on the small beach town, and that it ignores pressing issues that need to be addressed.

“In Chuburná, there are real needs – problems stemming from a lack of basic infrastructure and systematic neglect by the authorities,” Salvemos las Dunas, a local environmental activist group, told Mexico News Daily. “They want to foster the false belief that megaprojects bring economic benefits, but the question is: benefits for whom?”

‘A crime against biodiversity’

It’s not just Salvemos las Dunas that’s sounding the alarm.

Mexico’s Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) denied the project’s initial proposal in December 2023, as the site was deemed highly vulnerable. However, in April 2025, after adjustments were made to the proposal, the project was federally approved.

As the Las Dunas development began to take shape, the outcry from community members and activists was swift. Salvemos las Dunas launched a petition calling for a halt to the project and an official review of the proposed plan.

“[A]bove all, this area is not just a stretch of sand; it’s the history and identity of the people who already live there,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

Their concerns were supported by a three-day inspection led by the Federal Prosecutor’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) in late July. That report detailed multiple violations of federal regulations, some of which could carry criminal charges.

“Omissions, non-compliance and subsequent damage to species of wild flora and fauna protected by Official Mexican Standards may transcend the administrative scope and constitute a crime against biodiversity,” Profepa wrote in a statement shared with Mexico News Daily.

Profepa and the government of Yucatán have since paused the project while they verify its compliance. During a press conference in early August, Gov. Joaquín Díaz Mena said that the “protection of Yucatán’s natural heritage will prevail over any particular project.”

Meanwhile, Salvemos las Dunas’ petition to protect the dunes has garnered more than 140,000 signatures. A protest was also held at the Monumento a La Patria in nearby Mérida in late July.

The public opposition to the project appears to be working.

“Given the concern of citizens, the State Government formally requested, since last July 25, Semarnat and the Federal Attorney General’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) to verify the timely compliance with the project authorizations and delivered all the technical information it has,” Yucatán’s government wrote in a statement.

Designia Desarrollos, the development firm behind Las Dunas, declined to comment on the ongoing proceedings.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said. “The lack of regulation and the ease with which permits are granted to real estate developers have hijacked the state.”

How important are the Chuburná Dunes?

The Chuburná Dunes are an integral part of the coastal ecosystem, recognized as one of the most well-preserved in Yucatán. Hosting various endangered wildlife species, including some that are endemic to Yucatán, as well as a nesting ground for a tortoise species on the brink of global extinction, the current ecosystem is both fragile and consequential.

Among the animals that call the dunes home are the Mexican sheartail hummingbird (doricha eliza) and the Yucateca wren (campylorhynchus yucatanicus), both of which have been granted a protective status, as well as the hawksbill sea turtle (eretmochelys imbricata) and the green sea turtle (chelonia mydas).

The dunes also serve as a natural protector against wind, tides, hurricanes, erosion and other storm systems that frequently batter the area, meaning any damage to them could prove irreversible.

“We believe that progress can be achieved consciously, hand in hand with environmental protection and citizen participation, but above all, by safeguarding the interests of the people, not just a few families in Mérida,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

A stalled Royal Caribbean project

The Las Dunas tourist complex is just the latest in a string of recent developments that didn’t sit well with local activists and conservationists.

Earlier this year, a Royal Caribbean megaproject in Quintana Roo came to a halt after citizens and activists expressed concerns.

The project, known as “Perfect Day,” is a proposed amusement park in the municipality of Othón P. Blanco, in the small fishing village of Mahahual. The famous cruise line had purchased the property, located close to the port of Costa Maya, which Royal Caribbean also owns, for $292 million.

An online petition against the development has garnered more than 5 million signatures to date.

Royal Caribbean officially withdrew its environmental assessment application in May, citing Semarnat’s intentions to deny the project. The company said it was “disappointed” in Semarnat’s decision and would “respect the role of Mexico’s environmental authorities,” but stopped short of saying “Perfect Day” would be scrapped entirely.

“We continue to believe in Mexico, and are optimistic in the potential to advance our investment responsibly,” the company wrote in a statement at the time. “Over the coming weeks, we will re-engage stakeholders to move forward in a way that delivers shared prosperity through the development of essential environmental infrastructure, the creation of thousands of local jobs, and community programs that support the people of Mexico.”

Tren Maya’s 900-mile development

The activism surrounding both Las Dunas and Perfect Day is set against the backdrop of the Tren Maya megaproject, which was completed in 2024 under then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

So far, the 900-mile train route spread across five states in Mexico’s southeast has failed to realize its promised financial benefits for local communities, while also understating its overall environmental impact.

Tren Maya carried its first passengers in December 2023. Since then, 42 trains have been inaugurated, traveling more than 900 miles of track across Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

According to an August 2023 report by CartoCrítica, Tren Maya’s construction spans more than 26,000 acres, requiring deforestation efforts in 61% of the surrounding jungle. The report alleges that 87% of the deforestation was done without the necessary permits.

This, despite López Obrador’s assertions in a 2018 interview that “Not a single tree” would be cut down. Semarnat similarly released a statement in January 2023, saying that “More than 64,000 plants have been rescued with 85% survival.”

However, Priscila Alaniz Uribe, the general director for the Sélvame nonprofit, has a different take.

“About 12 million trees have been cut down, and around 125 cenotes have been damaged,” Alaniz Uribe told Sierra Club in July. “There are 15,000 piles of concrete poisoning the water in underground rivers – water we humans, animals, and plants use to live here.”

Such concerns define the environmental activism that has taken place around the Yucatán Peninsula in recent years.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said of the project they’re working to stop. “If this area is cleared, it will leave the residents who have cared for their city for years unprotected; not to mention that it is home to endemic species of the area that are in danger of extinction.”

Jesse Foley-Tapia is a writer and photographer living in the Yucatán Peninsula, where he has dedicated his time and energy to shedding light on issues affecting Indigenous communities. His biggest journalistic accomplishment is interviewing Kendrick Lamar in 2010. His work has appeared in The Sun Magazine and BreakThrough News.

World.title: A flavorful, vanilla-scented hideout awaits along Mexico’s Gulf Coast
World.content:
You may have seen it: a group of high-flying performers, dressed in a colorful array of traditional garments, climbing a 100-foot-tall pole in a group of four, before diving into the air, upside down, to spin as a human cyclone — held only by a rope tied to their feet — while a fifth member sits atop the pole, performing a ceremonial dance and song with a flute and small drum.

The UNESCO-recognized tradition can be traced back to Tajín, an archaeological site that once served as the capital of the Totonac Mesoamericans from A.D. 800. Today, it is one of Mexico’s most celebrated and active Indigenous rituals, known as the “Danza de los Voladores,” or “Dance of the Flyers.”

Interestingly, the Totonac did not invent the dance — that was likely the Nahua of Central Mexico — but they have preserved it, inextricably linking the practice to their history and culture in the process.

Ancient traditions in the modern world

These airborne avatars of the Totonac people are native to the northern region of Veracruz, where the modern Pueblo Mágico of Papantla can be found, roughly four hours northeast of Mexico City. They are famed throughout the country, with representatives performing their millennia-old routine in tourist centers such as Mexico City’s Bosque de Chapultepec and Xcaret Park in Playa del Carmen.

The voladores maintain their practices and Indigenous language through generations of flyers and community-supported programs, including the Escuela de Niños Voladores in Papantla. They are one of Veracruz’s greatest cultural exports and have inspired an inside joke among Mexicans, who sometimes shout “Papantla, tus hijos vuelan!” when something funny or unexpected happens in daily life.

And yet, as impressive and fun as the voladores are on a sweltering summer day, the region has also gifted Mexico, and the world, even more than its high-flying customs: Papantla is the global cradle and origin of vanilla.

I drove four hours north of Xalapa along the Gulf Coast to Papantla — admiring the decaying majesty of its tropical vastness and curving, mountainous shoreline — to visit the historical ruins and learn about its contemporary tastes.

‘The city that perfumed the world’

Papantla, a town of 55,452 inhabitants according to national census data, was once the global leader in vanilla exports. From 1870 to 1910, the modest pueblo in Veracruz state — located on steep, labyrinthine roads in the middle of a tropical forest — became the epicenter for vanilla, one of the most expensive spices in the global market. Much of it was exported to Europe and the United States, and the region was dubbed “the city that perfumed the world” for the sweet, refreshing scent that vanilla emits.

Sadly, naturally grown vanilla from Papantla — which a researcher at UNAM designated as one of Mexico’s greatest contributions to global cuisine, along with cacao, amaranth, chile peppers and tomatoes — is no longer what it used to be. Nowadays, artificial vanilla dominates, and the market value of small-batch vanilla bean production from Papantla is nowhere near what it once was — in many ways a metaphor for the greater significance of Veracruz as a state.

The rise and fall of the vanilla trade

Historical documents reveal that vanilla cultivation dates back to the Totonac peoples, who gathered the fruit of orchid plants in surrounding areas before any other known society. Writing in her journal article “The History and Ecology of Vanilla,” Dr. Mariana Hernández Apolinar, a biologist and faculty member in UNAM’s science department, notes that for more than 200 years, “Mexico was the world’s only supplier of vanilla, bringing the country considerable profit.”

That declined in the mid-19th century when Europeans intervened. According to Hernández Apolinar, “it was discovered that vanilla flowers could be fertilized manually. This made it possible to produce the fruit on plantations outside its natural area and led to intensive vanilla cultivation in different tropical regions, making its production intensely commercial.”

Fast-forward to today, and the vanilla economy has been at risk for more than a decade. As NPR reported in 2019, local farmers have found themselves the target of robberies and violence at the hands of organized criminal gangs. In addition, a group of Mexican professors and biologists have outlined how issues of deforestation, soil erosion, shifting weather patterns and the marginalization of rural communities have negatively impacted modern vanilla productivity in the region.

At the same time, efforts to restore vanilla’s potential within the Mexican agricultural sector have been underway, including Papantla’s growing tourism sector.

Exploring ‘The Vanilla Route’

Originally known as “xanat” or “xanath” in the local dialect, the region upholds a proud legacy of vanilla. Vanilla tours are widely available, allowing visitors to tour nearby plantations that grow the spice. Family-owned shops abound, selling everything under the sun with an added touch of vanilla: ground coffee mixed with vanilla extract, vanilla-flavored cigarillos, vanilla sodas, horchata with vanilla, bottled vanilla concentrate, vanilla-scented candles, vanilla perfumes, vanilla liqueurs and more. Each shop explains the benefits and uses of its products. For example, vanilla’s aroma is considered an effective aromatherapy treatment for stress, while eating it is believed to offer digestive and anti-aging properties.

For a deeper immersion, there are excursions like “The Vanilla Route,” which spans two days of history and includes guided visits to the Xanath ecological park, a 54-acre plot of land that is preserved for sustainable vanilla growing, as well as a visit to a family-owned vanilla farm, where guests can witness firsthand how vanilla is turned into artisanal products.

Savoring local gastronomy

I made it a point to find as much local gastronomy as I could during my visit. I stayed at a small hotel with classical architecture dating back to the 18th century, less than a block away from the town’s main plaza, which stays abuzz at all hours and where street vendors sell goods and regional treats, such as homemade vanilla ice cream and atole morado, an iced, purple corn beverage to stave off the jungle’s humidity.

For breakfast, a trek up the nearby hillsides led to Saberes Ancestrales de la Vainilla, a family-owned business with two locations, one of which offers a vanilla museum and sweeping vista of the town. “Saberes” is the Spanish word for “knowledge,” and embodies the spirit of the restaurant and museum, which was founded to preserve the culinary essence of vanilla in its multitudinous forms.

Here, I began my self-guided tour of Papantla with a café de olla, a traditional coffee brewed in a clay pot and doused with natural vanilla, giving it a rich, natural sweetness to balance the drink’s dark bitterness.

Indigenous flavors and regional dishes

To eat, we had bocoles, a Huastecan dish featuring girthy tortillas made from bean or chicharrón masa stuffed with a protein of choice, as well as espolvoreadas de pipián, a lard-rubbed heap of thick tortillas, served in a pancake-style stack, and topped with ground pumpkin seed powder. The dish is simple, but in its simplicity, the orchestra of corn, pumpkin and oily grease is a representation of Mexico’s indigenous flavors without any unnecessary pomp.

The meal was so good that my family and I returned to Saberes Ancestrales de la Vainilla’s original location near our hotel in the main zócalo, where I ordered a chicken breast simmered in a smoky vanilla-pepper sauce. It was tangy and piquant, reminiscent of an American Southern barbecue dish, but in a tropical context.

For dinner, we visited Nakú, a restaurant named in honor of the Totonac word for “heart.” Its outdoor eatery offers tours and artisanal products, while highlighting an indigenous diet specific to northern Veracruz.

Art, history and unforgettable flavors

There are hard-to-find dishes like zacahuil, served on Sundays only, and pulaklh, which are regional varieties of tamales with ingredients such as sesame seeds and acoyo, popularly known as hoja santa. Other unique offerings include tachula xa talhtsi, a bowl of buttery beans coated with crumbled pumpkin seeds; liwa xalak kakwin, rabbit in a spicy al chiltepín salsa; and pollo en salsa de vainilla y pulque, chicken bathed in a chilpaya, pulque and vanilla sauce, served with steamed vegetables and a stack of espolvoreadas de pipián.

Any visit to Papantla and nearby Tajín should include more than vanilla. One highlight that may surprise tourists is the murals and work of Teodoro Cano García, a Papanteco sculptor, painter and muralist who was mentored by Diego Rivera and who gifted the town a massive mural depicting the historical evolution of the Totonac people in the town square, to go along with a monument of the voladores de Papantla.

An overlooked attraction

In addition, the small but impressive Teodoro Cano Museum offers a rare contemporary art space in the pueblo, housing his paintings alongside Totonac artifacts, and is open to the public for free. Regardless of interests, Papantla is a historically significant, if not overlooked, part of Veracruz’s — and Mexico’s — rich past, and remains a culturally informative, intensely flavorful visit that will not break your bank.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

Guatemala: Property & Tax

Key Facts — Decreto 18-2026 sets the IUSI property tax to zero on residential and mixed-use property. It was published in the official gazette on 28 August 2026.

It was published in the official gazette on 28 August 2026. — Commercial buildings keep paying , at three, six and nine per thousand across three value bands — the top rate bites above Q1 million, about US$131,161.

, at three, six and nine per thousand across three value bands — the top rate bites above Q1 million, about US$131,161. — The ban on cutting services over unpaid tax starts in late November 2026 ; the zero rate and the new commercial table take effect on 8 January 2027, with income-tax and stamp-duty changes dated 1 January 2027.

; the zero rate and the new commercial table take effect on 8 January 2027, with income-tax and stamp-duty changes dated 1 January 2027. — Registration duties remain. A zero rate does not remove your obligation to register the property with your municipality.

A zero rate does not remove your obligation to register the property with your municipality. — Individuals selling a property are exempted from the 10 percent capital-gains tax, and municipalities can no longer cut water, rubbish collection or street lighting over unpaid tax.

Guatemala has just scrapped the annual property tax on homes — including homes owned by foreigners. If you own, rent out, or are thinking of buying in Antigua, the capital or the lake country, here is what Decreto 18-2026 actually does, when it bites, and what does not change.

A colonial doorway in Antigua Guatemala, the country’s most popular address for foreign homeowners. From 8 January 2027, the annual IUSI property tax on homes drops to zero. (Photo: Rio Times archive)

What the decree actually changes

Guatemala’s Congress approved Decreto 18-2026 on 29 July 2026, amending Decreto 15-98, the Ley del Impuesto Único Sobre Inmuebles — the IUSI, the single annual tax on real estate collected by municipalities. President Bernardo Arévalo signed it on 28 August, and the Diario de Centro América published it the same day. Publication started every clock in the reform.

The headline: the IUSI rate on residential and mixed-use property is now zero. Mixed use covers a home with a small business attached, a common arrangement in Guatemala. Whatever your house is worth, the annual bill from the town hall disappears once the change takes effect.

Commercial property moves the other way. Buildings used for business pay three per thousand of assessed value up to Q500,000, about US$65,580; six per thousand up to Q1 million, about US$131,161; and nine per thousand above that. Conversions here use the Banco de Guatemala reference rate of Q7.62422 per dollar for 29 August.

The timetable now running

The gazette text staggers three clocks. The ban on conditioning municipal services on IUSI payment takes effect 60 days after publication, in late November 2026. The IUSI changes themselves — the zero rate for homes and the new commercial table — take effect 90 working days after publication, which Congress’s first secretary calculates as 8 January 2027; until then, owners must keep paying 2026 and prior-year bills under the old rules. The income-tax and stamp-duty changes are dated 1 January 2027.

Inside that window, four bodies must rebuild their systems: the municipalities, the finance ministry, the SAT tax agency and the cadastre directorate. Expect uneven implementation across 340 municipalities — some will update bills promptly, others will need chasing.

What foreign owners should do now

Keep your registration current. The zero rate removes the bill, not the registry: the duty to register the property with your municipality stays in force, and an unregistered property remains the classic source of fines and paperwork trouble at sale time.

If you are selling, the decree helps twice. Individuals are exempted from the 10 percent tax on the capital gain, effective 1 January 2027, removing a cost that used to be priced into every private sale. Combined with the zero IUSI, the carrying and exit costs of a Guatemalan home both fall.

If you own commercial space, budget the other way. A shop or office assessed above Q1 million moves to nine per thousand — the sharpest end of the new table. And if a municipality ever threatens to cut your water, rubbish collection or street lighting over a disputed bill, the decree now expressly bars that tactic.

Why the town halls are unhappy

Finance minister Jonathan Menkos puts the loss to municipalities at about Q1.2 billion a year, roughly US$157.4 million, and says the constitutional transfer formula cannot be reopened to replace it. The partial offset is a 3 percent stamp duty on second and subsequent property transfers, routed to municipalities through the SAT.

The impact is wildly uneven. An analysis by Icefi, the Central American fiscal studies institute, found 45 of 340 municipalities collected nothing at all in 2025 and reckons roughly 300 come out ahead once the stamp duty flows. Five heavy losers sit in and around the capital, where values are highest: Guatemala City, Mixco, Villa Nueva, Santa Catarina Pinula and San Miguel Petapa. The municipalities’ association, ANAM, has warned that local finances are at risk.

Could the courts stop it?

Objections are already on record. Icefi’s director called the law technically flawed and noted it passed without opinions from the finance ministry or the SAT; a development-foundation economist argues the different treatment of residential and commercial property could be unconstitutional.

One case is already at the Constitutional Court — filed by the Cabal caucus on 12 May 2026 — but it targets the original IUSI statute, not this decree. No separate action against Decreto 18-2026 itself has been reported. Plan on the reform taking effect, and treat any court surprise as exactly that.

When does Guatemala’s property tax on homes actually end?

The decree was published on 28 August 2026. The zero IUSI rate for residential and mixed-use property takes effect 90 working days later, on 8 January 2027 — until then, 2026 bills still stand. A ban on cutting municipal services over unpaid tax starts in late November 2026, and the new commercial rate table also begins on 8 January 2027.

Do foreign owners in Guatemala still pay the IUSI?

Once the change takes effect, no — the zero rate applies to residential and mixed-use property regardless of the owner’s nationality. What does not disappear is registration with the municipality. Commercial property keeps paying, at three, six and nine per thousand across value bands, with the top rate above Q1 million, about US$131,161.

What changes if I sell a property in Guatemala?

Individuals are exempted from the 10 percent tax on the capital gain. Municipalities, for their part, are barred from cutting water, rubbish collection or street lighting over unpaid tax — and a 3 percent stamp duty on second and subsequent transfers now flows to them through the SAT to offset their lost IUSI revenue.

Sources

Diario de Centro América — Decreto 18-2026, published 28 August 2026

Prensa Libre — timetable, municipal impact and reaction, August 2026

Icefi — municipal collection analysis, 2025 data

Banco de Guatemala — reference exchange rate Q7.62422 per US dollar, 29 August 2026

The Short Version In short: Your LatAm expat and nomad daily guide for Sunday, August 30. American Airlines relaunches Miami–Caracas on Thursday with two daily flights — the deepest US–Venezuela connectivity in a decade, under a Level 3 travel advisory. The Warsh repricing holds all weekend: Colombia’s TRM fixing stays at 3,202.79 through Monday, Brazil’s PTAX closed Friday at 5.2005 and Mexico’s FIX at 17.0427. Guatemala has scrapped its property tax on homes, and Peru marks Santa Rosa de Lima today. 01 The Caracas air bridge is back this week. American Airlines resumes nonstop Miami–Caracas service on Thursday 3 September with two daily rotations — an Envoy Air Embraer E175 and a mainline Boeing 737-8 — lifting weekly seats to 3,472 in both directions, 63 percent above the pre-suspension schedule, pending final government approval. Round trips were showing from about US$757. The US advisory sits at Level 3, Reconsider Travel, with Level 4 zones along the Colombian border and in several rural states. 02 Guatemala abolishes its property tax on homes. Decreto 18-2026, signed by President Arévalo and published in the official gazette on Friday, sets the IUSI rate at zero for residential and mixed-use property. Commercial buildings keep paying, at three, six and nine per thousand. The zero rate takes effect on 8 January 2027 — 2026 bills still stand — and municipalities lose about Q1.2 billion a year, roughly US$157.4 million. 03 The dollar’s week, frozen until Monday. Friday’s hawkish Fed repricing — September hike odds near 57 percent — is locked into the region’s weekend fixings: the TRM at 3,202.79 through Monday, the PTAX at 5.2005, the FIX at 17.0427. If you earn in dollars, this is the strongest conversion weekend in weeks; local earners feel the squeeze on anything priced in dollars. What changed since yesterdayGuatemala’s gazette published the decree zeroing the property tax on homes. American’s Thursday Caracas restart went on sale, with Laser joining in September and United due from Houston in January 2027. Colombia’s Council of Ministers met Saturday in Barranquilla with the COP 21.9 trillion cut, about US$6.8 billion, on the table; details are expected this week. Honduras’s lempira broke 27 per dollar for the first time. And Chile’s red alert is now precise: the communes of Colbún and San Clemente, around the spilling reservoir.

Good morning. Your LatAm expat nomad daily guide for the last Sunday of August opens at 35,000 feet, because the week’s most concrete expat story is a flight: from Thursday, you can book Miami to Caracas twice a day again.

Regional air capacity keeps rebuilding: American Airlines returns to Caracas on Thursday, and GOL restarts São Paulo–Caracas on 15 September. (File photo: The Rio Times archive)

01 Getting Around: Caracas Goes Twice Daily, Rio Goes to the Football

American Airlines resumes Miami–Caracas on Thursday 3 September with two daily rotations — one flown by Envoy Air with an Embraer E175, one by a mainline Boeing 737-8 — for 3,472 weekly seats in both directions. That is 63 percent more than the 2,128 planned before June’s earthquakes closed Maiquetía, and the increase still awaits final government approval. Launch-period round trips were showing from about US$757 on aa.com. Travelers displaced by the suspension can still reroute via Maracaibo, which has had daily Miami service since 14 July. Laser Airlines joins the route in September, United plans Houston–Caracas from January 2027, and JetBlue from Fort Lauderdale is expected to follow. Full practical brief — fares, advisories, insurance and health prep — in our Venezuela flights standalone.

Chile, Maule corridor: the Colbún reservoir spill continues, and SENAPRED’s red alert is now precisely defined — the communes of Colbún and San Clemente, raised from yellow after the 50 cubic-metres-per-second discharge ran past its initial six-hour forecast. Constitución’s mayor reported no river impact in the first hours, but access to the mitigation park is banned. Stay off riverbanks and fords, and follow SENAPRED bulletins only.

Rio today: the Metrô runs normal Sunday hours, 7 a.m. to 11 p.m., at R$7.90 a ride, about US$1.52 at Friday’s PTAX; the VLT in Centro runs on reduced Sunday frequency. The big movement is to the Maracanã: Flamengo x Botafogo at 4 p.m., free-to-air on TV Globo — expect the line 1 and 2 platforms around the stadium to be packed from 2 p.m.

Bolivia, overland: the San Pablo bridge blockade on the Trinidad–Santa Cruz corridor has produced conflicting reports since police moved on Thursday. The diesel decree stands, fuel queues persist, and fresh blockades remain possible with little notice. Build in slack for any long road trip.

02 Cost of Living & Money: The Weekend Freeze

With markets shut, everything prices off Friday’s fixings — and Friday was the day Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole keynote pushed September hike odds to about 57 percent. The two-year Treasury rose above 4.3 percent, the ten-year closed at 4.72 percent, the dollar index rose 0.50 percent to 99.65, and the S&P 500 slipped 0.25 percent to 7,711.76. For the region, that meant a firmer dollar across the board; the numbers below are the official references your cards, transfers and rents actually settle on through Monday.

Currency Reference in force today Note Argentina (ARS) Official 1,485 / 1,535; wholesale 1,503 / 1,512; blue 1,535 / 1,555; MEP about 1,544; CCL about 1,604; tarjeta about 1,996 Official rates stamped Friday evening; blue, MEP and CCL updated Saturday. Country risk last published at 512 basis points on 28 August, up from 509. Mexico (MXN) FIX 17.0427 (Friday) Back over 17, from 16.9712 on Thursday. Chile (CLP) UF 40,872.45 today; last dólar observado 925.25 The UF is worth about US$44.17 at the observado. Heavy rain hits the central valley today. Peru (PEN) SUNAT 3.348 / 3.356 for Sunday The region’s quiet currency, steady all week. Uruguay (UYU) Retail about 39.05 / 41.55 Saturday’s retail board. Colombia remains the story. A US$1,000 transfer converts to COP 3,202,790 at the weekend fixing; a COP 3,000,000 rent costs about US$937. The COLCAP fell 1.28 percent to 2,458 on Friday as the government put its COP 21.9 trillion spending cut, about US$6.8 billion, in front of Saturday’s Council of Ministers in Barranquilla — details are expected this week — and Ecopetrol’s 15 September assembly will replace six of nine board members.

Brazil. The PTAX closed the week at 5.2005. A US$1,000 transfer buys about R$5,200 at the fix, against R$5,151 on Monday; a R$5,000 rent now costs about US$961. The Ibovespa still rose 0.30 percent to 175,665 on Friday — an eighth straight daily gain — with the Selic at 14.00 percent since the 5 August cut. Second-quarter GDP lands Tuesday, the last big data point before Copom on 15–16 September.

Mexico. The FIX is back over 17 at 17.0427, so a MXN 10,000 month of co-working and lunches costs about US$587. UNAM’s new academic year starts Monday — expect the city’s rental and traffic rhythms to snap back to term mode.

Argentina. The wholesale dollar sits at 1,512 and the blue at 1,555; a US$100 card spend now bills at about ARS 199,550 on the tarjeta rate. Country risk ticked up to 512 basis points on Friday.

03 Visas, Residency & Tax

Where What changed What it means for you Guatemala Decreto 18-2026, published Friday, sets the IUSI property tax to zero on residential and mixed-use property; commercial buildings pay three, six and nine per thousand. Individuals are exempted from the 10 percent capital-gains tax on property sales, and municipalities can no longer cut water, rubbish or lighting over unpaid tax. If you own a home in Guatemala, the zero rate takes effect on 8 January 2027 — until then, 2026 bills still stand, and municipal registration duties remain permanent. Commercial landlords face a sharper top rate of nine per thousand above Q1 million, about US$131,161. Full brief in our Guatemala standalone. Venezuela The US State Department lowered Venezuela to Level 3: Reconsider Travel on 19 March 2026, under the post-Maduro interim government. Level 4, Do Not Travel, still applies to the 20-mile strip along the Colombian border, Amazonas, Apure, Aragua outside Maracay, rural Bolívar, Guárico and Táchira. Flights resume Thursday, but check your insurance first: the UK foreign office warns that travelling against advice can invalidate cover, and Canada still advises avoiding all travel. Malaria prevention is recommended; bring any medication you depend on. Colombia Standing deadline: the permanent-visa transfer under Resolución 9316 of 2024 must be done by 31 October 2026. The salvoconducto requirement has been dropped. Nine weeks left. Without the transfer, Migración Colombia will not issue your cédula de extranjería. Panama Standing window: the US$300,000 real-estate route to day-one permanent residence runs until 15 October 2026, after which the threshold rises to US$500,000. Six and a half weeks to file at the lower threshold. The difference is US$200,000.

04 The Week’s News in Brief

Guatemala. Beyond the zero rate, the IUSI decree routes a 3 percent stamp duty on second and subsequent property transfers to municipalities via the SAT, to offset part of the Q1.2 billion annual loss, about US$157.4 million. Icefi counts 45 of 340 municipalities that collected nothing in 2025 and reckons roughly 300 come out ahead; five heavy losers cluster in and around the capital, including Guatemala City, Mixco and Villa Nueva.

Venezuela. Beyond American, GOL restarts São Paulo–Caracas on 15 September, and Copa and LATAM have already returned to Maiquetía. The season offers the deepest US–Venezuela connectivity in a decade.

Honduras. The central bank’s selling price for the dollar reached L27.0010 on Friday — the first reading above 27. The lempira has slid 1.87 percent this year, but net international reserves stand at a record US$11.59 billion, and remittances reached US$7.69 billion between January and July.

Peru. Today is Santa Rosa de Lima, a national holiday — falling on a Sunday, so no long weekend. Banks and government offices reopen Monday.

Colombia. The Council of Ministers met Saturday in Barranquilla with the COP 21.9 trillion spending cut on the table; the finance ministry is expected to publish the details this week.

Chile. The Colbún spill continues under red alert in the two reservoir communes. The UF, the unit that prices rents and insurance, stands at 40,872.45 today, about US$44.17.

05 Weather & Safety

A warm, mostly dry Sunday in the southeast and a wet one in the Andes and Mexico. Rio de Janeiro is sunny and humid at 27°C with a 20 percent rain chance, green flags and water at 22°C; sunset is 5:41 p.m. São Paulo reaches 31°C with an 80 percent chance of rain today, easing to 40 percent on Monday. Buenos Aires is dry and cool at 18°C. Santiago is the outlier: rain is near-certain today, with a 74 percent chance lingering on Monday. Mexico City sees 23°C and a 49 percent shower chance today, turning heavy on Monday. Bogotá and Caracas are both near-certain wet at 19.5°C and 28°C. Lima stays dry at 24°C, and Guatemala City reaches 29°C with a 65 percent shower chance.

On safety, the live advisories are Chile’s red alert in Colbún and San Clemente — stay off the Maule riverbanks and fords — and Venezuela’s Level 3, with Level 4 zones listed above. Bolivia remains under the state of emergency declared on 20 June, which lets the military clear road blockades.

06 What’s On — 30 August to 1 September

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I book a flight to Caracas again, and should I? If you go, book flexible fares, arrange malaria prevention, and carry any medication you depend on. What does Guatemala’s property-tax change mean for foreign homeowners? Decreto 18-2026, published on 28 August, sets the IUSI property tax to zero for residential and mixed-use property; the zero rate takes effect on 8 January 2027. Registration with your municipality does not disappear with the bill. Commercial landlords move to a three-step scale of three, six and nine per thousand, with the top rate above Q1 million, about US$131,161. Individuals selling property are exempted from the 10 percent capital-gains tax. What is the dollar doing to my money this weekend? Friday’s hawkish Fed repricing is locked into the weekend fixings. Colombia’s TRM is 3,202.79 through Monday, so US$1,000 converts to COP 3,202,790. Brazil’s PTAX closed at 5.2005, so US$1,000 buys about R$5,200. World.title: Brazil’s Gripen F Makes Its First Flight With an Air Force Pilot Aboard
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · DEFENCE

Key Facts — First flight The Gripen F first flight ran 40 minutes from Linköping on 28 August 2026.

— Crew Saab’s Jakob Högberg flew with Brazilian Air Force test pilot Abdon de Rezende Vasconcelos.

— Order Brazil contracted 36 jets in 2014, 28 single-seat F-39E and eight two-seat F-39F.

— Budget The 2026 federal line for the programme is about R$2.1 billion (US$403.8 million).

— Schedule The last of the 36 aircraft is now due for delivery in 2032.

The Gripen F first flight opens a test campaign that must finish before the jet reaches Brazil.

Saab flew the two-seat Gripen F for the first time on Friday, with a Brazilian Air Force test pilot aboard. The sortie lasted 40 minutes from the company airfield at Linköping in Sweden.

A Gripen in flight. The two-seat Gripen F, built only at Linköping in Sweden, flew for the first time on Friday. Photo: Milan Nykodym, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Flickr.

What Saab confirmed about the Gripen F first flight

The aircraft took off at 09:40 local time and stayed airborne for 40 minutes, Saab said. The sortie checked the fighter’s core systems and its initial flight performance.

Saab chief test pilot Jakob Högberg flew the aircraft with Brazilian Air Force test pilot Lieutenant Colonel Abdon de Rezende Vasconcelos. The company did not publish the airframe’s registration, nor the altitudes and speeds flown.

No matching notice appeared on the Brazilian Ministry of Defence news pages on the day of the flight. Brazilian aviation titles carried the same departure time and the same two pilot names.

Cavok, a Brazilian aviation outlet, reported the same 09:40 departure and roughly 40 minutes aloft. It described the Gripen F first flight as the opening of a wider test campaign.

Saab’s release carries the reference CU 26-034 and links to video of the departure. It gives no serial number for the airframe, a detail Brazilian outlets also left out.

Why the two-seat version matters to Brazil

The Gripen F is the two-seat version of the single-seat Gripen E, built to Brazilian requirements. It shares sensors, avionics, mission systems, weapons and logistics with the aircraft already in service.

Saab says the second cockpit lets a crew divide the workload during complex missions. The rear seat can manage sensors, mission systems and weapons rather than simply carrying an instructor.

For the Air Force the aircraft shortens the path from a training aeroplane to a front-line fighter. Pilots convert on the same platform they will fly in combat, cutting the need for an interim jet.

Brazilian reporting says the two-seater drops the 27 millimetre Mauser cannon carried by the single-seat version. The space it occupies is needed for the systems that sit behind the second cockpit.

Where the F-39 programme stands today

Brazil signed with Saab in 2014 for 36 aircraft, 28 single-seat F-39E and eight two-seat F-39F. Saab announced the deal at 39.3 billion Swedish kronor (about US$4.05 billion at 2014 values).

Ten aircraft were in service by late 2025, with one more kept for test work in Brazil. The first jet assembled in the country, registered FAB 4109, was rolled out in March 2026 as the twelfth.

The single-seaters fly with the 1st Air Defence Group at Ala 2, the Anápolis wing in Goiás. That unit, known as the Jaguar Squadron, shares the base with Embraer KC-390 transport aircraft.

Sweden builds 13 single-seaters and all eight of the two-seaters, according to Brazilian trade reporting. The other 15 single-seat jets are assembled at Embraer’s plant in Gavião Peixoto, São Paulo.

The Air Force has already flown the type abroad, sending six F-39E jets across the Andes to Chile this year. That deployment, for the Salitre 2026 exercise, was the fighter’s first large multinational outing.

The Embraer assembly line at Gavião Peixoto

Gavião Peixoto holds the only Gripen production line outside Sweden, according to Saab’s own account. The site also hosts the Gripen design and development centre that opened there in 2016.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva attended the March rollout of the first Brazilian-built fighter. Defence Minister José Múcio Monteiro and the Air Force commander were also at the ceremony.

Saab counts more than 350 Brazilian engineers, technicians and pilots trained under the programme. Embraer, Akaer and AEL Sistemas work on structures, systems integration and onboard electronics.

The two-seat variant itself is built only in Sweden, so the Gripen F first flight was always going to happen there. Brazilian engineers nonetheless worked on its structure and on its systems.

Money, amendments and a schedule that slipped to 2032

The contract has been amended twelve times, the Air Force told senators in September 2025. The original plan closed deliveries in 2024, yet the last aircraft is now due only in 2032.

Air Force chief of staff Walcyr Josué de Castilho Araújo told the committee that budgets fell short of the contract. He set out one delivery in 2026, four in 2027 and five in 2028.

The 2026 federal budget carries about R$2.1 billion (US$403.8 million) for the fighter programme. Roughly R$800 million (US$153.8 million) of that sum was blocked under this year’s fiscal squeeze.

Both conversions use the Banco Central do Brasil PTAX selling rate of R$5.2005 to the dollar on 28 August 2026. PTAX is the central bank’s official daily reference rate for the real.

The Air Force extended the life of its Northrop F-5 fleet to cover the gap left by the delays. Those older jets reached 50 years of Brazilian service during 2025.

When Brazil expects to fly the aircraft at home

Saab says the aircraft now enters production acceptance flights, then a step-by-step expansion of its flight envelope. Speed, altitude, G-load and angle of attack limits will be cleared in stages.

Rear cockpit functions and the tactical capabilities specific to the two-seater will be assessed in parallel. The campaign runs from the company’s flight test centre in Sweden.

An Air Force briefing in April 2026 put the arrival of the first two-seater in Brazil in 2028. The Gripen F first flight therefore opens a test phase lasting roughly two years.

Once it arrives, the Air Force plans to move pilots straight from the A-29 Super Tucano to the Gripen. That would remove the need for an intermediate lead-in fighter trainer aeroplane.

A possible second batch of twenty aircraft

Embraer and Saab signed a head of agreement in July 2026 to study building 20 more Gripen fighters. The work would go to Gavião Peixoto, complementing the existing line at Linköping.

The companies stressed that nothing is ordered until the Air Force signs a further contract amendment. Such a deal would take the Brazilian fleet to 56 aircraft.

The Air Force has told Congress that 36 fighters are not enough for a country of continental size. It puts the operational requirement at 66 aircraft.

For now the Gripen F first flight is the programme’s clearest step forward in a difficult budget year. Delivery to Brazil, and any second batch, both remain some way off.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where did the Gripen F first flight take place? It took place on 28 August 2026 at Saab’s airfield in Linköping, Sweden. The aircraft took off at 09:40 local time and flew for 40 minutes. Who was in the cockpit for the flight? Saab chief test pilot Jakob Högberg flew with Brazilian Air Force test pilot Lieutenant Colonel Abdon de Rezende Vasconcelos. Saab did not publish the aircraft’s registration. How many Gripen fighters has Brazil ordered and received? Brazil contracted 36 aircraft in 2014, 28 single-seat and eight two-seat. Ten were in service by late 2025, plus one more kept for testing.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief — Sunday, August 30, 2026
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro — Sunday opens with warm sun, light rain risk and a beach-ready breeze — ideal for a long shoreline morning.

The city slows down, so pair a free museum run in Centro with an early dinner as locals do.

The business mood is cautious after a hawkish Jackson Hole message; the board carries the exact settle.

It is the day for a slow wander through Rio’s monumental centre, followed by sea air.

Ipanema in the sun, with the Dois Irmãos peaks behind — Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief for Sunday, August 30, 2026. Photo: Christian Haugen, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr.

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — CENTRO CULTURAL LOOP A free, air-conditioned art morning where the city began Start at Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil on Rua Primeiro de Março, open 9am to 8pm and free. Walk ten minutes to Museu Nacional de Belas Artes on Avenida Rio Branco, open 10am to 6pm and free. From there, stroll to Paço Imperial on Praça XV, open noon to 6pm with free entry. Take the VLT or Metrô to Cinelândia; the whole loop is walkable and flat. This route gives you three serious art stops in one morning without spending a real.

OUTDOORS — SEA WALL AND SAND The shoreline afternoon that resets a long week After lunch, head to Ipanema or Copacabana for a late beach session. The sun is out, water temperature sits near 22°C, and waves stay small enough for easy swimming. The seafront ciclovia is open; rent a bike near Posto 9 and ride toward Arpoador before sunset.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — SOUTH ZONE Two laptop-friendly rooms for a slow Sunday Coffee Five in Ipanema opens early with good wifi and a calm upstairs table. Curto Café in Centro is a better fit if you stay near the museums; it is open on Sundays with strong espresso and fewer crowds. Both have reliable connections for light work, though Sunday hours can shorten in the late afternoon.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — LAPA NIGHT AIR A grittier, music-first alternative to the beach Skip the sand and cross to Lapa for an early evening walk under the Arcos. Bar Antigamente stays open Sunday with samba circles and cold beer. It is livelier after 7pm; go with a local friend and watch your phone on the street.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Early dinner, Botafogo boardwalk, then home before Monday Reserve a table at Comuna in Botafogo for burgers and craft beer before 8pm. Alternatively, Fogo de Chão in Botafogo serves a full rodízio for a proper Sunday feast. Walk the Botafogo waterfront afterwards; it stays busy and well-lit until late.

ALSO ON TODAY Parque Madureira riverside walk — Parque Madureira, Zona Norte — free, from 8am, easy cycling and running paths Jardim Botânico — Rua Jardim Botânico, 920 — 8am to 5pm, R$40 residents / R$80 foreigners Museu de Arte do Rio — Praça Mauá — 11am to 6pm, R$20, free on Tuesdays Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil — Rua Primeiro de Março, Centro — 9am to 8pm, free Arpoador sunset — Ipanema — around 5:30pm, free, arrive early for the rock

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô lines 1, 2 and 4 run normally on Sunday from 7am to 11pm. Single journey costs R$7.90.

The VLT is running in Centro with reduced Sunday frequency; check the Carioca station board before boarding.

If rain appears in the afternoon, ride-hailing fares may surge near the beach exits.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Try Cais do Oriente in Centro for a refined weekend lunch near the museums. Or grab a quick, honest plate at Bar Luiz on Rua da Carioca for under R$80.

Dinner: Book Comuna in Botafogo for burgers and local craft beer. For a long Brazilian feast, Fogo de Chão in Botafogo serves rodízio until late.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a light layer for air-conditioned museums and a water bottle for the afternoon walk.

Cards and Pix are widely accepted; keep R$60 in small notes for beach vendors and tips.

After dark, stay on the main streets in Lapa and Centro. Avoid the side alleys alone, especially after 9pm.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Digital nomads meet at Coffee Five in Ipanema on Sunday mornings for a quiet work hour.

Newcomers often join the weekly beach volleyball game at Posto 9 in Ipanema after 4pm — show up with water and introduce yourself.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

Flamengo host Botafogo at the Maracanã at 4pm today — a Rio derby that doubles as a title-race test for the visitors’ pursuit of leaders Palmeiras.

Fluminense are on the road at Athletico-PR at 11am. For tickets and last-minute entry rules, check the club channels this morning.

Watching in a bar? The Maracanã area fills early; in the South Zone, Bar do Adão in Botafogo and the waterfront bars are the usual spots.

If you want noise and a screen tonight, head to any bar on Rua Dias Ferreira in Ipanema.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The week ended with global risk assets on the back foot after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh held firm on the 2% inflation target at Jackson Hole.

His message pushed Treasury yields higher and cooled stocks, gold and several Latin American markets.

Local investors still found support in large Brazilian blue chips, leaving the Ibovespa with an eighth straight daily gain.

The coming week turns to US payrolls and any fresh sign of how hawkish the Fed will stay into September.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SUN 30 — Warm and partly cloudy; free Centro museum loop in the morning MON 31 — Dry and 28°C; good day for Jardim Botânico before work TUE 1 — Humid, 29°C; MAR free entry day in Praça Mauá WED 2 — Hotter, 31°C, afternoon rain possible; indoor plans in the afternoon THU 3 — Still warm; check midweek football fixtures if you want a live match

Background: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 29, 2026.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief — Saturday, August 29, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is it safe to visit Centro museums on a Sunday?

Yes, the main museum corridor around Cinelândia, Praça XV and Praça Mauá is busy and policed on Sunday afternoons. Stay on the main streets, avoid empty side alleys, and you will be fine.

Do I need cash or Pix for the beach and small cafés?

Pix is now the default for most small purchases, but beach vendors still prefer cash. Keep R$60 in small notes for water, coconuts and quick snacks.

What is actually open tonight after 7pm?

Restaurants and bars in Botafogo, Ipanema and Leblon stay open late on Sunday. Lapa starts later and feels busier after 8pm, but go with a local if you can.

TODAY’S PICK — FREE CULTURE Museum Sunday: Língua Portuguesa free, MASP and Pinacoteca worth the ticket Start at MASP on Avenida Paulista in Bela Vista. It opens at 10am and today is a paid day at R$85, with online booking recommended — free entry is on Tuesdays. The permanent collection of European masters hangs on glass easels, but the Brazilian modernists upstairs are the real reason to go. From Paulista, ride the metro Line 2 from Trianon-Masp to Paraíso, change to Line 1-Blue and get off at Luz. Pinacoteca’s grand brick building is a two-minute walk, opens at 10am and charges R$40 today — free entry is on Saturdays and the second Sunday of each month. Its soaring central hall and Brazilian 19th-century painting collection are unforgettable. Finish at Museu da Língua Portuguesa inside Estação da Luz, a two-minute walk away. Entry is free today — Sundays are its free day — and the interactive exhibits on Brazilian Portuguese feel more like a playground than a museum. It closes at 4:30pm, so aim to arrive by 2pm. All three sit on metro Lines 1 and 2. A single journey is R$5.40. The two paid tickets add about R$125; with metro, coffee and a pastel the day still lands under R$200. You will walk a lot, so wear soft shoes. This trio is the best culture day in the city. It covers Paulista avenue energy, historic Luz architecture and language as living art. You finish by 4pm, leaving time for the park or an early dinner.

OUTDOORS — PARK LIFE Ibirapuera at golden hour, then the lake path Parque Ibirapuera opens at 5am and stays open until midnight. The sweet spot is 4pm to 6pm, when the light turns golden and runners, cyclists and families fill the paths. Entry is free. Rent a shared bike via an app or just walk the loop around the lake. The Japanese pavilion area is quieter than the main entrances. MAC USP inside the park is free and open until 9pm on Sundays. This is the best outdoor reset for a Sunday. Bring water, wear sunscreen and expect crowds near the main gate.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — VILA MADALENA Slow wifi, strong coffee and a Sunday that actually works Coffee Lab on Rua Fradique Coutinho in Pinheiros is the city’s most serious coffee bar. This time of year the cold brew is excellent and the laptop-friendly tables fill up by 11am. Expect to spend R$18 to R$25 on a drink. For a quieter corner, try Sofá Café on Rua Harmonia in Vila Madalena. It has solid wifi, small tables and a calm Sunday crowd. It opens at 9am and is a good base before the street gets busy. Both are walking distance from the Vila Madalena metro station. Bring a charger and expect to share a table if you arrive after midday.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — CENTRO HISTÓRICO Mercadão, Farol Santander and a different São Paulo Skip Paulista and head to Centro instead. Mercado Municipal opens at 6am on Sundays and closes at 4pm. Go early for a mortadella sandwich or pastel de bacalhau upstairs. Entry is free. Then walk ten minutes to Farol Santander on Rua João Brícola. It opens at 9am and costs R$45. The 360-degree viewing deck from the 26th floor is the best skyline view in the city. This is grittier and busier than the west zone. It feels like old São Paulo. Go with a charged phone and keep your bag in front of you.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Samba in Vila Madalena, pizza in Pinheiros Vila Madalena wakes up late on Sundays. Head to Bar Salve Jorge on Rua Aspicuelta after 7pm for cold beer, feijoada and live samba that spills onto the street. Arrive early for a table. Nearby, Posto 6 on Rua Aspicuelta serves excellent petiscos and stays lively until late. It is less crowded than Salve Jorge and has better caipirinhas. For dinner, head to Pinheiros and try Bráz Pizzaria on Rua Grajaú. It opens until 11pm on Sundays and the margherita is around R$70. Book ahead or wait at the bar. The whole area is safe and walkable after dark on a Sunday. Keep your phone in your pocket on the busy bar streets.

ALSO ON TODAY MASP — Avenida Paulista, Bela Vista — 10am-6pm, R$85 today (free Tuesdays), European and Brazilian collections Pinacoteca de São Paulo — Praça da Luz, Luz — 10am-6pm, R$40 today (free Saturdays and second Sunday of the month), grand halls and Brazilian masters Museu da Língua Portuguesa — free — Praça da Luz, Luz — 9am-4:30pm, free today, interactive language exhibits Ibirapuera park walk — Ibirapuera — 5am-midnight, free, lake loop and golden hour light Mercado Municipal — Rua da Cantareira, Centro — 6am-4pm, free entry, mortadella sandwich and pastel stalls Farol Santander viewing deck — Rua João Brícola, Centro — 9am-8pm, R$45, 360° skyline view

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

The metro runs a Sunday timetable from around 4:40am to midnight. Single journey is R$5.40. Lines 1-Blue, 2-Green and 4-Yellow connect the main Sunday spots: Paulista, Luz, Pinheiros and Vila Madalena.

There is no rodízio on Sundays, so all license plates can circulate freely all day. Ride apps are plentiful and cheaper on Sunday mornings. Traffic builds after 5pm around Ibirapuera and the bar streets of Vila Madalena.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: At Mercadão, get the famous mortadella sandwich at Hocca Bar or the pastel de bacalhau from a stall upstairs. Budget R$35 to R$50. If you stay near Paulista, try Casa do Porco in Centro — expect a queue and around R$60 for the set lunch.

Dinner: For pizza, Bráz Pizzaria in Pinheiros is the city classic — R$70 a pizza, open until 11pm. For a meatier Sunday dinner, Fogo de Chão in Itaim Bibi does rodízio from around R$150, but book ahead.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a reusable water bottle and sunscreen — the sun is strong through 4pm and museum queues mean standing outside. Most places accept Pix and cards, but keep R$60 in cash for market stalls and street food.

Museu da Língua Portuguesa is free today, so its queue forms early — arrive 15 minutes before opening. MASP and Pinacoteca charge entry on Sundays, which keeps their lines shorter.

In Centro around Mercadão and Farol Santander, keep your phone and wallet in your front pocket and be aware of your surroundings. It is busier on Sundays but still a pickpocket zone.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

For expats and digital nomads, the Sunday morning run club in Ibirapuera starts near Portão 7 at 8am. It is a friendly mixed group and a good way to meet people without a formal event.

Check Internations and Meetup for Sunday board-game meetups in Vila Madalena or English-language samba nights in Pinheiros. The Café des Arts community board in Pinheiros often lists Sunday language exchanges.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

It is a big football Sunday in the city: Corinthians host Santos at Neo Química Arena in Itaquera at 4pm, the Alvinegro derby with Neymar confirmed to start for the visitors.

League leaders Palmeiras visit Mirassol at 6:30pm, while São Paulo FC are not in action today. Tickets for the derby were sold online only, with facial-recognition entry at the arena.

For watching on TV, try O’Malleys in Itaim Bibi or Blue Pub in Pinheiros. Both show Brazilian and European games and have a full Sunday crowd. Heading to Itaquera instead? Take metro Line 3-Red to Corinthians-Itaquera and arrive early.

The Libertadores quarter-finals start on September 8, with Corinthians and Palmeiras both still in the bracket. Plan ahead if you want tickets.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Markets were closed on Saturday and remain shut today, so Friday’s session stands as the week’s close. The mood among professionals is still cautious about US interest rates staying higher for longer.

The story behind the mood: a stronger dollar and firmer US Treasury yields put pressure on Latin American assets on Friday. Brazil’s main equity benchmark bucked the regional trend, which signals continued foreign interest in Brazilian stocks.

Ahead: Monday brings a fresh week of trading and any weekend policy headlines will set the tone. Keep an eye on the US dollar’s trajectory against the real — it shapes import costs and local inflation expectations.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SUN 30 — Sunny, 27°C. Free museums, Ibirapuera walk, samba in Vila Madalena tonight MON 31 — Warm, 28°C, mostly dry. Good day for a Paulista avenue work-from-café session TUE 1 — Still 29°C and dry. Last fully outdoor day before midweek change WED 2 — 26°C with 40% rain chance. Move plans indoors — Pinacoteca or MASP are smarter bets THU 3 — Chance of lingering showers. Check weekend fixtures and plan Saturday football viewing

Background: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 29, 2026.

Background: São Paulo Daily Brief — Saturday, August 29, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Which museums are actually free on a Sunday in São Paulo?

Museu da Língua Portuguesa is free on Sundays and open 9am-4:30pm. MAM, the modern art museum inside Ibirapuera, is also free on Sundays. MASP and Pinacoteca are paid on Sundays: MASP costs R$85 (free on Tuesdays) and Pinacoteca R$40 (free on Saturdays and the second Sunday of the month). MAC USP inside Ibirapuera is always free and open 10am-9pm on Sundays. Farol Santander is not free either — it costs R$45 and opens at 9am.

Is public transport running normally today?

Yes. The metro runs a Sunday timetable from around 4:40am to midnight. A single journey is R$5.40 and you can pay with a contactless card or bilhete único. There is no rodízio on Sundays, so cars with any plate can drive all day. Ride apps are readily available and cheaper before 5pm.

What can I do on a Sunday night if I don’t drink much?

Walk the calm side of Ibirapuera after dark — the main loop is well lit and safe until 10pm. The park officially closes at midnight. For food without a bar scene, go to Pinheiros for pizza at Bráz or an early dinner at any of the restaurants on Rua dos Pinheiros. They stay open to 11pm on Sundays.
