World.title: Danish Fund Buys Control of Moroccan Logistics Leader Globex
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Morocco · LOGISTICS & INVESTMENT

Key Facts — Deal Two A.P. Moller Capital funds signed an agreement on 17 August to buy a majority stake in Globex Investissement, a leading Moroccan logistics company. The price and the size of the stake were not disclosed.

— Target Casablanca-based Globex was founded in 1998 as the exclusive FedEx Express licensee in Morocco and employs more than 350 people.

— Continuity Founder and chief executive Omar El Kadiri will stay on, leading the business with his existing management team.

— Hurdle Completion needs merger-control clearance from Morocco’s Competition Council.

The investment arm of the Danish group behind Maersk is buying control of Morocco’s best-known independent logistics network, six months after setting up a dedicated Moroccan fund.

A.P. Moller Capital said on 17 August that two of its funds had signed an agreement to acquire a majority stake in Globex Investissement, a leading Moroccan logistics company. Neither the size of the stake nor the price was disclosed.

The deal is the first big move by a Morocco-only fund the Danish investor set up in February. It lands as the country consolidates its position as North Africa’s main logistics hub.

Container cranes at Tanger Med, the Moroccan port complex that handled more than 11 million containers last year. (Photo: NAC, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What was agreed

The buyers are the Emerging Markets Infrastructure Fund II, known as EMIF II, and the APM Capital Morocco Fund. Together they will take the majority holding and form a partnership with Omar El Kadiri, Globex’s founder and chief executive, who stays in place.

Completion is subject to the usual conditions, including merger-control clearance by the Moroccan Competition Council. Until that lands, the acquisition is agreed but not closed.

Kim Fejfer, the chief executive of A.P. Moller Capital, said the investment aligns directly with the firm’s core sector and geographic focus. He called Morocco a market that is rapidly developing into the leading North African logistics hub, supported by strong economic tailwinds.

What Globex actually does

Globex was founded in Casablanca in 1998 as the exclusive FedEx Express licensee in Morocco. That means it runs the American courier’s brand, pickups and deliveries in the country under licence.

The company now employs more than 350 people and works across express delivery, road freight, freight forwarding, customs brokerage and warehousing. It also holds FedEx and TNT licences in Senegal and Cameroon, and uses the FedEx network to serve more than 220 countries.

The private equity firm Amethis bought a 30.5 per cent stake in 2022 to fund expansion in Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa. A.P. Moller Capital did not say whether Amethis will sell as part of the new transaction.

Who the buyer is

A.P. Moller Capital is a Copenhagen-based institutional fund manager within A.P. Moller Holding, the Møller family holding company that also controls the shipping group A.P. Moller-Maersk. It manages infrastructure funds focused on transportation, logistics and the energy transition in emerging markets.

Its Moroccan arm, APM Capital Morocco S.A., is regulated by the country’s capital-market authority, the AMMC, and led by chief executive Ghislane Guedira. She said the combination of the Danish firm’s sector heritage and Globex’s management team would strengthen the company’s market position.

A fund raised just for this

The APM Capital Morocco Fund was established in February 2026, backed by leading Moroccan institutional investors. Its mandate is transport and logistics, with a pipeline spanning international express, third-party logistics, air cargo handling and cold storage.

The fund raised 1.6 billion dirhams (about US$178 million) in commitments, and EMIF II committed a further 600 million dirhams (about US$65 million) alongside it. That gives the two vehicles 2.2 billion dirhams (about US$243 million) to deploy, at roughly nine dirhams to the dollar.

Why Morocco, why now

The anchor is Tanger Med, the port complex on the Strait of Gibraltar that is the largest in Africa and the Mediterranean. Its four container terminals handled more than 11.1 million containers in 2025, up 8.4 per cent on the year, and 161 million tonnes of cargo overall.

A second Mediterranean deep-sea port, Nador West Med, is due to start operating in the last quarter of this year. Between them, the ports feed the automotive plants, run by Renault and Stellantis, that have made vehicles Morocco’s biggest export.

Under its new owners, Globex is meant to become a green logistics leader, with solar-powered hubs, an electric fleet and carbon reporting tools. The seller side is moving too: A.P. Moller Capital has separately agreed to sell its 49 per cent of grain-terminal operator Mass Céréales al Maghreb to the investors STOA and Africa50.

What to watch

The first marker is the Competition Council’s clearance, the only named obstacle between signing and completion. The second is whether Amethis stays in the shareholding or exits.

Beyond that, the fund’s own pipeline suggests more Moroccan deals in cold storage and air cargo. For a country selling itself as the logistics doorway between Europe and Africa, Danish money arriving at this scale is itself the story.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is A.P. Moller Capital part of Maersk? Not directly. It is the fund-management arm of A.P. Moller Holding, the family holding company that also controls the Maersk shipping group, so the two are sister businesses under the same owner. How much is the Globex deal worth? The price and the exact stake were not disclosed. The two buying funds hold about US$243 million in committed capital between them. What does Globex do? It is FedEx’s exclusive express licensee in Morocco, and also works in road freight, freight forwarding, customs brokerage and warehousing. It holds FedEx and TNT licences in Senegal and Cameroon as well. What still needs to happen before completion? The deal needs merger-control clearance from Morocco’s Competition Council, plus other customary conditions. Founder Omar El Kadiri stays on as chief executive either way.

World.title: Nigeria Tells Atiku the Land Borders Are Already Open
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

NIGERIA · POLITICS & TRADE

Key Facts —The rebuttal: Nigeria’s presidency says the country’s land borders are already open, dismissing a 2027 campaign pledge by opposition candidate Atiku Abubakar to “open the borders.” —Who said it: Sunday Dare, President Bola Tinubu’s special adviser on media, in a State House statement dated 28 August titled “Atiku and the Borders: Nigerians Deserve Facts, Not Campaign Slogans.” —The record: Most land borders were reopened on 14 March 2024, the statement says, and in February 2026 customs reopened the Kamba and Tsamiya corridors in Kebbi State on Tinubu’s directive. —The jab: Dare called Atiku “unhinged” and argued that an open border is not an uncontrolled border. —The backdrop: The late President Muhammadu Buhari shut Nigeria’s land borders in 2019-2020 to fight smuggling, squeezing trade with Benin, Niger, Cameroon and Chad.

Nigeria’s presidency says the country’s land borders are already open, rejecting a campaign promise by 2027 opposition candidate Atiku Abubakar to reopen them. The unusually sharp rebuttal turns one of Nigeria’s oldest economic grievances into an early election battleground.

What the presidency actually said

“The facts are straightforward: Nigeria’s land borders are already open,” the State House said in a statement issued on Friday, 28 August. It said the government announced the reopening of most of the country’s land borders on 14 March 2024 and has not reversed that position.

The statement, signed by media adviser Sunday Dare, also cited the Kamba border in Kebbi State, which it said President Tinubu opened in February 2026 “with attendant economic and diplomatic gains.” Customs officers formally reopened the Kamba and Tsamiya corridors that month, freeing about 2,000 trucks stranded at the frontier with Benin and Niger.

Then came the attack. “Atiku is unhinged now, and he would say or announce anything to attract and deceive the politically gullible,” Dare wrote, adding: “An open border is not an uncontrolled border.”

The statement leaned on security to make its case. Citing the Global Terrorism Index 2026, it said about 41 per cent of terrorist attacks occur within 50 kilometres of an international border and 64 per cent within 100 kilometres, arguing that troops on Nigeria’s northern corridors reflect border security, not closed borders.

What Atiku promised

Atiku Abubakar, a former vice president who won the African Democratic Congress presidential primary in May, has made border trade a plank of his 2027 campaign. He pledged to reopen any land borders still shut and to ease the importation and movement of goods.

He argues that border closures forced many businesses to shut down and deepened insecurity. He has also promised to develop seaports in Nigeria’s south, where the dominance of Lagos harbours has long been a grievance for coastal states such as Akwa Ibom and Bayelsa.

His claim has a kernel of truth. The presidency itself says only that “most” borders were reopened in 2024, leaving open the question of which crossings remain restricted and why.

How the borders became a campaign issue

In August 2019 the late President Muhammadu Buhari closed Nigeria’s land borders, saying rampant smuggling of rice, fuel and other goods was undercutting local producers. The blockade lasted about 16 months and strained relations with Benin and Niger, whose economies depend heavily on trade with their giant neighbour.

Abuja began unwinding the closure in December 2020, reopening four major posts: Seme on the Benin corridor, Illela and Maigatari toward Niger, and Mfum toward Cameroon. A phased reopening followed, and on 14 March 2024 the Tinubu administration announced that most remaining land borders were open again.

The Kebbi corridors are the newest chapter. Customs area controller Mahmud Matawalle-Ibrahim said the Kamba and Tsamiya posts reopened in February on presidential approval, after talks with Benin to let legitimate cargo move through to Niger’s Tunga Jado border.

Why it matters beyond the campaign

Nigeria’s frontiers with Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon carry one of Africa’s densest flows of informal trade, from petrol and rice to livestock and textiles. Seme, west of Lagos, is among the busiest land crossings in West Africa.

Open and predictable borders are also the backbone of Nigeria’s commitments under the African Continental Free Trade Area, the pact meant to create a single market across the continent. Every closure undercuts Abuja’s claim to leadership of that project.

Customs Comptroller-General Bashir Adeniyi has framed the recent reopenings as economic diplomacy: regulated crossings, the service argues, give better oversight and intelligence than closures that push trade into smugglers’ hands.

What is still unverified

Neither side has published a definitive list of which crossings remain restricted. Traders’ groups have long reported that some posts operate with de facto limits even after formal reopening, and the presidency’s “most borders” phrasing does not settle that.

The terrorism statistics are quoted from the presidency’s own statement and were not independently checked against the Global Terrorism Index 2026 report. Atiku’s camp had not responded to the “unhinged” remark at the time of writing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Nigeria’s land borders open right now? The presidency says yes, pointing to a 14 March 2024 decision reopening most land borders and the February 2026 reopening of the Kamba and Tsamiya corridors in Kebbi State. Opposition candidate Atiku Abubakar says some crossings remain shut, and neither side has published a full list. What did Atiku Abubakar promise about the borders? The ADC presidential candidate pledged to reopen any land borders still closed and ease the movement of goods if elected in 2027. He says past closures killed businesses and worsened insecurity, and he has also promised to develop seaports outside Lagos. When did Nigeria close its land borders? President Muhammadu Buhari closed them in August 2019 to fight smuggling. Reopening began in December 2020 at four posts, including Seme and Mfum, and the Tinubu administration announced that most borders were open again on 14 March 2024. What is the Kamba border? Kamba is a crossing in Kebbi State, northwest Nigeria, linking the country to Benin and, via the Tsamiya corridor, to Niger. Customs reopened it in February 2026 on President Tinubu’s directive, releasing about 2,000 stranded trucks.

World.title: Turkish Arms Ship Freed Off Somalia as Rescue Accounts Clash
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Somalia · MARITIME SECURITY

Key Facts — Seizure Eight armed men seized the Cameroon-flagged MV LUTUF on 17 August, about 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district.

— Crew The ten people aboard were six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards.

— Release Somalia’s defense ministry said a joint Somali-Turkish operation freed the ship on 29 August and killed 14 alleged pirates. Puntland’s security ministry says the pirates left after a ransom was paid.

— Context Before the release, the International Maritime Organization said six merchant ships and more than 90 seafarers were being held in the region.

A cargo ship carrying Turkish military equipment is free after twelve days off Somalia’s Puntland coast, but the two governments involved tell sharply different stories about how.

Somalia’s defense ministry said on 29 August that Somali and Turkish forces had freed the MV LUTUF, the Cameroon-flagged cargo ship held by pirates off the Puntland coast since 17 August. It said the operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four of their boats.

Puntland, the semi-autonomous region where the ship was held, immediately rejected that account. Its security ministry said no military operation took place and that the pirates left voluntarily after being paid.

A skiff carrying pirates leaves a hijacked merchant ship off Somalia during an earlier seizure, under naval observation. (Photo: US Navy, Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Jason R. Zalasky, via Wikimedia Commons)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

What Mogadishu says happened

The federal defense ministry said the vessel and its crew were freed in a joint operation by the Somali army and the Turkish navy that lasted ten days. It said the remaining pirates fled the vessel, allowing the forces to take control of the ship.

The operation was conducted under a defense cooperation agreement between Somalia and Turkey aimed at strengthening maritime security, protecting Somalia’s coastline and combating piracy, the ministry said. Turkey is one of Somalia’s closest security partners and trains thousands of Somali soldiers.

The ministry gave no details about casualties among its own forces or the well-being of the crew. Abdullahi Warsame, a local elder from the Jiifle community in the Godob Jiiraan district where the vessel was held, told the Associated Press that the vessel and its crew had been freed.

The hijacking itself

The LUTUF was seized on Monday 17 August, about 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district, a Somali official told the Associated Press. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, the Royal Navy’s shipping-alert desk, said eight armed individuals boarded the vessel and took control of it.

The ship, owned by Polar Movement Shipping, was sailing from Turkey toward Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. Its cargo was weapons, communications and satellite equipment bound for TURKSOM, the Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu that is Ankara’s largest overseas base.

The ten-member crew comprised six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards. Neither the Indian nor the Turkish authorities made any public statement while the ship was held.

The eight pirates were believed to belong to the same group that seized the merchant vessel Sward on 26 April. They steered the LUTUF toward the coast near Garmaal, in Puntland’s Dangoroyo district on the Nugaal shore.

Puntland tells a different story

Puntland’s Ministry of Security rejected the military-rescue account outright. It said the pirates freed the LUTUF voluntarily after receiving the ransom they had demanded.

The ministry said the payment was facilitated by members of the federal government, who it said had been in phone contact with the pirates since the day of the hijacking. Local media and journalists in Puntland put the ransom at US$2.5 million; earlier unconfirmed reports of the pirates’ demand had cited about US$2 million.

Puntland’s government condemned any ransom payment, warning that it risks emboldening pirates and undermining efforts to combat piracy along Somalia’s coast. Turkish authorities have not commented publicly on either version of the release.

The strike that killed four men

On 18 August, a day after the hijacking, a small boat delivered khat, a stimulant widely chewed in Somalia, to the held vessel. After the boat returned to shore, an airstrike hit the area, killing four men and wounding two.

The Associated Press could not establish who carried out the strike or whether the dead had any connection to the pirates. Turkish naval vessels, helicopters and drones had been reported monitoring the area, but Ankara has never publicly confirmed a strike on Somali territory.

Puntland says the dead were fishermen, and its president, Saeed Abdullahi Deni, accused Ankara of killing civilians in strikes on 18 and 20 August. Garmaal held burials for the men, and former foreign minister Abdisaed Muse Ali called the killings a brutal act of aggression by Turkey.

A piracy season like the old days

The LUTUF was the fifth merchant ship seized off Somalia since April, and not the last. Three days after it was taken, six armed men boarded the tanker Seamull about 136 nautical miles east of Mukalla in Yemen and diverted it toward Somalia.

That prompted the International Maritime Organization, the United Nations shipping agency, to warn that six vessels were being held in the region: the Honour 25, taken on 21 April; the Sward, on 26 April; the Eureka, on 2 May; the Asana, on 17 July; the LUTUF; and the Seamull. Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said more than 90 seafarers were captive and demanded their immediate release.

The resurgence has coincided with heavier traffic along the Somali coast. Security threats in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz have pushed carriers to reroute through the western Indian Ocean, putting more ships within reach of pirate groups operating from the shore.

What to watch now

The first open question is the crew. Ten men, most of them Indian, spent twelve days in pirate hands, and no government has yet confirmed their condition or where the LUTUF will be taken.

The second is money. If a ransom was paid, as Puntland insists, negotiators will have handed the region’s pirate networks fresh funding at the very moment the world’s navies are stretched between the Gulf of Aden and the Gulf.

Five of the six ships on the maritime agency’s list, and their crews, remain in pirate hands tonight. The LUTUF’s release, however it was bought, is the exception in this season, not the rule.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where exactly was the LUTUF hijacked? About 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district on 17 August. The pirates then moved the ship to the Nugaal coast near Garmaal, where it was held until 29 August. Was a ransom paid for the ship? That is disputed. Somalia’s defense ministry says a joint Somali-Turkish military operation freed the vessel, while Puntland’s security ministry and local media say a ransom of about US$2.5 million was paid. Turkey has not commented on either account. Who are the crew, and are they safe? Ten people: six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards. A local elder said the crew was freed with the ship, but no government has officially confirmed their condition. Is piracy off Somalia getting worse? Yes. Six merchant vessels were seized between April and August, and the International Maritime Organization counts more than 90 seafarers held hostage, the worst spell of Somali piracy in about a decade.

World.title: Belize stays hot and mostly dry this Sunday
World.content:
Belize stays hot and mostly dry this Sunday

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Warm and relatively dry conditions prevail over Belize today, according to the National Meteorological Service.

Expect sunny skies with a few cloudy intervals through the day and partly cloudy skies tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with a low chance of a few more over southern Toledo tonight.

Inland temperatures will reach 95 degrees Fahrenheit before dropping to 74 overnight. The coast reaches 90 with a low of 82, while the hills stay at 82 and fall to 68.

At sea, easterly winds will blow at 5 to 15 knots with a light chop and waves of 2 to 4 feet.

Monday and Monday night will continue mainly fair and warm with isolated shower activity.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

Sunrise was at 5:38am and sunset comes at 6:07pm.

The forecast was issued at 6am by forecaster Derrick Rudon.

World.title: You will be dead much longer than you will be tired, the Sunday arithmetic
World.content:
You will be dead much longer than you will be tired, the Sunday arithmetic

By Horace Palacio:

A line has been circulating this week, dressed in the name of Alexander the Great.

You will be dead much longer than you will be tired.

Did Alexander actually say it? Honesty first, as always in this column. No ancient historian records the sentence, and it carries the fingerprints of the internet, which loves to lend its best lines to famous corpses. But for once, the internet mailed the quote to the correct address. Because whether or not the words are his, no life in recorded history argues them harder.

Consider the record. A young man inherits a small kingdom at twenty. By thirty two he has marched an army more than twenty thousand miles, from Greece to the edge of India, never once losing a battle, founding cities from Egypt to Afghanistan that carry his name to this day. He fought at the front, not the rear. At one siege in India an arrow went through his chest into his lung, and the man got up and kept campaigning. Plutarch records that Alexander said it was sleep that reminded him he was mortal. Tiredness, to him, was weather. You do not negotiate with weather. You march through it.

Now sit with the sentence itself, because it is really a piece of arithmetic, and arithmetic is this column’s love language.

How long will you be tired? Tonight, perhaps. This season, maybe. Tiredness is a visitor. It arrives, it sits heavily, and it always, always leaves, usually by morning, sometimes by Monday, occasionally by next year.

How long will you be dead? Forever. Not a long time. Forever. Every year that has ever passed and every year that will ever come, stacked end to end, and then eternity after that. Death is not a visitor. Death is the address.

So the sentence is simply asking you to compare the two durations before you make any permanent decision based on the temporary one. And yet, look around Belize, and listen to the national anthem we actually sing daily. Mi tired.

Let me be careful here, because this column has spent a year honoring Belizean tiredness, and I will not insult it now. The mother working the hotel shift and the market stall, whose month is longer than her money, she is not the target of this sermon. She is its proof. She wakes exhausted every single morning and rises anyway. She has been living Alexander’s arithmetic her whole life without a meme to tell her so. Salute her.

No, the sentence aims at something else entirely. It aims at the dreams we execute with fatigue as the weapon. The business never registered, because mi tired. The course abandoned at module three. The field never planted. The application never sent. The apology never made, the book never opened, the savings circle never started. Ask the honest question, Belize. How many of our unlived lives were cancelled not by failure, not by enemies, not by lack of talent, but by a feeling that would have passed by Thursday?

We keep signing permanent resignations with temporary ink.

Now, the double edge, because this column never sells half a story, and Alexander’s own life carries the correction inside it.

Two facts about the undefeated general. First, the only force that ever beat him was tiredness itself, just not his own. At a river in India called the Hyphasis, his soldiers, eight years and twenty thousand miles from home, refused to take another step. The man who had conquered the known world stood before his own exhausted army, and lost. The mutiny of the weary turned him around. And second, he was dead at thirty two, burned through, feverish in Babylon, a torch that consumed itself entirely.

So hold both truths, because together they make the whole lesson. Tiredness must never cancel your purpose. And unmanaged fire consumes the torch. The sentence was never an instruction to skip sleep. Even Alexander slept, he simply never stopped. The instruction is finer than that. Rest, fully, nightly, guiltlessly, and never once resign. Rest is a pit stop. Quitting is a destination. The tragedy is not the Belizean who takes Sunday off. The tragedy is the one who mistook a Sunday feeling for a final answer.

Which gives us the practical tool, in the tradition of this column’s tests. Call it the tired-or-done test, and run it any night the towel feels ready to be thrown. Ask one question. Am I tired, or am I done? Tired needs a bed. Done needs a decision. And here is the iron rule that comes with the test. Decisions are never to be signed by fatigue. Never quit at night. Sleep first, and let the morning cast the deciding vote, because the morning has never once agreed with midnight.

And remember the ledger this column opened months ago, the one about your forty seconds on the radio. In the grave, understand, you will finally receive every hour of rest you ever skipped, refunded in full, with interest, and eternity added. Death is scrupulously fair about rest. It repays all of it. What death never refunds, not one, is a chance. The naps come back. The openings do not.

One last widening of the lens, because you know this column never leaves the nation out. Belize itself is tired. Tired of blackouts, tired of prices, tired of the same arguments in new jerseys. Fine. A tired country is entitled to sigh. It is not entitled to resign. Everything on this year’s blueprint, the scorecards, the megawatts, the classrooms, the ledgers, waits on the far side of a nation that decides its exhaustion is a visitor and not an address.

So here is your Sunday arithmetic, Belize, whoever first did the math.

Tonight, you will be tired for perhaps eight hours.

You will be dead for the rest of eternity, and eternity keeps no office hours and grants no appeals.

The tomb has already reserved your eternal rest, fully paid, no booking required.

Until it calls, there is light left, and work worth doing in it.

Sleep well tonight.

Rise anyway tomorrow.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.
