(Header image: Solar panels cover the mountains in Anshun, Guizhou province, Aug. 4, 2024.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018941/After ‘Sleep No More,’ What’s Next for Chinese Immersive Theater?
World.title: After ‘Sleep No More,’ What’s Next for Chinese Immersive Theater?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018941/After ‘Sleep No More,’ What’s Next for Chinese Immersive Theater?
World.content:
After 2,670 performances, the immersive theatrical production “Sleep No More,” co-produced by Shanghai Media Group and pioneering British theater company Punchdrunk, will conclude its 10-year run at the McKinnon Hotel in Shanghai on Aug. 30.

When it opened in Shanghai a decade ago, the production wowed local theatergoers with its novelty and impact. Audience members donned white masks and entered a dimly lit building where they could move freely between rooms: following Macbeth, searching for the witches, or wandering the corridors piecing together clues. No one could see the complete story, but “missing out” was part of the experience.

A decade on, immersive theater has blossomed across China, appearing in theaters, scenic areas, museums, shopping malls, and former factories. There are even purpose-built theatrical theme parks. “Unique Henan,” for example, in the suburbs of Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, features 21 performance spaces and nearly 1,000 actors performing almost 700 minutes of material each day. Visitors can spend an entire day exploring the park and still see only a fraction of what it offers. Meanwhile, “Unique Dream of Red Mansions” in Langfang, in the northern Hebei province, takes the classic Chinese novel “Dream of the Red Chamber” as its theme, with four large theaters, eight smaller ones, and 108 interconnected immersive spaces. Its daily performances total more than 800 minutes.

Was all this brought about by “Sleep No More”? Yes and no.

In traditional theater, the theatrical world is confined to the other side of the stage, while the audience sits in darkness and watches a carefully framed reality. This model came under scrutiny in the 20th century. Avant-garde theater pioneers, including Antonin Artaud, Jerzy Grotowski, Peter Brook, and Richard Schechner, reexamined the body, space, presence, and the relationship between audiences and performers. Schechner, in particular, developed the concept of “environmental theater,” emphasizing that a theatrical event encompasses not only performers and text but also the audience, sensory stimuli, architecture, and other elements of the performance space. Modern theater has since continued to seek ways to move audiences beyond fixed seats and into cities, rivers, markets, and historical settings, making space part of the work itself.

Such practices are nothing new in Chinese theater. From 1932 to 1937, playwright Xiong Foxi went to Ding County in Hebei as part of a movement to popularize theater in rural China. His productions integrated stage scenery with the real sky and surrounding forest, while audiences crossed the fourth wall to participate directly in the performance.

Since the early 2000s, director Wang Chaoge’s pioneering “Impression” and “Encore” series have reshaped the spatial aesthetics of China’s cultural tourism performances through large-scale live productions. They took theater beyond the proscenium arch and into outdoor landscapes, familiarizing audiences with expansive, panoramic, and interactive performances. “Encore Pingyao,” which premiered in 2013 in Pingyao, in the northern Shanxi province, went further by dispensing with the traditional stage entirely. Audiences walked through streets, courtyards, and indoor spaces alongside the actors.

“Sleep No More” was therefore by no means the starting point for immersive theater in China. Long before its arrival, Chinese audiences were already familiar with shared spaces, physical participation, and collective rituals. Nevertheless, it marked an important watershed. It gave Chinese theater practitioners an internationally influential model: a mature, replicable, sustainable, and long-running production. By combining free movement, multiple narratives, repeat viewings, and word-of-mouth recommendations, it demonstrated that audiences were willing to pay for highly personalized live experiences.

Before “Sleep No More,” even China’s grandest immersive productions were generally guided by their creators, with audiences moving through history as a group. It gave individuals greater agency, allowing each person to follow different characters and leave with an incomplete but unique story. These approaches represent two important strands in Chinese immersive theater: one emphasizes group movement, local history, and collective memory, while the other focuses on individual choice, free exploration, and fragmented narratives. Both, however, make the performance environment part of the show, place audiences and performers in the same space and time, and allow them to experience together a theatrical event unfolding “here and now.”

Over the past decade, many Chinese productions have emerged between these two approaches. Theater has moved beyond the traditional stage into public squares and parks, forests and lakesides, warehouses and factories, and historical sites. Its forms range from parades in theme parks and rituals at village temple fairs to farmers singing together in fields or an individual quietly grieving in a museum before onlookers.

Chinese immersive theater has not simply imitated “Sleep No More.” Instead, it has converged with China’s established traditions of live performance, experiential theater, and cultural tourism, gradually forming a distinctly local style. At destinations such as “Unique Henan” and “Unique Dream of Red Mansions,” theater has expanded from a single work into an entire cultural attraction. Productions of different scales and formats coexist, while architecture, landscapes, dining, and travel all become part of the experience.

This form of theater draws on China’s rich resources of local history, classic literature, and cultural heritage, while also being closely linked to urban renewal, scenic-area development, and destination tourism. Compared with Western immersive productions, which tend to emphasize individual exploration and unfamiliar experiences, Chinese productions more often combine historical resources, collective viewing, and large-scale spaces.

Yet the proliferation of such productions has also exposed problems. A bigger space does not necessarily mean deeper immersion. Enormous scale can accommodate more narratives, but it can also allow architectural spectacle to overshadow the drama. Likewise, local culture can provide rich material, but it can also be compressed into a handful of easily recognizable symbols.

Now that “immersive” has become a ubiquitous cultural label, perhaps we theater practitioners need to reconsider a fundamental question: Why do we need immersion?

Immersion is not the purpose of theater, but a way of establishing a relationship between the audience and the work. It shortens not only the physical distance between audiences and performers but also the psychological distance between audiences and characters, environments, history, and real-life situations. Audiences should enter a theatrical space for the novelty of “being there” as well as to better understand the characters’ environment, the pressures they face, and why they make particular choices at a particular time and place. Physical presence is only the starting point. Meaningful immersion moves from presence to understanding, and then to empathy, identification, or reflection.

As the boundaries of spatial spectacle continue to expand, the future value of immersive theater in China should not be measured by architectural scale or technological sophistication. Instead, it should be judged by whether it can transform space into narrative and the audience’s presence into understanding.

At its best, immersive theater is not about temporarily transporting audiences to another world but about ensuring that the characters, history, and culture they encounter remain with them after they leave, creating connections with their own lives. In this sense, even as “Sleep No More” ends its Shanghai run, its influence on contemporary Chinese theater will continue.

(Header image: A promotional image for “Sleep No More.”From @SleepNoMore上海 on Shanghai)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018953/Hundreds Still Missing After Deadly China-Nepal Border Mudslide
World.title: Hundreds Still Missing After Deadly China-Nepal Border Mudslide
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018953/Hundreds Still Missing After Deadly China-Nepal Border Mudslide
World.content:
On Monday, Zhao Jianing rode his motorcycle through the Gyirong border checkpoint under clear skies, inching past export trucks and lines of BYD vehicles as traffic backed up along the China-Nepal border. He recalled seeing at least a dozen uniformed workers at their posts.

Two days later, a massive surge of water, mud, and debris descended from the Nepali side of the Himalayas and tore through the border area at around 11 a.m. Wednesday. Funneled through a steep valley toward southwestern China’s Xizang Autonomous Region, the torrent swept away police posts and buried the Gyirong checkpoint.

Surveillance footage from outside the checkpoint showed muddy floodwaters surging above the border gates and engulfing the area within seconds as people fled. Aerial footage from state broadcaster CCTV later showed the border zone blanketed in mud, with no buildings visible.

By Thursday, three people had been confirmed dead and 558 remained missing in Gyirong County on the Chinese side, while two people had been rescued. Across the affected area, at least 273 people were dead and 1,384 remained missing.

China’s Ministry of Water Resources told CCTV that a landslide dam had formed upstream, creating a lake containing an estimated 2 million cubic meters of water. The lake was already overflowing, and another 3 million cubic meters were expected to channel into it over the next three days, raising the risk that the dam could fail.

The threat further complicated rescue efforts already hampered by damaged roads and communications infrastructure.

Xizang activated its highest-level emergency response, deploying military transport aircraft, more than 800 firefighters, and armed police officers to the area. Central authorities also allocated 220 million yuan ($30.7 million) for disaster relief, recovery, and reconstruction.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived in the mudslide-hit area of Gyirong Township on Thursday to oversee rescue and relief efforts, state news agency Xinhua reported. He visited on behalf of President Xi Jinping and met rescue workers and people displaced by the disaster.

Wang Qian, an official with the Shigatse military sub-command, told CCTV that the edge of the mudslide was about 2.5 kilometers from the Gyirong checkpoint, where mud was nearly 1.5 meters deep.

Gyirong is Xizang’s largest land port and a major gateway for trade and travel between China and Nepal. As of June 23, the checkpoint had recorded more than 100,000 entries and exits this year, up 12.85% from the same period in 2025.

Crossing into Nepal two days earlier, Zhao, a 26-year-old motorcyclist from Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, remembered the checkpoint as busy but ordinary, with clear skies, lines of export vehicles, and workers directing traffic.

One of those workers, a uniformed man Zhao estimated to be in his 30s, had briefly argued with him over his speed.

After seeing footage of police posts being swept away, Zhao said he kept thinking about the encounter. “I never imagined that just one or two days later, everything would be gone,” Zhao told Sixth Tone. “It happened so fast. I think he probably had no chance to escape. I feel really guilty and upset.”

The road on the Nepalese side beyond the checkpoint was extremely difficult to navigate, he said. In some places, the mud was “as deep as half the length of an arm,” he said, forcing him to use both feet to keep the motorcycle moving. His shoes even came off.

“The cliff was on the right and the muddy road was on the left. I could barely ride. I thought I was going to die there,” he said.

No official investigation has established the cause of Wednesday’s disaster, but several experts said preliminary evidence points to a possible high-altitude ice-rock avalanche originating from a tributary of the Donglin Tsangpo River in Nepal.

Fan Xuanmei, director of the State Key Laboratory of Geohazard Prevention and Geoenvironment Protection at Chengdu University of Technology, told Southern Weekly that a high-altitude mass of ice and rock may have destabilized and collapsed before rapidly descending into the valley.

As it moved downstream, the mass could have mixed with water and scraped loose material from the valley floor, Fan said, expanding into a much larger flood and mudslide. Such a mechanism would differ from a conventional glacial-lake outburst flood.

The terrain may have amplified the destruction. Yi Shaoliang, an expert at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development based in Nepal, said the enormous volume of water may have struck hard rock formations on the opposite side of the Lhende River, generating powerful turbulence and redirecting the flow toward buildings at the Chinese checkpoint, according to Southern Weekly.

The border corridor has faced destructive flooding before. In July 2025, a flood destroyed the Friendship Bridge linking China’s Gyirong Port with Rasuwa Fort in Nepal. Research across the Himalayan region has linked warming to expanding glacial lakes and greater instability in high mountain environments, though experts cautioned that Wednesday’s disaster may have followed a different mechanism.

Kang Shichang, director of the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Chengdu, told domestic media that if an upstream ice-rock avalanche were detected quickly enough, downstream communities could theoretically receive about 20 minutes of warning.

In the remote Himalayan valleys around Gyirong, however, limited monitoring and the speed of such events can leave little time between detection and disaster.

Additional reporting: Jiang Xinyi; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A landslide-dammed lake near Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, Aug. 27, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018944/Eye of the Storm: Viral Podcaster Breaks Silence Over Plagiarism Scandal
World.title: Eye of the Storm: Viral Podcaster Breaks Silence Over Plagiarism Scandal
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018944/Eye of the Storm: Viral Podcaster Breaks Silence Over Plagiarism Scandal
World.content:
“Every time fishermen head out to sea, they have to face the uncertainty of the ocean. When a storm hits — you can only head back to port.”

Zhuge Yiyang, an essayist and podcaster better known online as Zhong Shu, stares lost in thought from the pier at Jiaoshan Fishing Port Town, part of Wenling City in the eastern Zhejiang province.

Facing her own storm, she’s returned home.

In early August, the 29-year-old rode a wave of global fame after a viral interview with British-American filmmaker Christopher Nolan about his latest blockbuster, “The Odyssey.” Yet things quickly came crashing down when she was accused of plagiarism, sparking widespread criticism.

In the wake of the controversy, almost all of Zhuge’s public appearances in China were canceled. Yet on Aug. 18, she agreed to meet with reporters from Jiefang Daily in her hometown, taking in the alleyways, docks, and fish markets she frequented as a child.

In her own words

Zhuge has released three episodes of her hit podcast “Monologues of a Committed Observer” since the plagiarism accusations emerged, discussing Shakespeare and Plutarch. The show has more than 970,000 subscribers on the Chinese podcast platform Xiaoyuzhou.

While she acknowledges that she draws on media reports and international podcasts, she firmly denies copying any content.

“When I talk about the Canadian election, for example, I’ll read reports from the American and Canadian media, and compile that information into an episode. I’m not a journalist,” says Zhuge, who is currently studying toward a Ph.D. in political philosophy at Boston College in the United States. “A lot of my information I get from listening to overseas podcasts.”

Yet the claims against her have drawn intense public scrutiny. On Aug. 19, business news outlet Caixin removed from its website a recent column Zhuge wrote on universities dealing with student use of artificial intelligence. This came after several online users remarked on the column’s similarity to a piece published in The Atlantic magazine in May. (Editor’s note: Sixth Tone can verify that the first two paragraphs published on Caixin closely match The Atlantic’s first two, as well as parts of its third.)

Until now, Zhuge has refused to respond publicly to the plagiarism accusations, preferring instead not to get involved in the “maelstrom of online harassment.”

“I don’t know how to respond. … There’s no point in trying to clarify things at a moment like this,” she says. “People have claimed that I stay up every night deleting comments. I haven’t deleted a single comment. I do want to find out who is really behind all this, who is pulling the strings, but there’s simply nothing I can do.”

For her most recent podcasts, Zhuge says she wrote the script on a plane, without referring to any materials. But when the episodes were released, people began claiming that specific passages had been plagiarized.

“Some people have set up a website that lays out what they claim are examples of ‘article spinning,’ word by word. I’ve looked at it. The English and Chinese don’t match; not a single example is a word-for-word translation,” she says. “There are some passages from sources that I haven’t even read, and they don’t correspond to the material they are being compared with.”

(Sixth Tone has listened to several episodes highlighted on the website and noted multiple instances where Zhuge’s scripts closely match content from overseas podcasts. In not all instances does she credit her source.)

“Once this started circulating online, my comment section began getting hundreds of comments every hour, many of them mentioning this website,” Zhuge adds. “This is the storm I’m going through.”

So is that why most of her upcoming public appearances have been canceled?

“That has nothing to do with any of the conjecture,” she insists. “I canceled (the events) a long time ago, but the organizers only announced it recently. These events had already been called off before this wave of controversy.

“Some of my elderly relatives aren’t in good health, and with the controversy surrounding me online, I’ve also been feeling emotionally drained. So I wanted to come back and spend more time with them.”

Humble beginnings

Zhuge is no stranger to criticism. In the past, she’s been branded arrogant and condescending, particularly for repeatedly calling Wenling “uncultured” on her podcast.

However, she insists the term isn’t derogatory, but rather an objective fact. With a strong tradition in commerce, the people of Wenling are more interested in pursuing wealth than reading or academic pursuits, she says. As a result, being “uncultured” is inevitable.

“When I was growing up, there was only one Xinhua Bookstore (a state-owned chain), and almost everything it sold was study materials,” Zhuge recalls.

She says speaking bluntly is also common among Wenling people. Her grandmother, for example, alternates between telling her she is “as fat as a pig” and “as skinny as a refugee.” She believes this way of speaking has influenced her own manner of expression, making her come across at times as blunt or even offensive.

“People in big cities wouldn’t talk like this, but no one here thinks there’s anything wrong with it — it’s simply the truth.”

After finishing elementary school, Zhuge left Wenling for a boarding school in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang. She later completed high school and university in the U.S., when she eventually began her career as a translator, writer, and podcaster.

She often refers to herself as a “small-town girl,” yet critics argue that Zhuge uses her background as a “shield” to justify her arrogance, saying that her “manufactured persona” hardly fits with someone who attended the elite Groton School in Massachusetts, U.S.

“I don’t think coming from a small city is something to be ashamed of,” Zhuge says, “nor do I think it means you’ve overcome some kind of hardship or that you have to prove something to people from big cities.”

However, her origins did have an impact when she arrived at Groton at age 15. The few Chinese students at the school were from first-tier cities like Beijing and Shanghai. Through them, Zhuge says she was exposed to an “elite discourse” she had never encountered before.

“I’ve never deliberately constructed any persona, but I know that there’s been a change — not intentional; my circumstances were simply different back then,” she says.

Zhuge was living in the U.S. when she first rose to prominence on Zhihu, China’s Quora-like platform, writing on political theory. Later, she began posting on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, about the meals she cooked for her husband and the books they were reading, as well as podcasting about her academic research.

“Then I went through a divorce, racked up a large amount of legal fees, and spent a period living a fairly miserable life,” she says. “At this point, the narrative online changed, and I became this ‘strong, independent woman.’ But I still cook, I still enjoy cleaning, I still post about sports. I’m still very happy — the only difference is that I no longer have a husband.”

But after her interview with Nolan went viral, Zhuge says she no longer felt as comfortable posting about her daily life, as it could be easily misinterpreted.

“For example, my father has a softshell turtle, and we often visit the nearby stream to catch fish and shrimp to feed it. I’d posted about that before, only now people were saying I was trying to construct a persona,” she says. “There seems to be a stereotype about intellectuals — people think it’s OK for me to hold events in big cities, but I shouldn’t go back to my hometown. But that’s my life.”

What lies ahead

Standing by the Jiaoshan pier, Zhuge begins reminiscing about her childhood. She would often visit the harbor with her parents on weekends, sometimes sailing out on a small fishing boat.

Today, the dock is dominated by larger, more advanced vessels. Yet the fishermen must still brave the same rough sea, never knowing whether they will return with a lucrative haul or be forced back to shore by high winds.

For Zhuge, this is the fundamental element of coastal life: You never know what will come — you can only eat what there is to eat.

“That’s what life by the sea is like. When the winds and waves come, you can’t go out to sea, and you never know when a storm will hit,” she says. “When I was going through my divorce, that’s how I comforted myself: this is just the stormy sea of life.”

The legal proceedings in 2024 consumed a great deal of time, money, and energy, affecting her Ph.D. studies. It was around this time that she began podcasting more frequently.

“I wanted to speak out on a public platform, and a podcast is a place where you can talk for 40 minutes and still be well listened to,” Zhuge says, adding that she has no interest in fame or wealth — she simply eats what there is to eat. “If I wanted to make money, I definitely wouldn’t be podcasting.”

However, the popularity of “Monologues of a Committed Observer” has helped her foster connections with Chinese media outlets and publishers, eventually leading to her being asked to translate works by the philosophers Hannah Arendt, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and Plutarch. The income has alleviated some of the financial burden from her divorce.

In the face of the online storm, she is now considering whether to halt the podcast entirely. “I’m seriously considering giving it up,” Zhuge says. “Maybe tomorrow I’ll decide I’m done, and quit. I don’t have a team, so I don’t have to force myself to keep going. That’s my advantage here.”

Reported by Yu Liang, Zhu Lingjun, and Zhou Liya.

A version of this article originally appeared in Jiefang Daily. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from Zhou Liya and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018948/Who Let the Dogs In? Chinese Universities Open Dorms to Pets
World.title: Who Let the Dogs In? Chinese Universities Open Dorms to Pets
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018948/Who Let the Dogs In? Chinese Universities Open Dorms to Pets
World.content:
A growing number of Chinese universities are allowing student pets both on campus and in university dormitories, drawing online support and sparking sharp debate over the safety, equity, and cost of campus pet ownership.

This past weekend, both Shanghai Lida University and Kunming City University in the southwestern Yunnan province announced on their official WeChat accounts that they would now allow student pets on campus. At least five other universities across China — mostly private institutions with pet-related programs — have also rolled out similar policies since Monday.

Previously, Chinese universities did not allow pets in dorms or on campus — not even to visit. With the recent policy shifts, that is now changing.

The new policies come amid China’s booming pet industry and the advancement of related professional training and services. According to the 2026 China Pet Industry White Paper, the consumer market for dogs and cats in urban areas reached 312.6 billion yuan ($43.2 billion) in 2025, up roughly 4% from the previous year. The market is expected to surpass 400 billion yuan by 2028.

On Saturday, Kunming City University announced that students can now bring dogs, cats, rabbits, hamsters, and legally permitted exotic pets to campus. Banned dog breeds — such as pit bulls and Rottweilers — and “pets that pose health risks” are not allowed, however.

The university plans to roll out pet-friendly dormitories, a pet daycare center, and partner with professional institutions to establish an on-campus pet health station. Faculty and students from the university’s School of Pet Technology will also regularly offer free pet health checkups and consultation services, the university said.

Campus-wide amenities will include waste bags, water stations, and fenced play areas, with most outdoor spaces except cafeterias open to pets. Per-semester pet registration and vaccine checks will also be implemented.

A dedicated fund will support stray animal rescue and student volunteer work, while “pet companionship therapy” will be available to help students relieve stress.

Online, users hotly contested the new policies, with supporters arguing that pets provide important emotional comfort for students far away from home, helping to alleviate loneliness and stress in academic and daily life. Many voiced approval of the universities’ detailed regulations, such as providing centralized pet care facilities and pet-friendly dormitories separate from other student housing.

Others questioned whether the new policies would infringe on other students’ rights, pointing to issues such as allergies, noise, and safety.

A university student in Shanghai who had previously secretly kept a cat in her dormitory told Sixth Tone that the new rules — which require pets to be housed in dedicated pet-boarding facilities and ban them from dorms — are “no different from not being allowed to keep a cat at all.”

Her roommate, surnamed Chen, instead called the new policy a “very loving move” that shows the school is “warm and humane.”

“While it doesn’t meet most people’s needs, I think it’s a good first step that will spark discussion and encourage other schools to follow suit and make better policies in the future,” she told Sixth Tone.

Wu Qi, founder of Shanghai-based animal therapy nonprofit Paw for Heal, said the core challenge of keeping pets on campus is balancing companionship needs with public safety and collective rights.

“(Universities need to) respect (pet owners’) companionship needs while protecting students with allergies or a fear of animals,” he told Sixth Tone.

Wu advised restricting pets on campus to certain zones and recommended implementing a registration system so that students bear responsibility in the event of pet-related disputes. He also recommended that universities have clear protocols for removing animals when necessary.

He noted, however, that owning a pet as a university student has its own educational value, teaching responsibility and pet knowledge, while also cultivating empathy.



Additional reporting: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018940/Underground No More: China’s ‘History Fangirls’ Stand Up
World.title: Underground No More: China’s ‘History Fangirls’ Stand Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018940/Underground No More: China’s ‘History Fangirls’ Stand Up
World.content:
“Serve the dead as one serves the living.”

This principle has shaped Chinese funeral and ancestral rites for over two millennia. Traditionally, it meant visiting tombs with food and wine and burning joss paper or paper effigies to honor the deceased. In recent years, however, some rather unexpected offerings have started appearing at the burial sites of famous historical figures.

For example, visitors to the tomb of Guo Rong, also known as Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou (r. 951–960), have left offerings of Beijing soil. A copy of a book on child psychology was discovered at the grave of Zhang Juzheng, a high official during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). And custodians of the tomb of Cao Cao, a warlord during the Three Kingdoms period (220–280), have been inundated with ibuprofen packets — one of which was accompanied by a heartfelt instruction: “General Cao, these are to help with your migraines. Take half a tablet when the pain strikes.”

These unconventional offerings may seem absurd, but each one has a story behind it. For example, it is well known in China that Cao Cao suffered from persistent headaches. And Guo Rong fell ill and died during an expedition north to reclaim lost territory, so well-wishers now bring the north to him. Meanwhile, the book on children’s psychology left for Zhang Juzheng was a more tongue-in-cheek offering. After serving for 10 years as a stern tutor and father figure to a young emperor, Zhang was posthumously stripped of all titles, ranks, and property by the ruler he’d helped raise. Perhaps a more modern approach could have helped him navigate their power imbalance.

In every case, however, the offerings centered on some aspect of the deceased’s life — a well-known habit, a historical anecdote, or an unfulfilled ambition. And they were all carried out by members of an unlikely, yet increasingly popular subculture in China: shitong nü, or “history fangirls.”

The shitong nü movement has its roots in fanfiction — specifically Japanese doujin — but with a focus on history instead of pop culture. But unlike historical fiction, which tends to ask what historical figures did or might have done, history fangirls are often more interested in who they were: who they loved, how they behaved, what they might have said to a friend, or what it would have been like to know them.

The result is something that closely resembles modern fandom culture, but instead of young singers or movie stars, fans fixate on people who’ve been dead for centuries, if not longer.

Members of the community are not blind to these parallels. Indeed, they will sometimes jokingly describe themselves as fans of “underground idols” — a term taken from the Japanese “chika aidoru,” referring to idol groups that have yet to break into the mainstream. This Japanese loanword has taken on an additional layer of meaning in China: Since the people being admired are six feet under, they are quite literally underground idols.

The ways in which these enthusiasts relate to historical figures generally fall into two categories. The first are “solo stans,” who focus all their time and energy on a single celebrity. Some even become what is known as a “dream girl,” imagining romantic relationships with their favorite historical figure through various kinds of fan-made works.

The other major type are “shippers,” who invent emotional relationships between two or more historical figures.

These two categories are not exclusive. For example, a history fangirl might have a favorite emperor, while also being deeply invested in imagining his close relationship with one of his generals.

As for why, to many history fangirls, historical figures are the ideal subjects for the emotional investment required by contemporary fandom. Loving a living celebrity comes with a certain amount of risk, since there will inevitably be a gap between the carefully curated public image and the real individual. Even fictional characters are at the mercy of their creators, who may do or say something that fans find unacceptable.

Historical figures, however, are different. Their lives have already been extensively documented, and there are few surprises in store. There is little risk at this point that the deceased will fall from grace, for example, or betray their fans or disappoint them by revealing some hidden side.

Moreover, the sparseness of the historical record leaves plenty of space for imagination. Official histories rarely describe how someone walked, sat, or conversed with a close friend. As such, history fangirls are free to fill in the blanks, attach their own understandings, and invest themselves emotionally. Importantly, since the deceased can never contradict them, there is no one to reject fans’ interpretations or deny their emotional projection, making them unusually safe objects of affection.

Deciding which historical figure to stan and how to express one’s affection varies from person to person. However, the practice generally follows a similar pattern: reading historical materials, creating fan works, and making pilgrimages to historical sites.

When you care deeply about someone, it is natural to want to learn everything you can about them, and so history fangirls typically spend a lot of time reading up on their underground idols. In some cases, publishers of obscure old books have been surprised by sudden sales spikes, with some works even selling out the moment they are put on sale. On platforms like Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, fans swap tips for how to buy rare books like the “Complete Collected Works of Cao Pi,” Cao Cao’s son and a particularly popular underground idol.

In addition to reading up on history, fans mark special occasions such as Tomb-sweeping Day and the Dragon Boat Festival, as well as birthdays and death anniversaries, with collaborative online creative projects or offline pilgrimages. Even the most secluded tombs and little-known ruins can now be found using guides posted on social media. Many leave handwritten notes or gifts connected to the figure’s life as a way of making the visit feel more personal, as if the deceased were capable of “receiving” this kindness.

Because their focus is history — a serious and important field of knowledge — the fandom enjoys cultural legitimacy that other forms of celebrity obsession don’t receive. Its economic potential has also encouraged wider acceptance. Various cemeteries have gradually adapted to and encouraged the subculture, while museums and cultural institutions have started producing related merchandise and collaborating with games aimed at fans. Even state media outlets have lauded enthusiasts for “strengthening cultural confidence” and “promoting national heritage.”

Critics, however, worry that fandom is turning history into entertainment. The most common concern is the “fandomization” of history, with critics worrying that fan-made creations will ultimately distort the public’s understanding of the past.

Yet both sides risk missing the fandom’s essence. History fangirls are not trying to produce historical knowledge or advance a social agenda. They are enthusiasts practicing a personal hobby, with the simple goal of enjoying themselves.

Take, for example, the popularity of “underworld couples” — pairings understood to be toxic, or which romanticize violent or unequal relationships. One well-known example is between Cao Pi and one of his wives, Lady Zhen, whom he later had killed. Some fan-made works imagine the deep, tragic love between the pair, while others attempt to give Lady Zhen — whose personal name is not recorded in the historical records — greater subjectivity, or even place her in a parallel universe where she can choose her own fate. The fandom has no single, central discourse. Morality is not the primary standard; chemistry is.

Ultimately, the subculture’s power lies precisely in these intimate, personal acts of imagination that grand historical narratives cannot co-opt. As the 16th-century poet-official Yang Shen once wrote: “The history books contain but a handful of names, while the hills are strewn with countless forgotten tombs.” Yet, through the imaginations of the living, these historical figures continue to walk among us.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A woman takes a photo of a display dedicated to Cao Cao at the Cao Cao Mausoleum Site Museum in Anyang, Henan province, May 2026. VCG)

World.title: Tracing the Route of ‘Cathay’
World.content:
Eighty years ago, Roy Farrell and Sydney de Kantzow — two ex-air force pilots who had supported China’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression during World War II — purchased a Douglas DC-3 twin-engine propeller airplane. After establishing an import-export company in Shanghai, they soon relocated to Hong Kong and officially registered their new venture: Cathay Pacific Airways.

Today, Cathay Pacific is ranked as a 5-star airline and flies to 60 countries worldwide. Less recognized is the origin of “Cathay” as a common term. Chosen by the founders as a nod to their China connection alongside “Pacific” to capture their ambition for their enterprise to one day cross the world’s largest ocean, the word itself tells a story of communication and misunderstanding between ancient China and the West.

Indeed, for centuries, the name “Cathay” haunted the European imagination. It conjured visions of a distant, mythical realm of silk and spices beyond China — even as European merchants and missionaries quietly traded with the immense state. The great irony is that for nearly 300 years, Europe operated under the profound delusion that these two magnificent empires were separate neighbors, and perhaps even rivals.

This mismatch in geographical understanding can be traced back to a difference in terminology, itself a byproduct of accounts from travelers who visited different parts of the region amid shifting names for the north and south. According to the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), “Cathay” can be traced back to “Khitan,” the name of the nomadic people who established the Liao dynasty in the north from the 10th to the early 12th century. The Khitan name was then absorbed by the powerful Kara-Khanid Khanate to the west along the Silk Road, which subtly altered its pronunciation. As the word flowed westward into Persian (as Katā), then post-classical Latin (Cataia or Cathaia), and in Marco Polo’s accounts as Catai, “Cathay” came into being.

And yet, a linguistic rift began to appear as Europeans who landed on China’s southern coast found themselves dealing with a country named “China,” an older word derived from Sanskrit. On 16th-century maps, “China” was thus often depicted as a mere coastal strip known to Portuguese sailors, while “Cathay” loomed as a vast, mysterious inland empire to the north.

This was no mere academic error; it had monumental, real-world consequences. In fact, this geographical schism served as the very engine of the Age of Discovery. When Christopher Columbus and John Cabot set sail for the New World — with a heavily annotated copy of Marco Polo’s book of travels — they were convinced they were heading toward Cathay. Driven by the desperate hope of finding this elusive northern empire, Humphrey Gilbert penned his 1576 treatise, “A Discourse of a Discoverie for a New Passage to Cataia.”

Yet, the human drive to uncover the truth is a powerful instinct. The reconciliation of “Cathay” and “China” belongs not to kings or cartographers, but to the walkers — specifically, the missionaries who refused to accept that the map was complete. When Matteo Ricci arrived in China in the late 16th century, he noticed that the “Cathay” described by Polo perfectly matched the empire of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). To settle any lingering doubts, the Portuguese Jesuit missionary Bento de Góis then embarked on a grueling overland expedition from India. Crossing the unforgiving Pamir Mountains and the Gobi Desert, he searched for the legendary kingdom of Cathay. Though he died waiting for permission to enter Beijing, his ultimate sacrifice proved that the Silk Road led directly to the seat of the Ming’s rule, not the separate land of “Cathay.”

By the early 17th century, Western travelers like Ricci, de Góis, and Martín de Rada had conclusively established that the China reached by sea could be accessed by following Marco Polo’s land route across Central Asia. When their letters finally reached Europe, the phantom of “Cathay” vanished from the maps, leaving behind only the tangible reality of China.

One might expect the word “Cathay” to have perished alongside that geographical revelation. Instead, it transformed. As the OED notes, from the beginning of the 17th century, “Cathay” was gradually superseded by “China,” and by the century’s end, the process was complete. Stripped of its geographical necessity, the word was reborn as an archaic, highly connotative strand of poetic use. In the early 18th century, poet James Thomson wrote of caravans bending “to the golden coast of rich Cathay/With news of human-kind.” By 1823, Lord Byron was similarly invoking “far Cathay” alongside Ceylon and Inde in “Don Juan.” In 1859, Harper’s Magazine placed Cathay alongside Atlantis and El Dorado as a land now “peopled with beings of flesh and blood.” By 1871, Joaquin Miller mused, “Where the winds come in from the far Cathay/With odor of spices and balm and bay.” Through these verses, the word had become a timeless vessel for exotic mystery and richness.

Perhaps most fascinating is the OED’s entry for the phrase “cycle of Cathay,” defined as “a period of time which is long-lasting but during which little changes.” Popularized by Lord Tennyson’s poem “Locksley Hall” (“Better fifty years of Europe than a cycle of Cathay”), the phrase reflects a complex, heavily Eurocentric Western gaze assuming cultural superiority. This cultural bias was further cemented in an 1886 issue of the North American Review, which claimed that “the world has made more progress in that time [...] than in many cycles of Cathay.”

The name then found a romantic revival in the bustling commercial heart of the East. In the cosmopolitan Shanghai of the 1930s, “Cathay” was embraced as a symbol of ultimate luxury and modernity. The legendary Cathay Theatre and the grand Cathay Hotel (now the Fairmont Peace Hotel) adopted the ancient name to evoke timeless elegance and prestige. When the theater’s name was localized into the Chinese characters pronounced Guotai, evoking an auspicious idiom meaning “peace and prosperity,” it marked a brilliant fusion of Western phonetics and Eastern cultural values. Here, Cathay was no longer just a distant Western fantasy, but a glamorous reality woven into the very fabric of the city’s urban memory.

Decades later, this evocative name took flight, finding its most enduring manifestation in the clouds. By reusing the beloved “Guotai” moniker, Cathay Pacific’s founders seamlessly carried that century-old promise of peace and prosperity into the jet age.

The story of Cathay teaches us that names are far more than mere labels; they are the enduring vessels of our shared history. The long journey from “Cathay” to “China” charted a passage from fragmentation to wholeness, from distant myth to tangible reality. It serves as a poignant reminder that while maps and misunderstandings may carve the world into “us” and “them,” the human spirit — propelled by the footsteps of explorers and the verses of poets — can’t help but try to blur such divides. In the end, we are all, in some way, still searching for Cathay, hoping to discover that behind the ancient myth lies a shared humanity.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: China’s Beloved Beef Noodles Are Getting a Rebrand
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018933/China’s Beloved Beef Noodles Are Getting a Rebrand
World.content:
China’s signature local specialty Lanzhou lamian, or Lanzhou pulled noodles — named after the capital city of the northwestern Gansu province — are undergoing a rebranding. At many noodle shops across the country, the dish will now be known as “Qinghai lamian,” as the northwestern Qinghai province strives to build its own regional brand.

More than 1,000 noodle shops nationwide have made the shift, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Saturday. In June, 72 noodle shops in the northern port city of Tianjin first changed their names to bear the words “Qinghai lamian,” followed by hundreds of shops in several other provinces in the months since.

Composed of hand-pulled noodles in a clear broth, sliced beef and radish, and chili oil, the dish traces its history back to the turn of the 19th century in the central Henan province. After being brought west, they took on the name of Gansu’s capital, a stop on the old Silk Road — where the halal noodles first became a hit in part owing to its significant Muslim Hui population. They were further popularized as a local specialty by Hui noodle maker Ma Baozi in the 1910s.

Later, as China opened up in the 1980s, entrepreneurs from poverty-stricken counties in Qinghai, such as Hualong, began capitalizing on the noodles’ popularity, opening small, mom-and-pop restaurants across the country.

“There was little brand awareness back then, and hardly anyone had heard of Hualong, Qinghai. However, Lanzhou is close by, so (noodle shop owners) thought they’d just call them ‘Lanzhou noodles,’ because everyone knows Lanzhou,” Ma Liping, president of the Qinghai Noodles Industry Association, told local media.

The shops have become a familiar sight nationwide. As of the end of February 2026, there were 31,000 noodle restaurants operated by owners from Qinghai in more than 330 cities across China, generating more than 24 billion yuan ($3.5 billion) in annual revenue, according to data from the Qinghai Noodle Industry Association.

But tensions over the use of the dish’s name have grown among Lanzhou and Qinghai residents, as people from Lanzhou call it “Lanzhou niurou mian” — Lanzhou beef noodles — while people from Qinghai call it “Lanzhou lamian,” or “Lanzhou pulled noodles.”

The dish has also evolved two differing preparation methods among Gansu and Qinghai restaurant owners, fueling debate. Lanzhou noodle makers have made efforts to preserve its traditional flavors, while Qinghai shop owners have adapted to local tastes — for instance by using less oil and salt in Guangdong, or adding more pepper in the southwestern Sichuan province.

To distinguish their wares from the noodles sold by people from Qinghai, local authorities in Lanzhou registered a trademark featuring a bull’s head for “Lanzhou Beef Noodles” in 2007, marking the city’s first step toward building a formal regional brand.

The recent rebrandings are part of Qinghai’s broader effort to build a provincial brand. About one-fifth of the rebranded shops have adopted a “three-in-one” model, adding in-restaurant sales of local specialties such as yak jerky and highland barley products, as well as tourism promotion, as new revenue streams.

Online, users voiced their support for the change. “After all, the two noodle dishes differ significantly in taste and texture, so distinguishing them clearly will help consumers make informed choices,” one user wrote on microblogging platform Weibo.

In a commentary, state-backed Haibao news wrote that “the rebranding reflects the growing push to standardize China’s grassroots food industry.”

The push is evidenced by multiple regions recently moving to standardize the production of local dishes. Gansu began regulating Lanzhou lamian in 2023, while a vocational college in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region launched a course dedicated to standardizing and promoting its river snail rice noodles in 2020. In July, the catering industry association of the eastern Zhejiang province also introduced a standard for preparing duck heads, a Quzhou city specialty.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A Lanzhou lamian shop in Yichang, Hubei province, Aug. 11, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Heroes aplenty as Gilas Pilipinas turns back Iran to complete home sweep
World.content:
Dwight Ramos, Juan Gomez de Liaño, Kai Sotto, and AJ Edu join hands in a superb finish as Gilas Pilipinas beats Iran in FIBA play for the first time in over a decade

MANILA, Philippines – Gilas Pilipinas leaned on a strong finish and completed a sweep of its two-game homestand in the fourth window of the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers after a 68-56 win over Iran on Sunday, August 30, at the Mall of Asia Arena.

Similar to its gritty 82-81 victory over Jordan two days prior, heroes were aplenty for the Philippines as Dwight Ramos, Juan Gomez de Liaño, Kai Sotto, and AJ Edu joined hands in a 19-4 finishing run that allowed the hosts to even their record to 4-4 in Group E.

Iran momentarily took a 52-49 lead behind Mobin Sheikhi early in the fourth quarter before the Filipinos dominated the rest of the way.

Gomez de Liaño came off the bench and produced 16 points on 5-of-9 shooting and Ramos also finished with 16 points, 7 rebounds, and 2 steals, including a three-pointer that broke a 54-54 deadlock and sparked the Philippines’ breakaway.

Sotto once again turned in a double-double of 13 points and 16 rebounds, while Edu protected the paint with 8 points, 8 rebounds, and 3 blocks.

The win marked the first time Gilas Pilipinas beat Iran in FIBA play in over a decade, or since its 87-73 victory over Team Melli in the 2015 Asia Championship, where it captured the silver medal.

Playing in likely his final game for the national team, June Mar Fajardo made the most of his brief stint, contributing 6 points in a little over seven minutes of play as he proved pivotal in Gilas Pilipinas’ resurgence from a lethargic start.

The Filipinos got buried by as deep as 13 points, 5-18, and trailed 7-18 at the end of the opening quarter before they flipped the script in the second period behind Ramos and Fajardo to seize the upper hand at halftime, 36-34.

Sheikhi, the smallest player on the court standing at 5-foot-8, surprised the Philippines and led Iran with 21 points on a 5-of-8 clip from beyond the arc.

But with no other Iranian player scoring in double figures, Team Melli fell to 5-3 as they dropped both their fourth-window games after also losing to New Zealand.

Gilas Pilipinas returns to action in the Asian Qualifiers in November when it battles Syria and Iran again. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pilandok maintains strength, enhances southwest monsoon
World.content:
WEATHER. Tropical Depression Pilandok and southwest monsoon inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of August 30, 2026, 5:40 pm.

The enhanced southwest monsoon or habagat is bringing monsoon rain to Ilocos Region, Abra, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga

MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Depression Pilandok maintained its strength on Sunday afternoon, August 30, and is enhancing the southwest monsoon or habagat.

In its 5 pm bulletin on Sunday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Pilandok was located 1,180 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon. It is moving northwestward slowly, with maximum sustained winds of 45 kilometers per hour and gustiness of up to 55 km/h.

PAGASA said Pilandok is seen to move west northwestward on Monday, August 31, before turning generally northwestward.

It is less likely to make landfall and is expected to be a short-lived tropical cyclone, remaining a tropical depression before weakening into a remnant low over the Philippine Sea south of the southern islands of Japan on Tuesday, September 1.

While it is not directly affecting the country, Pilandok is enhancing the southwest monsoon, which is bringing monsoon rain to Ilocos Region, Abra, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga, and occasional rain to Metro Manila, the rest of Cordillera Administrative Region, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro.

It is also causing scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of Luzon, Western Visayas, and Negros Island Region, and isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of Visayas.

Below is PAGASA’s latest heavy rainfall outlook due to the southwest monsoon for the next three days:

Sunday afternoon, August 30, Monday afternoon, August 31:

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 millimeters): Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Abra, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Metro Manila, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro

Monday afternoon, August 31, to Tuesday afternoon, September 1:

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Pangasinan, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Batanes, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, and Cavite

Tuesday afternoon, September 1, to Wednesday afternoon, September 2:

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Abra, and Benguet

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, La Union, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Zambales, and Bataan

These areas should watch out for flash floods and landslides.

The enhanced southwest monsoon is also bringing strong to gale-force gusts over the following areas, especially in coastal and upland areas exposed to winds:

Sunday, August 30:

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Oriental, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, and Davao Oriental

Monday, August 31:

most of the country

Tuesday, September 1:

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Oriental, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, and Davao Oriental

Moderate to rough seas will also persist in the following areas:

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Western seaboard of Babuyan Islands — waves up to 4 meters high

Seaboards of Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, and Zambales; the northern seaboard of Babuyan Islands; the western seaboards of Pangasinan and Bataan — waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboard of Lubang Islands; the western seaboards of northern La Union, Cavite, Batangas, northern Occidental Mindoro, and Kalayaan Islands — waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Western seaboard of northern Palawan including Calamian Islands; the eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; the remaining seaboard of Kalayaan Islands; the remaining western seaboard of Occidental Mindoro — waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboards of Isabela, Antique, Surigao del Sur, and Davao Occidental; the southern seaboards of Iloilo and Guimaras; the western seaboard of Negros Occidental; the remaining seaboards of Babuyan Islands and Davao Oriental; the remaining western seaboard of mainland Palawan — waves up to 2 meters high

Aside from Tropical Depression Pilandok, PAGASA is also monitoring the low pressure area that was formerly Saudel, which has a “medium” chance of redeveloping into a tropical depression, and another low pressure area, which also has a “medium” chance of developing into a tropical depression. Both are outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Trust and public funds: why and how we obsess over the national budget
World.content:
There are reasons why 'trust' should never be something you assume when it comes to the people’s money, even if (and maybe, particularly if) they are labelled confidential or intelligence funds

Ten years ago, when funds allocated to confidential and intelligence expenditures skyrocketed under the Duterte administration, I asked then Budget Secretary Benjamin Diokno for his thoughts on what safeguards should be put in place to prevent potential abuse of these funds.

Diokno’s response then: “We just have to trust him (President Rodrigo Duterte) na mabuting tao siya (that he is a good person),” he said.

I was astounded. Trust? Journalists are trained to be skeptical and suspicious, particularly when it comes to matters that involve power and money.

The word “trust” is also anathema to the checks and balances that is embedded in our system of government.

It therefore felt surreal that — 10 years later — there is that word again: trust.

People reporting to Duterte’s daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, are saying the same thing before an impeachment court: they trusted Colonel Raymund Lachica, the VP’s chief security officer. They trusted the Vice President.

Hello! I am Gemma Mendoza, head for strategic programs at Rappler. As a journalist, I am particularly obsessed with the budget process. I have been scrutinizing budget, procurement, and audit documents for over two decades now.

There are reasons why “trust” should never be something you assume when it comes to the people’s money, even if (and maybe, particularly if) they are labelled confidential or intelligence funds.

Former heads of the Commission on Audit (COA) have already said that confidential and intelligence funds are difficult to audit.

Prior to that specific interview with Diokno, I co-wrote the book The Enemy Within with Aries Rufo and Glenda Gloria. That book dived deep into how the military top brass abused confidential and intelligence funds allocated to the armed forces and, among other things, diverted these funds to their pabaon retirement system.

A former military general took his own life following congressional investigations into this scandal.

While there are legitimate reasons why certain funds cannot go through the usual processes, the Constitution is explicit about subjecting all kinds of funds to audit.

It says: “No law shall be passed exempting any entity of the Government or its subsidiary in any guise whatever, or any investment of public funds, from the jurisdiction of the Commission on Audit.”

This was precisely why in 2015 the budget department and COA worked with the local government and defense departments to come up with Joint Circular No. 2015-01.

Within each government office, each vote and signature in the budget request, procurement, and liquidation process is supposed to represent checks to misuse. Each signatory is supposed to be responsible. They are not supposed to “trust” each other.

The fact that the confidential funds of Sara Duterte are now at the center of an impeachment trial is a demonstration of how various steps in this process of checks and balances failed the Filipino people. Rappler has reported on this every step of the way.

This is why we require every journalist at Rappler to be familiar with the national budget and the budget process. We remind our reporters that the scrutiny of how public funds are allocated and spent needs to happen at each phase of the process: planning and formulation, approval, implementation, and audit.

Beyond the numbers themselves, everything requires sharp eyes: the logic of the budget, the expected outcomes, the process of fund release up to the point the project funded by said item is marked as completed.

This is not an easy endeavor. Many parts of this process remain opaque, despite various transparency initiatives. And so journalists need to learn not just how the formal and informal processes work, where to get paper trail, and how to read between the lines of each document.

In the past couple of weeks, our team went through another budget refresher sessions for this purpose.

Spotting issues requires the ability to analyze budget data over a period of time. Formats in which data is made available is not always consistent, and so we have been training our journalists in data processing and analysis.

We have gone a step further. On RappLearn, we now have a training module on understanding the budget process, which serves as a supplement to onground training for staff, fellows, and stakeholders. Budget toplines as well as granular budget data are now available and visualized on our website.

If you want to know how much each department received for its staff since 2020, you should be able to see that on our #BudgetWatch page.

Our pages for each department now have the department’s detailed budget. For example, if you want to know if the public high school in your city received funding for internet services, then you may check our topic page for the Department of Education.

All of these require resources. And this is where we need support.

If you have not yet signed up for Rappler Plus, please do so, and please ask your friends to do the same. If you want to give further assistance, please consider donating or volunteering.

Work with us to ensure that every peso spent from the public treasury counts, connects to improvements in the lives of Filipinos, and is not lost to corruption or misuse. – Rappler.com
