World.title: Sydney dining heavy hitter takes over iconic Gerard’s site
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outRestaurant news Sydney dining heavy hitter takes over iconic Gerard’s site Rebecca Yazbek is bringing Nomad to Queensland, adding a third state to her expanding portfolio – in another big play after her partner made national news. Matt Shea August 31, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The way Rebecca Yazbek tells it, she’s used to taking leaps. Her first, as far as restaurants go, was opening Nomad in Sydney in 2013. An interior architect by background, she had no hospitality experience at the time. Then there were the Melbourne openings of Nomad in 2021 and the sumptuous Reine & La Rue in the heritage-listed former Melbourne Stock Exchange building in 2023, and the purchase of Victorian dining institution Grossi Florentino last year. Rebecca Yazbek’s Edition Hospitality will open a Nomad in Brisbane in the premises previously occupied by Gerard’s. Steven Siewert In that sense, opening Nomad in Brisbane, in the space previously occupied by Gerard’s, is just another leap for the Edition Hospitality founder and chief executive.





Gerard’s rammed-earth walls will be retained but the space will feel more open. Morgan Roberts Now, taking over yet another institution feels like a statement of intent: “The first time I looked at Brisbane sites was 10 years ago. I know because I had a four-month-old strapped to my chest who just turned 10,” she says. “You do those big leaps and hope for the best. I don’t think about the worst case. I think, ‘if we do what we do really well, then people will come’,” she says. Apart from retaining Gerard’s rammed-earth walls, J.AR Office’s Jared Webb is returning to the premises he redesigned in 2023 with a simple brief: “Do Nomad for 2026 in Brisbane. Go!” Yazbek says. “He understands that space. He understands the environment.” For those familiar with the space, Nomad will feel more open, with a lengthy bar, a large wine wall, and a kitchen that better communes with the restaurant floor. There will be Australian art and Australian pottery, and while it will feel like a Nomad, “it’s not a replica”, she says.



Rebecca Yazbek with Edition’s group general manager, Ged Bellis (left), and Michael Greenlaw. Ethan Smart for Ediition In charge of food is Edition culinary director Michael Greenlaw and current Nomad Melbourne head chef Jeremy Swann. The venue manager will be long-time Nomad Melbourne staffer Robbie Pyke-Marcou, and drinks will be overseen by group bar manager Felix Woods and group sommelier Steve Senturk. Like the other Nomads, the still wines by the glass will all be Australian. “It’s a great opportunity to put wines in front of people that they haven’t necessarily seen before,” says Yazbek. The food is yet to be finalised, but it’ll be the same wood-fired approach of the Sydney and Melbourne editions, but informed by Queensland produce. “For 10 years, Nomad was all I did because that’s what I knew and that’s what I loved. So pushing to see how far we can take that is really exciting.” Nomad Brisbane is scheduled to open in late spring.

World.title: ‘Miraculous gift’: Family of Australian who survived Nepalese floods rejoices
World.content:
The family of an Australian woman thought to have been missing in the Nepalese floods said her survival was a “miracle” as they thanked the Australian government and Nepalese hiking partners who got her out safely. Cara Severino, 26, was listed as missing following the devastating floods that swept across regions in Nepal and China on Wednesday. Australian Cara Severino was located by Australian consular officials after hiking in Nepal. Facebook The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade on Sunday confirmed there were 42 Australians missing in floods that have left thousands dead and unaccounted for. That number includes six Australians who Chinese state authorities said were missing on the Chinese side of the border, among a total of 261 foreign nationals who remain unaccounted for. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a statement on Sunday: “This is an extremely anxious time for their families and loved ones. They are understandably desperate for news, and our thoughts are very much with them.”



The death toll in Nepal and Tibet on Sunday (Monday AEST) climbed to 804 with 3048 missing. The Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster. The Australian government will deploy a further $3 million in humanitarian assistance. The Royal Australian Air Force will transport supplies from Queensland later this week. Nepalese flood survivor Cara Severino with Australian consular officials in Nepal. Senator Penny Wong on X Severino contacted her parents on Friday after two days hiking through the devastated area. She was located by consular officials in Nepal on Saturday, who drove out from Kathmandu to meet her. Severino’s parents, Debbie and Frank, said they were “beyond relieved and elated” that she had been found safe. “We can’t wait to hold her in our loving arms,” they said in a statement distributed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade on Sunday.



“Seeing Cara’s name appear on my MessageBank, hearing her voice and now seeing her photo and speaking with her has been the most miraculous gift.” The pair thanked their church, Jesus, family and friends who had prayed for the “miracle”, as well as the Australian consular response teams and local teams. Loading “We are so grateful to her Nepalese hiking partners who saw her through a harrowing several days of hiking in very difficult terrain – so thankful that they have all made it to safety,” they said. “The scale of this tragedy is staggering, and amidst our personal joy we continue to stand in prayer with the many families here in Australia, in Nepal and around the world who have lost loved ones or are still waiting to hear from them … We know that the waiting is horrendous.”



Related Article Floods In Nepal, once-busy towns are turned to wastelands of mud The pair encouraged people to donate via the Emergency Action Alliance webpage. Cara Severino in a statement on Saturday said she felt “blessed” to be Australian and to have support from the embassy and the government. “I’m so grateful for the crew we formed on that first day when we entered the national park on the tractor. Sudha, Lucas, Samir and Saugat. It’s thanks to these amazing people I got out safely,” she said. “I feel for the families of those still missing. I know how much my family and friends went through.”



Meanwhile, relatives of one missing Australian family are desperately hoping to find their loved ones among the survivors of the disaster. More than 7000 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Speaking to this masthead in Nepal, one of the four brothers of Sreedharan Iyer, 53, said they were yet to get a “concrete” lead on what had happened to his brother from authorities carrying out search and rescue operations. Iyer, from the Sydney suburb of Cherrybrook, his wife, Lakshmi, 49, and the couple’s two sons – Rudhra, 20, and Rishab, 23 – were travelling with a group of about 15 Australian friends to the Hindu sacred site of Mount Kailash. Relatives arrive in a remote area to search for the missing Iyer family. KATE GERAGHTY “They were on their way towards the border check post [to get to Mount Kalaish],” Ganesh Gopalakrishnan said.



The missing Sydney family in Nepal: (From L-R) Rudhra Iyer, 20, the father Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife Lakshmi, 49, and Rishab, 23. “It could have been they were face to face with the floods coming at them, and we just hope they managed to park their cars and escape to an elevated area.” Ganesh was at work in Bangalore when he first learned the shocking news that a disaster was unfolding exactly where his family members were travelling. “We didn’t have the itinerary with us, so we had to start from scratch, starting with the tour operator,” he said. “From there, we found the itinerary and the place they spent that last night and morning, and then when they would have checked out. That was 8.45am.” Lakshmi runs the Leap Pad Early Learning Centre in Riverstone, the brothers said. Sreedharan is a mortgage broker. Their eldest son, Rishab, is a doctor and Rudhra is studying medicine at a university in Sydney.



“It is [Sreedharan’s] dream to get his children to become doctors,” Ganesh said. “He’s been very successful in getting two fine boys.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Sunday said his “thoughts and prayers” were with the families of those missing and the people of Nepal. “The tragedy in Nepal [has] resulted in such devastation, loss of life, potentially including so many Australians still among the missing,” he said at the Queensland Labor state conference. “That something so devastating could occur in such an awesome and inspiring corner of the world during times of pilgrimage and holiday makes the blow seem even more heartbreaking. Australia is responding with significant consular rescue and humanitarian aid.” Loading



Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was concerned about the Australians still missing. “There remain grave concerns for the other Australians who are still unaccounted for, given the tremendous scale of the flooding and its impact,” Wong said on Saturday. Most of the Australians still missing were pilgrims on a journey to one of the most spiritually significant locations in the world. The list of Australians missing can be found here. Australia has announced a $5 million assistance package for affected communities. Nepal’s government has said it does not need foreign help for general rescue, but Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said the country needed assistance in such areas as tunnel rescue, DNA testing, refrigerated storage for bodies and forensic identification of decomposed remains.



He said Indian and Chinese experts were on the ground helping efforts to open tunnels. Rescue efforts in Nepal are focused on extracting hundreds of people believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower plants. Nepal has mobilised more than 18,500 military and police personnel on rescue missions. Opening the tunnel entrance at the Trishuli 3 A Hydropower Project located in Rasuwa is a particular focus. View post on X China has mobilised more than 2100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($32.7 million) to support relief efforts. Chinese tunnelling experts have arrived in Nepal to assist with the rescue operations. Kate Geraghty



It is also providing emergency cash aid, disaster relief supplies, satellite and hydrological data and tunnel rescue experts to Nepal, CCTV said. China used heavy-lift drones as helicopters began airdropping equipment and supplies to rescuers near the border crossing. Soldiers have used life-detection equipment, drones and a navigation system to continue searching for the missing. With Reuters/Bloomberg Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas). World.title: This Emmy nominee is a star in America. At home in Australia, no one knows his name
World.content:
You may never have heard of Michael Cusack. Chances are, that’s about to change.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Michael Cusack is a big deal in America, but in Australia, few outside the avid fandom of adult animation have heard his name. Though that could soon change. Cusack, 35, is a nominee at next weekend’s Emmys (the craft component, held a week before the main event, the Primetime Emmys) for his show Smiling Friends, co-created with American Zach Hadel. “It feels very surreal because I’ve never won any award, not even at school,” he says from Wollongong, where he grew up, and to where he has returned from his base in Melbourne for a short burst of writing before flying to LA on Thursday. “To be nominated for the Emmys before even being nominated for an Australian awards show feels huge, elite, almost too far,” he adds. “I’m very honoured, of course, it’s very nice. But I do find it funny that I don’t even know if someone at the Logies would know who I am.” Cusack is self-taught, his work in the rough-and-ready vein familiar to watchers of Adult Swim, but with a distinctively Australian edge, perhaps best described as a lack of affect. “I think it’s a little bit looser,” he says of his style, and of Australian animation more generally. “Americans love their really polished, kid-meets-adult kind of thing that’s going on right now. Our animation is rough and observational, sometimes grounded and boring, but that’s the joke. Like, that’s definitely my kind of thing because Aussies are just kind of like that.”



Cusack left high school with an ambition to be a filmmaker, and put $15,000 saved from his job at Subway towards a live-action feature, All Night Gaming, when he was 20 (he also got a bank loan for $10,000 to top up the budget, and later took a job washing dishes in a Queensland mining town to pay it off). “It was very much like a Clerks, Kevin Smith, Richard Linklater kind of thing,” he says. “It was the best film school I could ever have because I just learned. Like, it was hell.” Among the things the experience taught him was that much of the cost of making a movie goes on catering, and you’re often at the mercy of the weather. “So I was like, ‘I just want to draw what’s in my mind rather than having to film it’. So I taught myself animation.” Cusack is gunning for a future in which Australian broadcasters might actually commission Australian adult animation. George Chan Once his first effort, a two-minute short made for the gaming community, caught fire, he was hooked. “It got 400,000 views in a few days, and that blew my mind,” he says. “‘Yeah, I’m gonna just keep doing this’.” Cusack still releases material on YouTube, where Damo and Darren (better known as Ciggy Butt Brain), about a couple of drug-addled losers squabbling over a lighter, found him a huge audience more than a decade ago. But he’s also scored with the major broadcasters, with Yolo (originally a short about two nightclubbing women in Wollongong) and Smiling Friends both on Adult Swim and HBO Max, Koala Man (with a voice cast including Hugh Jackman, Hugo Weaving, Miranda Otto and Sarah Snook) on Hulu and Disney+, and the forthcoming Dad’s House on its way to Netflix. Notably, all these commissions came from the States.

World.title: ASX set to slide as Wall Street retreats; Fed chief talks up inflation fight
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide as Wall Street retreats; Fed chief talks up inflation fight Stan Choe August 31, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The bond market swung Friday as investors built bets that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates soon to get the nation’s high inflation under control. US stocks, meanwhile, dipped but not by much after economists said a speech by Chairman Kevin Warsh helped strengthen faith that the Fed will do what’s needed to bring inflation down, even if it causes pain for the economy in the short term. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent after flipping between modest gains and losses through the morning. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 9 points, or less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.5 per cent. There is strengthening faith that the Fed will do what’s needed to bring inflation down, even if it causes pain for the economy in the short term. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures on Saturday pointing to a fall of 36 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.60¢. The reaction was stronger in the bond market following Warsh’s first speech as chairman of the Fed at an annual economic symposium held in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The mountain setting has been the backdrop for major Fed policy announcements in the past, and the pressure was on Warsh.



Worries had grown that his tough talk about getting inflation down to the Fed’s 2 per cent target may be just that, unless the Fed backs it up with action. The Fed could hike short-term interest rates to get inflation under control, but it could also feel deterred from doing so because that would slow the economy and hurt prices for investments. And President Donald Trump, who appointed Warsh, has been vocal about wanting interest rates to be lower rather than higher. Related Article Opinion

Climate crisis Oil giant’s retreat on clean energy shows limits of investor pressure Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Warsh was adamant again on Friday that he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed plans to do with rates for its two jobs of keeping inflation low and the job market strong. He has said he wants markets to react to what incoming data says about the economy and inflation rather than what the Fed says. But Warsh also said Friday that “short-term interest rates are the predominant tool” for the Fed to do its job. And he said, “I would be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive,” an implication that short-term interest rates may not be high enough to tamp down the economy and inflation. The yield on the two-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for what the Fed will do with its federal funds rate, jumped to 4.35 per cent from 4.22 per cent just before the speech.



That’s a big move for the bond market, and it was because traders upped their forecasts that the Fed will hike its federal funds rate as soon as next month. They’re now betting on a nearly 58 per cent probability of that, up from the 35 per cent seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. Longer-term yields also rose following some initial zigzags, but not by as much as shorter-term yields. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.72 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday, and the 30-year Treasury yield got to 5.21 per cent from 5.19 per cent. All the moves, including the modest ones for stocks even though higher interest rates tend to hurt them, indicate investors “pricing a more credible Fed,” according to economists at Bank of America led by Aditya Bhave. “The positive market reaction highlights that investors place a premium on policy clarity, even when that clarity carries” a message implying higher interest rates, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. Yields had gotten so high for longer-term bonds this summer, in part because of worries about inflation staying high in the future, that the US Treasury Department made an unusual move last week and said it would buy back more bonds, though analysts said it will likely have only a limited effect.



On Wall Street, Gap jumped 12.9 per cent after the retailer reported stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also said Michael Francis, an industry veteran who began his career on the retail sales floor, will take over as head of its Old Navy stores. Related Article Building insurance Home owners are being short-changed by insurers’ cash payouts Marvell Technology fell 10.3 per cent even though the chip company reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations. CEO Matt Murphy said its business related to artificial-intelligence technology is strong, and it raised its forecasts for upcoming revenue growth. But analysts said much of that optimism may have already been baked into Marvell’s stock price, which came into the day with a surge of 184 per cent for the year so far. After rocketing higher for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks across the industry are confronting skepticism that they shot too high and that booming demand for AI chips may fade if the AI revolution does not produce as much profit as promised.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 19.23 points to 7,711.76. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 9.45 to 53,559.99, and the Nasdaq composite sank 138.93 to 26,402.42. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.8 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 1 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: One of the world’s greatest walks can now begin in an unusual place
World.content:
InspirationEurope One of the world’s greatest walks can now begin in an unusual place Billy Cantwell August 31, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m not a great fan of Irish jokes, but there’s one that makes me chuckle. When a lost tourist in a remote Irish village stops to ask directions to Dublin, she’s told “well, I wouldn’t start from here”. If “doing the Camino” is something you’re planning, beginning the hike in Ireland may not be front of mind. But now you can begin your camino (the Spanish word for “way”) in Ireland, and it contributes towards “el camino”, the popular pilgrimage that terminates at the shrine of St James (Santiago in Spanish) in the Galitian capital of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain. Walkers on the slopes of Croagh Patrick, above Clew Bay in County Mayo, Ireland. Pilgrimages to the shrine date to medieval times when the so-called “cult of St James” took root across Western Europe following the discovery of what was determined to be the burial place of the apostle in Spain. A cathedral – the imposing Catedral Basílica de Santiago de Compostela – was completed in the 13th century on the spot where his remains were found. Pilgrimages from as far away as Ireland became popular in medieval times, but only wealthier believers could afford the trip. According to historian Turlough O’Donnell, the earliest reference we have to the Irish pilgrimage to Santiago is in 1219, just six years after the cathedral was consecrated.



St James’ Gate in Dublin, made famous more recently as the site of the Guinness brewery, was one of the traditional departure points for Irish pilgrims pursuing The Way of St James. Others included Cork, Waterford, Galway and the Kerry town of Dingle. Pilgrims would travel from one of these Irish ports to A Coruna or Ferrol on the north-western tip of the Iberian Peninsula. From there, pilgrims continued on foot to the sacred site about 75 kilometres away. This “way” has become a unique pilgrimage route known as the Celtic Camino. 



For instance, the 63-kilometre Croagh Patrick Heritage Trail in County Mayo on Ireland’s Atlantic coast extends from the town of Balla, an early Christian monastic site, westwards via the gloriously named Ballintubber to the picturesque seaside village of Murrisk which sits at the foot of Croagh Patrick (764 metres), a popular pilgrimage destination in its own right. Hikers on Croagh Patrick in County Mayo, part of the camino. Further south, the 57-kilometre Kerry Camino, part of the Kerry Way, stretches from Tralee to Dingle and is usually navigated over three days. It follows in the footsteps of St Brendan the Navigator (the locals, if you believe them, will tell you St Brendan reached the Americas 1000 years before Columbus) and crosses rugged mountain and coastal landscapes. Happily, it’s punctuated by cosy pubs in the villages of Camp and Annascaul. Nearer the capital, St Kevin’s Way (32 kilometres) takes you through the hills of Wicklow to the stunning valley of Glendalough where the saint spent the last part of his life in solitary prayer and contemplation. After Kevin’s death in AD618, what had been a humble hermit’s retreat developed into an impressive monastic city, the ruins of which – including Glendalough’s magnificent round tower – are still standing. I took on the Boyne Valley Camino, a 25-kilometre picturesque hike that stretches from the haunting ruins of the 12th century Old Mellifont Abbey – Ireland’s first Cistercian monastery – through the riverside Townley Hall Woods and past the site of the Battle of the Boyne, a pivotal conflict that was to leave a profound legacy for both Britain and Ireland. It was here in 1690 that the Protestant King William of Orange defeated King James II, the last Catholic monarch of England. A visitor centre is now housed in the stately Oldbridge House, where you can find out more about the battle and its legacy.



The Boyne Valley contains many extraordinary heritage sites and a short diversion from the camino takes you to Newgrange – a 5200-year-old passage tomb that predates both Stonehenge and the Great Pyramids of Giza. Related Article Europe There’s a better way to do one of the world’s greatest walks: Don’t walk Back on the trail, you can get your “passport” stamped at sites along the way, including at the Morning Star pub in the sleepy village of Tullyallen. At the time I visited, the pub, sadly, was closed. Never mind, it’s a perfect excuse to go back, and then I can worry about the Spanish bit. THE DETAILS WALK

Self-guided Celtic Camino walk packages including accommodation and luggage transfer are available through operators such as Hilltop Treks. See hilltoptreks.com

You can order your pilgrim passport (€10/$16.50) online from Camino Society Ireland or pick one up in person by visiting the sacristy at St James’ Church, James Street, Dublin 8.

See caminosociety.ie



FLY

Airlines including Qatar, Etihad and Emirates offer one-stop flights to Dublin from Sydney and Melbourne. The writer travelled at his own expense.

World.title: Pressure builds on board, minister as Powerhouse contract goes to company of former trustee
World.content:
Exclusive CultureArt & designCity life Pressure builds on board, minister as Powerhouse contract goes to company of former trustee Linda Morris August 31, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Powerhouse Museum awarded an uncontested $2 million marketing contract to a boutique agency co-founded by a former board trustee, part of more than $5 million spent on drumming up publicity before the opening of its landmark Parramatta site. The bespoke agency, Ki Community, was appointed by former chief executive Lisa Havilah, who abruptly departed the billion-dollar project two months before the November 7 opening of western Sydney’s first state significant cultural institution. David Borger, president of the board of the Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences. Sam Mooy The agency was hired in December to develop a “complex marketing, communications, and engagement plan” following a selective tender process in which, the museum confirmed, Ki Community was the only applicant. The Sydney Morning Herald had been pressing the museum and the board’s chair David Borger about the contract in the days before Havilah’s shock departure.



Arts Minister John Graham and Department of Creative Industries, Tourism and Hospitality secretary Melanie Hawyes will be under pressure at Monday’s budget estimates committee to explain their role in Havilah standing aside, the adequacy of their response to complaints of procurement issues and their oversight of the museum’s preopening spending, which is expected to surpass $100 million, inclusive of the $70 million cost of its five opening exhibitions. Graham wrote to the board of trustees on June 15, outlining his expectations that the project be delivered on time, on budget and fully compliant with procurement policies that delivered value for money for taxpayers. The new Powerhouse at Parramatta. SMH He called for the board’s co-operation in a Treasury review of the Ultimo and Parramatta projects. He said a review initiated by the department had identified “deficiencies” with three major contracts, and that security and catering needed to be “reconsidered”. Ki Community was founded by Mark Hassell, Graeme Wills, who headed Mojo Australia and is described as the company’s visionary force, and Michael Dole. Hassell was a trustee for four years before departing in December 2024 in a board refresh in which Borger, a business lobbyist and former Labor minister, was appointed president.



Hassell has denied any conflict of interest, saying he was not involved in the tender or the delivery of the communications project and that the company had made a declaration to that effect to the museum as part of due process. The appointment of Ki Community over established industry heavyweights Ogilvy Australia and Heard baffled insiders in the media and marketing sectors at the time and it sidelined the Powerhouse’s internal communications team. Relations between Powerhouse staff and the representatives of Ki Community have deteriorated due to frustration and disagreement over strategy and delivery. (From left) Outgoing Powerhouse Parramatta boss Lisa Havilah, and newly appointed interim chief executive Abbie Galvin, and strategic adviser Louise Herron. The Sydney Morning Herald As well as Ki Community’s $2 million contract, Sydney-based specialist arts agency Articulate is being paid $288,718 plus expenses for strategic public relations and communications services, and London’s Bolton & Quinn is being paid $275,000 for international public and media relations. The Powerhouse commissioned a $1.7 million-plus documentary about the new building’s construction and design for television and cinematic release.



Borger told the Herald the board had not endorsed the marketing contract when it was brought to it in May. He said the contract had fallen within the chief executive officer’s delegations. “When the board was made aware of this contract, it raised concerns around conflict of interest and potential unfair advantage and asked for these to be reviewed and managed appropriately,” he said in a statement. “The board recently resolved to not endorse the decision that had already been taken by the CEO to approve this contract. Further, the board resolved to refer this matter to Procurement NSW for review.” Ki Community bills itself as a “community of world-class creative thinkers, who see value where others don’t”. It does not list any clients on its website and it has a minimal social media presence. Graham cited “fresh allegations” in announcing Havilah’s departure, believed to relate to a year-old investigation into a protected whistleblower complaint alleging systemic cronyism and unethical procurement practices.



The museum said in a statement issued before Havilah’s departure that, to meet audience targets, significant industry expertise and work had been required outside the “business as usual” work of the Powerhouse team. “Ki Community has successfully leveraged industry partnerships to drive further value back to the Powerhouse with additional in-kind and partnership marketing and advertising support for the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta,” the museum said. Premier Chris Minns, with Parramatta MP Donna Davis (left) and Powerhouse museum chief executive Lisa Havilah (right), tours the museum in 2025. Sitthixay Ditthavong Asked to specify the partnerships and advertising support it had provided, the museum responded: “Ki Community have supported Powerhouse staff to develop the marketing campaign.” According to a Powerhouse spokesperson, an eight-person assessment panel chaired by the museum’s chief operating officer had evaluated the submission on capability, methodology, strategy and risk. Panel members declared prior professional ties where relevant.



The museum said Ki Community had provided formal declarations that Hassell had been ring-fenced from the process. It said it was assured by the company that Hassell had not contributed directly or indirectly to the tender process. The Ki Community tender raises broader questions around public sector procurement. The Public Service Association has complained repeatedly to Graham about the “excessive use of external labour and consultants”, and it has urged an independent financial audit of the spending and recruitment methods that had been used by senior management at the Powerhouse. Related Article Exclusive

City life Powerhouse commissioned a documentary about its move. It will cost more than $1.7 million Bill Browne, director of the Democracy and Accountability Program at The Australia Institute, said heavy reliance on external consultants risked eroding public sector capacity. He said that, where possible, the work of government should be done in-house. “It’s particularly important when spending taxpayer money that perceived conflicts of interest are managed or, ideally, avoided altogether. Open, competitive tender processes can help reassure the community that public money is being spent well and fairly.”



Powerhouse said the Ki Community appointment had been fully vetted by independent probity adviser O’Connor Marsden and that it had been executed in line with government rules. When asked if senior leadership had personally met with the former trustee before the tender, the museum said Hassell had been present for “unrelated” in-office meetings. Hassell said he had “no involvement in the tender process and [I] have had no involvement in the project”. Ki Community had provided the museum a signed declaration of his “non-involvement” in the selective request for tender response to comply with NSW government probity and conflict of interest requirements. “Ki Community is a small team of experienced individuals focused on creating and unlocking value for clients across diverse sectors, through looking at their challenges and opportunities quite differently,” he said. “Members of our team have been associated with and guided communication strategies and campaigns for many of Australia’s leading companies.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Seven inexpensive sources of fibre to add to your grocery list
World.content:
Tips & adviceHealthy eating Seven inexpensive sources of fibre to add to your grocery list Meeting daily fibre targets is easier to do with these versatile and low-cost ingredients that can be found at almost any supermarket. Audrey Bruno August 31, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dietary fibre is often praised for its positive effects on digestion, most notably helping prevent constipation, but it also provides a number of other surprising health benefits — such as lowering cholesterol and helping control blood sugar. Yet, despite trends such as fibremaxxing and a growing awareness of its importance, many people still aren’t meeting their fibre needs. Eat more canned beans in dishes like this tomato, bean and chicken tray bake. James Moffatt The fact that fibre comes from plants could be a limiting factor, said Whitney Linsenmeyer, an assistant professor and director of the Didactic Program in Dietetics at St Louis University. Studies show plants are notoriously undereaten, with accessibility — and perhaps more consequentially, cost — being key contributors. Fresh produce isn’t a prerequisite for adequate fibre consumption, though, said Wendy Lopez, a registered dietitian, diabetes educator and co-founder of Diabetes Digital. Neither is a large monetary investment. In fact, the foods that registered dietitians most frequently encourage their clients to lean on aren’t pricey nut butters, tropical fruits or fresh berries that get the most credit for their fibre content, but rather the unsung heroes of the shelf-stable aisles - as well as a couple of standout, budget produce picks. Here are the fibre-rich ingredients they recommend to help reach the recommended 25-30g daily fibre intake per day without busting the budget.



Canned beans means cheap, nutritious meals. iStock The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Canned beans Beans offer one of the biggest returns on investment in regard to fibre. The fibre count of these legumes can climb up to almost 16 grams per one-cup serving depending on the variety. Uses for them are practically limitless, with their most famous applications covering everything from soups and stews to dips such as hummus, Lopez said. There are also many creative ways to sneak them into dishes where they might not normally appear. Lindsay Malone, a registered dietitian and instructor at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, said some of the easiest, stealthy tricks include adding them to recipes that call for ground meat. “You don’t even have to replace all of your meat but let’s say you’re making tacos: use half meat, half beans,” she said. Related Recipe collection 18 healthy meals to make with a can of beans, lentils or chickpeas



Dried lentils The lentil is another fibre-rich food that’s easy to slip into and boost the fibre count of traditionally meat-based meals without drawing undue attention, Malone said. What’s more, lentils may be easier to digest than most beans, thanks to their thinner skins and lower amounts of fermentable carbohydrates, which may cause bloating and gas in large amounts. What’s really special about lentils is just how inexpensive they are. “If you’re buying the dried version versus the canned version, those will be a few cents per serving,” Linsenmeyer said. A typical 1kg bar of lentils carries around 20 servings, so it can contribute meaningfully to fibre intake for weeks. Oat bran is an inexpensive way to get more fibre in your diet. Getty Images Oat bran



Oatmeal is widely considered to be one of the most inexpensive, fibre-rich foods, and while that’s largely true, there’s an important caveat: instant oats, the type many to choose for convenience, don’t offer as much as slower-cooking, whole grain varieties, Malone said. Malone recommends choosing oat bran — the fibrous part of oats, found in the same supermarket aisle — because it retains some of the fibre content that instant oats lose during processing. Its creamy texture makes it the perfect option for hot cereal, and you can combine it with the same toppings you’d use on other kinds of oats, such as berries, seeds and nut butters. Additionally, you can add oat bran to baked goods, to boost fibre content without drastically altering taste. Chia pots with fresh fruit: fibre central. William Meppem Styling: Hannah Meppem Chia seeds



Chia seeds require more of an up-front investment than some of the other items on this list, but the fibre offerings per serving are impressive all the same, said Linsenmeyer. Beyond the cost, Malone is a chia seed advocate because of its versatile taste and texture and how well the ingredient regulates bowel movements. She warns that consuming the seeds with a liquid is important to avoid unintended consequences such as constipation, as they can absorb up to 15 times their weight in water. But because many popular recipes prioritise soaking or blending them — such as chia pots or smoothies — that doesn’t tend to be too much of an issue. Popcorn is a good source of fibre. iStock Popcorn A surefire way to ensure your daily fibre needs are met is to keep fibre-rich snacks on hand to fill in the gaps, Lopez said. Popcorn is a solid choice because it’s low in cost, long-lasting, infinitely customisable and generally a healthy choice, provided you’re limiting intake of microwave options with excess sodium and saturated fats.



Related Recipe collection Five fun popcorn mixes to make this weekend (featuring Adam Liaw’s Hawaiian recipe) Apples When it comes to fresh produce that’s rich in fibre and cheap to boot, apples can’t be beat, Linsenmeyer said. This fruit has both types of fibre — the flesh is soluble and the skin insoluble — and contains roughly five grams of fibre on average. Plus, the fact that apples are transportable and relatively long-lasting when compared with other fresh fruits makes them an especially good option for high-fibre snacking throughout the day. Related Recipe collection 50 awesome apple recipes



Sweet potatoes have more fibre than white potatoes. James Moffatt Sweet Potatoes These bright orange spuds have an extended shelf life and a solid amount of fibre without the high price tag, Malone says. Her tip is to keep the skin on for an added gram or two of the nutrient. Using it as a base for an already fibre-rich dish, such as chili or a lentil-based stew, is a tried-and-true technique for ensuring a lunch or dinner hits that 10-gram-per-meal recommendation. A few of our favourite recipes to try: skillet sweet potatoes with brown butter and sage, a sweet potato and ground beef chili and this creamy sweet potato and mushroom gratin. Related Recipe collection 20 sweet potato recipes to brighten up weeknight dinners



How to start eating more fibre While fibre is a non negotiable for regular and consistent bowel movements, adding too much to your diet too quickly can backfire, said Malone. “The analogy that I give my patients is that if the conveyor belt is not moving, putting more boxes on the conveyor belt is not going to help our situation,” she said. She recommends aiming to include 10 grams of fibre in each meal but suggests starting with about half of that if you don’t already have a habit of eating very much. Another option is to introduce one new fibre-rich food into your dining routine every couple days, Linsenmeyer said. That way, “you’re basically giving your intestines time to adapt to that significantly larger bulk that it’s not used to,” she explained. However you choose to go about increasing your fibre intake, staying hydrated throughout the process is one point all of our sources could get behind. “We need the conveyor belt to be moving for everything to work, and that requires adequate hydration,” Malone said. Washington Post

World.title: Shane Jones accuses kiwifruit industry of 'slave practices', slams National over regional shakeup
World.content:
NZ First deputy leader Shane Jones has accused the Bay of Plenty kiwifruit industry of "medieval slave practices" at a public meeting, and called for a review of the laws governing Zespri.

The self-proclaimed champion of the regions has also promised New Zealand First will campaign on abolishing regional councils, and criticised National's approach - saying it has never had New Zealand First's backing and the mandate for it should be tested at the election.

Jones was railing against the India Free Trade deal and "blockchain migration" in his speech to about 130 people at the Victory Christian Centre in Lower Hutt when he turned his attention to "a deeper question".

"I don't know about you, but I'm sick to death of what I've seen up in the kiwifruit industry: medieval slave practices," he said.

"When the United States is calling out New Zealand as being responsible for the provision of goods and services that are associated with slave labour, look no further than the egregious cases of what we're seeing in the Bay of Plenty and the migrant groups that are being exploited there."

Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 8m

He said that could not be afforded and it was about time "we started to train more of our own young people".

Trade Minister Todd McClay in July rejected the United States administration's justification for newly reimposed 12.5 percent tariffs on the basis of "forced labour" in New Zealand.

"They are just looking for any means that they can to put tariffs back on... I strongly reject that there is any support at all in the New Zealand system for forced labour. We're not involved in it. It doesn't happen through our trade. It doesn't exist in New Zealand," McClay said at the time.

Jones told reporters after the public meeting that the kiwifruit industry "dominated by Zespri, is losing its social licence" and the next government should review the legislation which grants Zespri a legal export monopoly.

"It is riddled with cases of mediaeval labour practices, egregious taxation practices, and I fear that allegations of slave labour that are made from time to time by America against New Zealand are traceable back to migrant gangs exploiting the goodwill of Kiwis and ruining the reputation of an important industry called the kiwifruit industry. But that also can be shot home to the Zespri company and the orchard owners."

He believed "more systemic change" was needed than merely increasing the Labour Inspectorate's resources to deal with what he called "industrial-scale corruption".

"Casey Costello, who's been involved in this, has already got a model for us. It's the anti-corruption model," he said.

"All state agencies, as the IRD are now doing by issuing a red alert, should join forces and root out these cases of potential slave labour ... look no further than kiwifruit industry and those egregious cases that need to be not only terminated but the people associated with it, they need to be 501'd out to where they come from."

A Zespri spokesperson said the company had have extensive systems in place to both keep the wrong people out of the industry and remove them when they are found. Zespri

The NZ Herald reported last May on an illegal migrant allegedly exploited as a "money mule" to funnel more than $3 million through his bank accounts and withdrawn as cash.

At the time, Customs and Associate Police Minister Costello - a former police detective sergeant who later worked on investigating labour exploitation, and entered Parliament at third on NZ First's list at the last election - pointed to the Ministerial Advisory Group on organised crime she set up earlier in 2025.

"I saw these issues first-hand when I was working to prevent migrant exploitation before entering politics," she said.

"Numerous countries have introduced statutory requirements to ensure that wage payments are made through verifiable, electronic means, to enhance compliance and combat financial misconduct."

She had also called for an end to cash payments for professions like lawyers and immigration consultants, and a joint approach to investigations and prosecutions.

"It's time for a review of the Zespri legislation," Jones said on Sunday, "because I fear that they have trivialised their social licence, and we mean to do something about it if we come back into power."

Zespri responds

A Zespri spokesperson said the company wanted everyone in the industry to be safe and well looked after no matter where they were working.

"Any allegations of poor working conditions are taken seriously and investigated, with action taken wherever possible, including proactive on reporting to government agencies to consider further enforcement action.

"We have extensive systems in place to both keep the wrong people out of the industry and then to remove them when they are found."

The spokesperson said all growers supplying the company were certified to internationally recognised independent certification system GLOBALG.A.P and compulsory employer module GRASP which includes requirements for worker safety and health and welfare.

"All potential contractors go through a vetting process administered by independent private ethical labour investigators AIM CRI Ltd during the application process to assess if they will be able to meet the required standards.

"These contractors must also hold a CAV (Compliance Assessment Verification). To get this, they must show they have the appropriate systems in place to meet GAP and GRASP requirements including providing a safe work environment, with inspections taking place annually to observe that these systems are operating effectively."

Zespri said any who failed to comply were removed from its published list of approved contractors, and a separate list of such contractors was also published to the industry.

"To address issues when they arise, we work closely with government agencies and use AIM CRI Ltd to robustly investigate allegations of misconduct and to support a strong response. These investigations will often result in us passing files on to enforcement agencies to take action.

"To help ensure issues are brought to our attention Zespri also has a dedicated Speak Up Line in place for anyone who has concerns about poor practice taking place within the industry and we encourage anyone with concerns to contact this confidential information line. We also have a dedicated Industry Compliance team which continues its work to strengthen our compliance programme."

Zespri said its discussions with authorities about removing operators failing to meet its standards had previously led to successful prosecutions, "removing poor operators from the industry".

"The vast majority of employers in the industry look after their people. Any exploitation of workers is unacceptable and alongside the government and NZKGI we will continue to do everything we can to ensure an industry free from exploitation and one where people are valued, supported and safe in their jobs."

NZ First favours catchment groups to replace regional councils

Jones had also spoken of his party's plans to "do away with your regional councils", but would not "shoehorn you into a single model".

"That's on you, the community, to work with your ratepayer associations, to work with your community boards and your elected representatives to identify a type of reform model that improves not only responsiveness but your sense of confidence as to where you live," he told the gathered congregation.

"Other parties might be trying to force rapid change. We are going to campaign on it and then after the election we will feel - depending on the quality of the voting result - that we have a mandate."

Speaking to reporters, he said regional councils would be "no longer fit for purpose" thanks to the councils' "chequered history" and the changes to resource management laws.

Using Wairau as an example, he said far too much authority was placed with "distant bureaucratic offices such as Napier and Hawke's Bay".

"We're very taken with catchment boards and catchment groups having more authority. It worked in the past. It ensures that more local ownership is exercised for rivers, for other catchment features, rather than it being centralised in a bureaucracy," he said.

That contrasted with the government's approach to reforming regional councils, where National Party ministers Chris Bishop and Simon Watts had handed down an ultimatum for councils to "lead your own reform, or we will do it for you".

Watts this month confirmed to RNZ more than two thirds of councils had submitted proposals for reorganisation - but nearly 20 had not.

Jones on Sunday suggested that approach should have been campaigned on.

World.title: Do children play on the street anymore?
World.content: Woods believes the decline in outdoor play is about more than the allure of screen time. Where neighbours don't know one another, there can be less trust in allowing children out independently, and children may be reluctant to go outside if no one else is there. She recalls one child telling her he’d rather be outside than playing Minecraft but wasn’t allowed to be out alone.

World.title: Solomon Island PM Wale rushes home from Palau after confidence challenge launched
World.content:
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale made an emergency trip back to Honiara on Sunday morning from Palau after a motion of no confidence was filed against him.

Wale, 57, was elected prime minister of the country on 15 May and has been in office for just over 100 days.

The no-confidence motion against him on over the weekend has been filed by East Malaita MP and Minister of Home Affairs Manasseh Maelanga. The Solomon Islands parliament has confirmed it has received the notice.

Maelanga is accusing Wale of making unilateral decisions without proper consultation and without taking matters through cabinet.

"The Motion follows concerns that the Prime Minister has repeatedly made decisions on matters of national importance without properly consulting Cabinet or obtaining its approval," Maelanga said in the statement.

"I have taken this step with confidence in our democratic institutions and a firm commitment to stable, transparent and accountable government."

Maelanga has also rejected claims that the challenge against Wales leadership was intended to derail ongoing investigations.

The motion is the first major political challenge for Wale since coming to power.

Wale was in Palau to attend the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting as its current chair. He was suppose to hand over the chairmanship to Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr in Palau.

He had only just landed in Palau when news of the no-confidence motion back home reached him. When questioned at the airport by a Solomon Islands journalist on the matter.

"When I go, I will tell you more, " Wale said. He was gone the next day in the early hours of the morning.

Wale was elected prime minister of the country on 15 May. Pacific Islands Forum

Other Solomon Islands officials who travelled with the prime minister to Palau were surprised to hear about the leadership challenge.

Local media have described the no-confidence motion against Wale as an "internal coalition revolt".

"There appears to be split within the GREAT Coalition. Few Ministers and MPs within the GREAT Coalition are likely to tender their resignations," according to a report by Solomon Star.

World.title: Older Kiwis struggle with basic living expenses: 'We are living in a very bad time'
World.content:
Over-50s advocacy group calls for cost of living support Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Grey Power wants government policies to address the needs of an increasing number of older New Zealanders struggling to meet the most basic living expenses.

West Auckland's Waitākere Grey Power recently invited politicians representing six political parties to a members' meeting at the Te-Atatu South Community Centre, located in West Auckland.

"A good budget would actually cover our real necessities. We are living in a very bad time at the moment financially, being an older person," Grey Power member Gayleen Maurice, also known locally as Auntie G, said.

She said was struggling to afford her private rental accommodation, which was difficult with only super to live on.

"On super, you keep getting these top-ups which you have to apply for. It's the only way that you can survive. So we are probably not as well off as people who still struggle to pay their mortgage, but at the end of the day, they at least have an asset, whereas I don't have an asset at all."

Auckland-based charity Commnicare manager Mike Matthews said the charitable organisation ran 16 friendship centres in Auckland for older people and another six on Auckland's North Shore run by CMA - Companionship and Morning Activities.

Matthews said the focus was creating a community for older people who would otherwise be alone.

Politicians address the Waitākere Grey Power meeting. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"In terms of lonely, isolated, vulnerable, and it's a major, major issue.

"And it's a forgotten community. It's not a child. It's not a sports team. It's not an animal. Those are very attractive for funders. They make good headlines. They do good TV."

He said the situation for many older people was dire and was unlikely to get any better without more supportive policies.

Matthews said the feedback out of Wellington was that Auckland's network for seniors was not as well coordinated as it needed to be.

"Grey Power was a real voice and power 40 years ago when it started through the 80s and 90s and everything like that, and it needs to be back there again, so people will start to listen, because it is a block that can influence the politicians."

Grey Power members at the meeting. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Matthews said the government needed to deal with the issue because there were more than 900,000 (900k) people over the age of 65 and 300k had just the super to live on.

"And that's forecast to grow over next 13 to 14 years to about 1.3 million."

Waitakere Grey Power president Vincent Naidu said the challenges were plain to see.

They included:

Superannuation: There is a demand for clear policy statements regarding the sustainability of superannuation, which should be viewed as an earned entitlement rather than welfare.

There is a demand for clear policy statements regarding the sustainability of superannuation, which should be viewed as an earned entitlement rather than welfare. Housing: A significant number of elderly people lack mortgage-free homes and rely on private rentals, making survival on superannuation difficult. There is a need for policies that facilitate downsizing to release larger family homes.

A significant number of elderly people lack mortgage-free homes and rely on private rentals, making survival on superannuation difficult. There is a need for policies that facilitate downsizing to release larger family homes. Healthcare and aged care : Concerns were raised regarding the rising costs of residential care, the difficulty of finding available aged care placements, and the need for better support for independent living at home.

: Concerns were raised regarding the rising costs of residential care, the difficulty of finding available aged care placements, and the need for better support for independent living at home. Cost of living: High power bills and the general cost of living crisis were impacting health, leading to increased hospitalisations during severe winters.

"I think a state which cares for its citizens needs to care for its elderly folks. We owe it to them," Naidu said.

Auntie G said she was also doing what she could to help other older people in the community.

She said it was particularly difficult for people no longer able to care for themselves.

"It's extremely difficult to find them a place," she said.

"Some stay in the hospital, just waiting and waiting to find a place. I hope I'm not going to be in that situation, but it looks like that's the way it's going to be.

World.title: Seven things GP owners say will fix primary healthcare
World.content:
GP group calls for more support for in-person visits Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Funding, face-to-face consultations and a sustainable workforce are among the seven things GenPro says are needed to restore general practice.

The General Practice Owners Association, which represents the owners of independent general practices and urgent care centres, has launched its manifesto amid a surge of winter illness, compounding years of underfunding and recent staff shortages in the health sector.

It is calling on political parties to make the long-term sustainability of frontline general practice a priority at November's election.

GenPro chair Dr Angus Chambers said practices across New Zealand were under sustained financial and workforce pressure.

"General practice is the front door to our health system. When people can access the right care at the right time in their local community, they are more likely to stay well and less likely to need hospital care.

"But that depends on having a financially sustainable general practice sector with enough doctors, nurses and other health professionals to meet demand. Political parties have an opportunity at this election to put general practice on a sustainable footing for the long term," he said.

GenPro has asked for several actions:

1. Invest in frontline general practice

A 30 percent cumulative increase in general practice funding over three years.

An independent mechanism to adjust funding for the true cost of delivering care.

A five-year funding pathway to provide certainty for practices.

Targeted funding for patients with complex health needs.

Targeted funding for rural and remote practices.

2. Support long-term GP-patient relationships

For continuity of care to be recognised as a core quality measure, with every enrolled patient having access to a named GP or nurse practitioner.

Face-to-face consultations to remain the foundation of primary care, with telehealth used to complement rather than replace in-person care.

3. Strengthen rural and urgent after-hours care

Increased rural funding.

Stronger support for rural workforce recruitment and retention.

Investment in infrastructure and digital connectivity.

The General Practice Owners Association is calling on political parties to make the long-term sustainability of frontline general practice a priority at November's election 123rf

4. Less bureaucracy and greater funding transparency - reducing unnecessary administration and ensuring more health funding reaches frontline patient care

5. Support for independent, community-owned general practice - protecting the owner-operated model providing continuity of care and ensuring government policy supports a diverse, community-based primary care sector

6. A stronger voice for general practice

Ensure GenPro is meaningfully consulted early on significant changes to funding, service design and policy.

7. A sustainable general practice workforce

Improve funding so general practice can offer competitive employment conditions.

Support internationally qualified clinicians.

Help the next generation of GPs buy into independent practices.

Chambers said the manifesto was designed to provide political parties with a roadmap rather than simply identify problems.

"These seven steps would help strengthen access to care, reduce avoidable pressure on hospitals and deliver better value for taxpayers," he said.

Chambers said the evidence was clear - people live better, healthier lives when they're seen by the same doctor or nurse practitioner.

He said continuity of care and face-to-face consultations must be a priority. He said there was a place for tele-health, but that it should complement, rather than replace in-person care.

"We get a lot more information with [patients] being in-person. A very key part of detecting illness and making sure somebody is okay ... is actually a physical examination.

"There's only so much you can achieve via tele-health."

Chambers wanted to see more GPs, particularly in rural areas, and said investing in primary care would help reduce the strain on emergency departments.

Staff at Auckland and Wellington hospital emergency departments have reported struggling to keep up with a surge in demand in recent weeks.

Chambers said a key part of primary care was prevention and early intervention.

"Managing chronic disease well, so people don't deteriorate so much, that will keep people out of hospitals."

He said every election was critical to healthcare and hoped political parties would take note of the manifesto before finalising their policies.

World.title: 'We're really starting to scrape the surface of the bottom' - NZ waters searched for skincare breakthroughs
World.content:
Scientists search NZ waters for secret skincare ingredients Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Scientists are searching New Zealand waters for marine organisms that could be the secret breakthrough ingredient for skincare products such as sunscreen and anti-aging creams.

Cawthron Institute and Callaghan Innovation's Biotechnologies Group are New Zealand partners in OCEOMICS, a Horizon Europe-funded project involving 12 organisations across eight countries, led by Spanish research institute AINIA.

Cawthron will lead research into marine microalgae, while Callaghan Innovation's Biotechnologies Group will study marine bacteria from New Zealand waters - including samples from pristine coastal, sub-Antarctic and subtropical environments.

The kiwi scientists have just collected their first batch of marine organism samples, from Whakaari White Island where Cawthron scientist Karthiga Kumanan used a variety of different methods.

"We collected samples from 10 different locations, so 10 times a one litre container of direct water. We also collected concentrated samples so using a plankton net which is like a fishing net. We dragged the net 300 metres to concentrate whatever is in the water," said Karthiga.

The laboratory was already processing the samples, and she was excited about what they might find.

"I just spoke to the lab teams and they have plenty of dead and live algal cells," she said.

Whakaari White Island. Supplied

Johan Svenson is the science impact manager at the Cawthron Institute and in charge of the project. He told RNZ the organisms they are looking for are mostly microscopic.

"So the stuff you don't really see in the ocean - we're talking about plankton, micro algae and bacteria."

He describes the ocean as having "massive untapped potential".

"We've used terrestrial plants for thousands of years in medicine, but we only looked at marine for the last maybe 70 years.. we're really starting to scrape the surface of the bottom to find bioactive compounds in the ocean compared to on land," he said.

The sample sites on Whakaari White Island. Supplied

The project will use artificial intelligence, genomic screening and biotechnology tools to identify future ingredients for high-value skincare formulations - including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, UV-protecting and skin barrier products.

"We want to see if they can produce commercially valuable compounds. At the end of this project we have Unilever as a commercial partner who would be willing to pick up any promising leads," said Svenson.

The scientists are looking for specific chemical targets to understand how, and if, valuable compounds produced by the marine organisms can be mimicked in future.

"So the goal is to understand the genetic information that is used and producing the compound using other organisms.. using recombant technologies - it's pretty fancy and science fictioney," said Svenson.

The sample sites on Whakaari White Island. Supplied

Cawthron Institute's Pou Arataki Anaru Luke said the project has been designed from the outset in accordance with New Zealand's legal, ethical and Treaty obligations.

"What's unique about this project is that sampling will proceed subject to agreement with iwi, guided by Te Tiriti-based principles including partnership, kaitiakitanga, and respect for mātauranga Māori."

"Critically, no organisms will leave New Zealand. Only extracts and genomic data will be shared with consortium partners, and all genomic and metabolomic data will be stored and stewarded in New Zealand to support data sovereignty."

Any commercially promising strains will be characterised in New Zealand, and downstream commercial benefits will be shared with participating iwi.

World.title: 'Not here for a holiday': What standards RSE workers should expect
World.content:
RSE workers want to maximise their earnings Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Police highlight risk of unsafe and unreasonable RSE accommodation

Academic says bad employers are the exception, and workers are focused on maximising pay over good housing

Accommodation standards need to be standardised and monitored, says union

Accommodation for seasonal rural workers should be focused on low cost, not high quality to maximise wages, according to an academic.

But a union warns that some housing is already substandard, especially with 'barracks'-style accommodation in winter.

Police identified "unsafe and unreasonable accommodation" as one of the biggest risks in the RSE system, according to a May government briefing.

The government last month announced changes to the recognised seasonal employer (RSE) scheme, which allows short-term recruitment from Asia and the Pacific to pick crops on farms, and in orchards and vineyards.

Some 'exemplary' employers could have six-year accreditation periods, and staff would be able to apply for migrant exploitation visas to leave abusive employers.

Immigration minister Erica Stanford signalled accommodation proposals will be announced next month, and the appeal of an Employment Court finding of unlawful deductions from wages of RSE workers in Hawkes Bay is also expected soon.

Waikato university emeritus Professor Richard Bedford - who specialises in migration and has previously advised the government on RSE - welcomed the accreditation change.

But he said accommodation would be a harder issue to deal with.

"The worst thing from a worker's point of view in the accommodation question is not really whether there's a toilet for every six people, or a shower for every five, or 4.3 square metres of space, the really big issue for them is how much of my wages are going to be spent on living in New Zealand, because I've come here to earn money and to take the maximum amount home. I haven't come here for a holiday."

About 200 employers use Pacific and Asian RSE workers, a small percentage of New Zealand's estimated 4300 fruit and vegetable growers.

Both employers and workers - who spend about seven months here at a time - want accommodation charges minimised, he said, but some of the costs are dictated by the market and peak periods for tourism.

"Building purpose-built accommodation for a workforce that is only with you for half a year or a bit over half is a real challenge," said Bedford. "So not surprisingly, a great number of RSEs rely on third party providers to deliver the accommodation for their workers.

"If you're using a motel or a backpackers or some entity external to you to provide accommodation, then to a large extent you're bound very much by what you can negotiate as a deal for your workers. At the end of March, which is a really high peak time, we could have an extra 10,000 workers. Well, they're competing for accommodation with backpackers, with Kiwis, who also want accommodation in these places."

The bad apples

As well as the police warning about poor accommodation, ministers were warned it remained a key concern for the Pacific, and undermined public acceptance of RSE in New Zealand.

An International Labour Organisation (ILO) report in April highlighted blacklisting of workers who make complaints, and concerns about wage deductions.

Bedford believes most employers are compliant, but that isolated breaches dominate debate - obscuring the scheme's wider benefits to workers, home countries, and horticulture.

"There'll always be people on the edges that are trying to game the rules," he said. "It's just a bit sad sometimes that the exception that you might find out there becomes the narrative in the public discourse. And I just feel a bit sad sometimes that some of the really good practice that's gone on, like for example the growers that build a primary school in a village or build a wharf - that doesn't get any reference at all."

Facilities and regulations - bunk beds, curfews, transport and toilets at home and work - needed to be pragmatic.

"An academic who's never been involved with working with seasonal workers before might think it's a bit rough, or, 'I wouldn't like to live in this space'. What isn't resolved in the accommodation area and this is the recent thing, is what are the limits on what you can charge? And what do you have to provide?

"On the orchard, 90 percent of the workforce that comes are males. I think it's been quite a challenge for some growers. If you drive down through Blenheim, you drive past hectares of grapes, you don't see any buildings. Well, somebody's got to prune those grapes. So where do those guys go to the loo? What are the facilities that are available for those men?"

Imposing expensive regulations would make the scheme unattractive, he said.

Workers' concerns

The question of what are 'reasonable' wage deductions is part of a long-running Hawkes Bay employment case which was won by workers, and is being appealed. The decision is expected soon, and could affect what employers or labour hire companies charge for accommodation.

Workers First union wants housing standardised and properly monitored, and clarity over the use and accreditation of labour hire companies.

General secretary Dennis Maga said accommodation standards and worksite transport were still among the biggest concerns raised by workers, as some housing still lacked heating, ventilation, or had curfews.

"Because this is no longer about money, it's about how they are being treated as a human being. So, if the accommodation is not up to the standard, it's also degrading for them. In fact, those Pasifica workers that we interviewed who decided not to pursue their case - something that I vividly remember when they told us about their case - is that they're not going back to New Zealand because they are not treated as human beings."
